airbus.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We continue its production in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family, and we put fleet safety and operational integrity above all. The people and suppliers who deliver both remain protected.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We keep studying the options for its future on our own technology and industrial clock. We will take decisions when the technology and the case are mature, and not before.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain, with long-term agreements sized to our own programmes. We also continue to recruit the engineers who will build the next generations of Airbus aircraft.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
**Decision: the company default.** NGSA hold, engine code None (the only code on the menu), A350 hold, Delay Tactics none.
- Grid: +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2.
- No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item.

**1. Red-line and pillars screen (the team rule's first step)**
Neither option breaks a company red line or the five pillars.
- Rule 1 is met: NGSA entered service in 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year.
- Rules 2 and 7: there is no NGSA cancel on the menu.
- Rule 3 is not binding: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
- Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are closed, and none is the only value.
- Rule 6 is met: a 2045 A350 Re-engine would be one launch with zero overlap with NGSA.
- Wagner confirms safety and quality pass on both options. The brief reports no safety, quality or supply problem and no inject.
Both options therefore go on to the colleagues' tests.

**2. Survivors**
- **Plan A (hold)** passes all of Toepfer's tests: peak cash $0, robustness +23.26 in the worst column, net cash and rating proxy. It passes all of Wagner's: safety and quality, ramp shield, engine code, integrity, rule 1.
- **Plan B (A350 Re-engine, entry into service 2050)** fails two binding soft vetoes:
  1. Toepfer's added-move gate, which is also the company's $1B launch test. The item is +0.89 in S1, $0.11B short of $1B, and -0.50 in S2, negative in the worst plausible column.
  2. Wagner's production-readiness test. No widebody engine on the record is ready by 2050: Rolls-Royce spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine, an UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, and there is no fallback.
  Neither failure is a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch result. Both are soft vetoes.
- **Override.** None is available. B's margin over A, the best passing option, is +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2: under $1B in both columns. The Board's override review would also fail it, as a Qualified Majority item that trails hold in its worst column. The game's single override stays unused. I concur on the merits in any case.

A is the only survivor. It is also the doctrine default: within $1B of the best grid row in my expected column, a $0.89B gap in S1.

**3. Tie-breaks** all point to A: less strain, a later capex start, and fewer Board items (0 against 1).

**4. My read of Boeing, and the expected column**
Expected column: S1, at about 60%. S2 at about 40%, within a 30-50% range.
- For S2: in 2035 Boeing said "We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service". fps has been in service since 2040. Boeing also said the 787 "has room to grow from our Charleston capacity".
- Against S2: "We're not starting a second development alongside this one", "Doing less and doing it better", and debt reduction with a solid investment-grade rating as its priority.
S2 stays the worst plausible column.

At 40%, the launch is worth about +0.33 in expectation (+0.40 at 35%, +0.20 at 50%). It breaks even at 64%. Even at 0% for S2 it is only +0.89, under the $1B test. **The decision rests on our own tests, not on our read of Boeing.** That keeps us on our own clock and ties no widebody step to Boeing.

**5. The staged widebody case the Board asked for in 2035, gate by gate**
| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| Rule 3 | Met. No 787 Re-engine is on the record. |
| A350F in service and Spirit A350 packages at rate | Passes on the game proxy only. The record is silent after 2025 and Wagner has no line data, so the Board's condition that he confirm both is not met. |
| Widebody engine ready by entry into service | Fails. The gap is built into the clocks: an engine launched alongside the airframe is ready at launch + 6, the airframe enters service at launch + 5. |
| Grid gate (at least $1B in the expected column, not negative in the 787 column) | Fails at +0.89 / -0.50. |
| Peak cash | Passes: $1.0B a year over 2045-49, $4.2B under the $5.2B line. |
| Qualified Majority | Required. |

The option to wait: on Toepfer's reconstruction (an inference), a like-for-like 2050 launch is worth about +0.6 in a rivals-hold column. It is still under $1B. A 787 Re-engine in 2045 would close it under rule 3, and the company already named 2035-37 as the last window. The case stays staged and is not launched.

**6. Board-gate line**
There is no Board item this round. For the record, the hold package:
- five pillars: pass;
- Toepfer: pass, with a peak programme cash of $0 against the $5.2B line;
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the ramp shield and integrity;
- grid: +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2.
The Board says hold is never vetoed.

**7. Cost and objective**
- Holding gives up $0.89B in S1, about $0.33B in expectation at 40% for S2. It gains $0.50B against B in S2.
- Plan A's worst column (+23.26) is better than plan B's (+22.76), so it meets the robustness preference.
- No PV is traded for the 60/40 objective, which no order on this menu can move.

**8. Operating actions**
- Supply agreements are resized down to our own falling needs (Wagner).
- The Joint Venture engine is carried as a watch item, with CFM as backstop.
- Buybacks are sized after programme cash (Toepfer).
- Studies stay studies, below EUR 300m each until a Board gate.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer's tests are role-derived (Low confidence), and I weighed them as such. His arithmetic matches the brief.

Plan A: passes everything.
- Peak programme cash $0 against the $5.2B line.
- Robustness +23.37 / +23.26.
- Net-cash proxy positive through 2049 in both the base case (+$43.6B) and the stress case (+$3.7B), with the full buyback.
- No Board items.

Plan B:
- Passes peak cash ($1.0B a year, $4.2B of headroom), rule 6 (zero overlap, one launch) and the plan-level robustness test (positive in both columns).
- Fails his added-move gate, the company's $1B launch test: +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2. Soft veto, binding.
- His expected-value schedule confirms my figures: +0.33 at 40% for S2, break-even at 64%. Even at 0% the item is +0.89, under $1B.
- His override arithmetic confirms that no override can carry B, under the team rule or the Board's review.

Accepted: the veto is binding, no override is allowed, and I agree on the merits. I also adopted:
- his rule that buybacks are sized after programme cash, the trim he would make first under stress;
- his staged sizing of the studies, below EUR 300m each and about EUR 0.9bn in aggregate;
- his option-to-wait estimate (about +0.6 for a 2050 launch, still under $1B);
- his finance line for the public statement.

He uses proxies he labels as inference: operating profit for EBIT Adjusted, an FCF/EBIT ratio of 0.667, and net cash at or above zero standing in for the agency thresholds, which are not in his record. I take them as indicative.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner's tests are role-derived (Very low confidence), and I weighed them as such. Where his record is silent, he says so.

Results:
- Safety and quality: pass on both options. It is a pillars result, but there is no line data after 2025, so it rests on the brief reporting no issue.
- NGSA ramp shield and A320neo transition: pass. A ramp result.
- Supply crunch: not applicable, as none is reported.
- Engineering capacity and rule 6: pass for B, on two conditions: a named widebody team ring-fenced from NGSA and the A320neo, and the studies staying studies.
- A350F and Spirit absorption: pass on the game proxy only. The record is silent, so he cannot confirm the Board's condition from data.
- Production readiness: fail for B. No widebody engine is ready by a 2050 entry into service. UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, and there is no fallback. Soft veto, binding. It is not a safety, quality, ramp or supply result, and it moves the window rather than closing the idea.
- Engine code: None only; the fitted CFM + P&W + RR set stands.
- Integrity and Delay Tactics: pass.
- Rule 1: pass.

Accepted: B's margin over hold (+0.89 / -0.50) is under $1B, so no override is allowed. On the merits, an entry into service without a ready engine is the very discipline we hold NGSA to under rule 1.

I adopted:
- his finding that the supply agreements must be resized down from the 2039 peak (1,260) to our own falling needs (1,140 in 2045, 1,060 from 2049). Holding slots at the peak would be over-contracting;
- his Joint Venture watch item, with CFM as backstop;

frame.situation:
Round 3, decision year 2045.

**Public record (bulletin)**
- **Boeing.** fps launched in 2030 on the 10-year path and has been in service since 2040 on CFM. No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase is on the record.
  - In 2035 Boeing said "We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service" and "We're not starting a second development alongside this one". It also said debt reduction and a solid investment-grade rating stay its priorities.
  - fps has now been in service for five years, so that look is due. S2 is a live column.
- **Airbus.** NGSA has been in service since 2037, three years ahead of fps. It flies CFM, P&W and RR (code 7).
- **Engines.**
  - CFM ducted: in service since 2036.
  - P&W-RR Joint Venture: formed in 2035, with GTF2 and UltraFan NB folded in. Its engine has been in service since 2036.

vetoes.plan: B. Plan A + A350 Re-engine launched 2045 (entry into service 2050)
vetoes.ground: Failed robustness (my 2035 added-move gate and the company's $1B launch test). The item is +0.89 in S1, under $1B, and -0.50 in S2, negative in the worst plausible column. Peak cash passes ($1.0B a year, $4.2B of headroom); this is not a red line and not a pillars breach. Margin over the best passing option (plan A): +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2. It is under $1B in both columns, so the team rule allows no override. The Board's override review would also fail it, since it trails hold in S2. The override is Faury's to weigh, not mine to pre-clear, but the arithmetic does not reach it.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: (1) A grid on which the A350 Re-engine is worth at least $1B over hold in the expected column and is not negative in the 787 Re-engine column. This grid cannot show that: +0.89 is its ceiling, at 0% for S2. (2) A Board decision. (3) For 2050: Boeing holds this round and the 2050 brief prices a 2055 entry into service at or above $1B over hold and not negative in its 787 column. On the five-year discount (about +0.6) I do not expect that. A 787 Re-engine on the record closes the case under rule 3. (4) On returns rather than the order: if free cash flow runs near FY2025's $5.2B while a 50% payout and the full €5bn buyback continue, the stress proxy turns net cash negative from 2047 with the A350 Re-engine. I would then trim the buyback first, never the programme gate. (5) A safety, quality or supply finding from Wagner would only strengthen hold.
cfo.memo:
Board paper, 2045 (CFO). The line is one year's free cash flow: €4,753m, about $5.2B [AX-0104].

Cash. Plan A carries no programme cash; NGSA's spend ended in 2036. Plan B spends $1.0B a year over 2045-49, with no overlap and no strain: $4.2B under the line. Both pass. Cash is not the constraint.

Value. Plan A: +23.37 / +23.26, positive in its worst column, S2. Plan B: +24.26 / +22.76. The launch alone is +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2; it breaks even at a 64% chance of S2 and is worth +0.33 at 40%. It fails my added-move gate on both counts. Soft veto, binding. Its margin over plan A, the best passing option, is +0.89 / -0.50, so no override can carry it. Even at 0% for S2 it is only +0.89.

Balance sheet. Base-case 2045 free cash flow is about $11.4B; the stress case holds it at $5.2B. The A350 Re-engine would take 9% or 19%. The payout stays inside 30-50%; buybacks are sized after programme cash. In stress, a 50% payout plus the A350 Re-engine leaves $1.4B, below the €5bn programme's $1.8B a year. No equity raise; state money upside only. Agency thresholds are not in my record.

Waiting. A like-for-like 2050 launch is worth about +0.6 in a rivals-hold column: smaller, still under $1B.

Recommendation: plan A. Engine code None, on Wagner's call.

Public line: disciplined investments in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

tests.name: Safety and quality, both options (a quality result: neither the CEO nor the Board overrides it)
tests.threshold: No open safety or quality issue on NGSA, the A320neo or the A350, and no order whose public explanation would contradict safety and quality
tests.numbers: The brief reports no safety, quality or supply problem and no inject. My record stops at the end-2025 technical issues under root-cause investigation and the A320 quality reports [AX-0056, AX-0057], and nothing since then is on the board. I can therefore confirm that no issue is open on the record, but I have no line data to confirm it from. Plan A adds nothing to review. Plan B's order stands on the pillars, but its public line must not give a window the engine cannot meet: 'around the turn of the decade' would be read as 2050, and the only widebody engine path is ready in 2051 (see the readiness test). This result should go to the Board's twice-yearly safety review together with the NGSA ramp report and the A320neo transition report.

tests.name: NGSA ramp after entry into service, and the A320neo transition: ramp shield (a ramp result: neither the CEO nor the Board overrides it)
tests.threshold: Nothing added draws on the people or supplier slots that carry the NGSA ramp or the A320neo transition. On this board the test passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem
tests.numbers:
NGSA has been in service since 2037, eight years. Our narrowbody deliveries on the board were 1,220 in 2037 and peaked at 1,260 in 2039. They are 1,140 in 2045 and fall to 1,060 from 2049, as share moves from 61% to 63%, then 57%, then 53% on the long-run 47/53 split. That fall is share, not a ramp or quality problem. The board carries no monthly rate, so I give no rate figure. It also does not split NGSA deliveries from A320neo deliveries, so for the A320neo transition I can report only that no problem is reported.

Plan A adds no demand. Plan B: NGSA development ran 2030-37 and an A350 Re-engine would run 2045-50, so it competes with no NGSA development. B passes on two conditions: it is staffed from the widebody teams, and it draws neither on NGSA in-service support nor on narrowbody supplier slots.

Operating consequence for both options: our narrowbody needs fall by about 16% from the 2039 peak to 2049 (1,260 to 1,060), so the ramp supply agreements must be resized down to our own needs.

tests.name: Supply crunch (a supply result: neither the CEO nor the Board overrides it)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency
tests.numbers: No crunch, shortfall or inject is reported. Narrowbody engine shares in 2044 were CFM 53.7%, P&W 23.2% and RR 23.2%, a stable three-way split since 2037. If a crunch is reported before orders are due, B fails outright and hold stands.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and rule 6, plan B (a red line if failed)
tests.threshold: One new launch per round, and a development overlap between NGSA and an A350 Re-engine of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more
tests.numbers:
B is the only launch this round. NGSA development ran 2030-37 and the A350 Re-engine would run 2045-50, so the overlap is 0 years and the strain is $3B x 0/5 = $0. The $1.0B a year of cash over 2045-49 is Toepfer's line, not mine.

Can it be staffed? On the board, yes, from the widebody teams. Off the board, talent binds [A-0366, A-0485, A-0423], and the record has no headcount. B passes on two conditions:
- a named widebody team, ring-fenced from NGSA in-service support and from the A320neo transition;
- the unpriced studies (an NGSA derivative, an A220 variant, research and technology for the next generation) stay studies, so that none becomes a second programme drawing on the same engineers.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption, plan B (a soft-veto ground)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: 2035 at the earliest (company window 2033-35). For 2045 I asked to see the A350F in service and the Spirit A350 packages at rate
tests.numbers: B passes on the game proxy only: 2045 is ten years past the 2035 floor. My record stops in 2025, with the A350F in its industrial phase and its first two prototypes in final assembly [AX-0082], and the Spirit A350 packages acquired [AX-0060]. The brief gives no A350F or Spirit status for any later year. Widebody share has been flat at 41.2%, 70 aircraft a year, since 2026. I cannot confirm either gate from data, because the record is silent. The Board's approval condition that I confirm both is therefore not met from the record. Twenty years on, I would expect both to be absorbed, but that is inference.

tests.name: Production readiness: a widebody engine ready by the A350 Re-engine's entry into service, plan B (a soft-veto ground; not priced on the board)
tests.threshold: Launch an A350 Re-engine only with a named engine on the record that is ready at or before the airframe's entry into service. This is the discipline of rule 1 for NGSA (no entry into service before the technology is ready) applied to the widebody
tests.numbers:
Launched in 2045, the A350 Re-engine enters service in 2050 (launch + 5).

The engine:
- Rolls-Royce is the A350's incumbent with the Trent XWB [A-0253]. It says: 'There is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine.'
- An UltraFan WB launched alongside us in 2045 would be ready in 2051 (launch + 6), one year after our entry into service.
- The other new engines on the record do not fit. The GEnx upgrade serves 787 customers (in service since 2033), and the CFM ducted, CFM-Embraer and Joint Venture engines are narrowbody engines.
- No second widebody engine is on the record, and no Trent XWB derivative with a ready date. There is no fallback.

So a 2050 entry into service has no engine. The real window opens in 2051 at the earliest, which the board's launch + 5 Re-engine cannot represent.

The gap is built into the clocks; 2045 is not special. If Rolls-Royce launches only alongside a Re-engine, a 2050 launch (entry into service 2055) meets an engine ready in 2056. The gap closes only if the engine is committed a year ahead of the airframe.

Grid margin against the best option that passes (A, hold): +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2, under $1B in both columns.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports one, re-time so that entry into service stays at or after the new technology-ready year; never cancel
tests.numbers: No slip is reported, and all of NGSA's engines are in service. The A350 Re-engine's problem is not a slip: no engine has been committed in time (see the readiness test).

tests.name: NGSA engines and supply; engine code (a recommendation, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: CFM in the set plus at least one second maker; flag any supply watch item
tests.numbers:
The only code on the menu is None. The fitted set, CFM + P&W + RR, stands and meets my rule with three sources.

The CFM ducted and P&W-RR Joint Venture engines have been in service since 2036, and NGSA since 2037. Narrowbody engine shares in 2044 were CFM 53.7%, P&W 23.2% and RR 23.2%. No shortfall is reported, so I can confirm delivery on the board but not from line data.

Watch items:
1. P&W said in 2035 that its GTF fleet keeps first call on its parts, shops and engineers. That priority now sits inside the Joint Venture.
2. Our P&W and RR positions on NGSA both ride on the one Joint Venture engine, since GTF2 and UltraFan NB were folded into it. A single Joint Venture problem would therefore hit two of our three engine sources. CFM is the backstop.

tests.name: Integrity limits and Delay Tactics, rules 4 and 5, for the ECSC review (a pillars result)
tests.threshold: Supply agreements sized to our own NGSA and A320neo needs and never over-contracted; hiring that never targets rival teams; pricing within ordinary competition; Delay Tactics none
tests.numbers:
Delay Tactics: none, the only value on the menu. The window closed when fps entered service in 2040, and no move was ordered in round 1 or round 2.

Supply: the agreements were sized for the ramp to the 2039 peak of 1,260 aircraft. Our needs fall to 1,140 in 2045 and 1,060 from 2049. The ECSC should resize the engine, wing-package, titanium and rare-earth agreements to those needs. Holding slots at the peak while our needs fall would be over-contracting, which is what a bottleneck looks like.

Hiring: open European hiring, sized to NGSA in-service support and any approved widebody work, never aimed at rival teams.

Pricing is Faury's call. From my side, no supply or hiring lever is used to do what Delay Tactics would do.

tests.name: Rule 1 and NGSA readiness (red line)
tests.threshold: No NGSA entry into service before the 2035 technology-ready year
tests.numbers: NGSA entered service in 2037, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Nothing in 2045 re-times it: ngsa is hold only, and no cancel is on the menu.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No programme reaction to Boeing's rate; we keep our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: No Rate Increase is on the record, and the order existed only in 2030.

vetoes.plan: B. Plan A plus an A350 Re-engine launched in 2045 (entry into service 2050)
vetoes.ground:
Production readiness, a soft veto: no widebody engine on the record is ready by a 2050 entry into service.
- Rolls-Royce, the A350 incumbent, spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine.
- An UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, one year late.
- No fallback engine is on the record.

Grid margin against the best option that passes my tests (A, hold): +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2. That is under $1B in both columns, so the team's override rule cannot carry B. The override budget is intact: none was used in round 1 or round 2.

This is not a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch result. It moves the window; it does not close the case. Re-test once an engine has been committed that is ready by the airframe's entry into service.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
1. A widebody engine on the record that is ready at or before the A350 Re-engine's entry into service. That could be Rolls-Royce committing UltraFan WB (or a Trent XWB derivative with a ready date) a year ahead of the airframe, or a second maker offering an engine. Readiness would then pass, and the launch would turn on the grid tests (the $1B launch test and Toepfer's gate), which are not mine. On today's grid (+0.89 / -0.50) it would still fail those.
2. Data confirming that the A350F is in service and the Spirit A350 packages are at rate. The Board needs this for its condition, and it would strengthen any future case.
3. A reported supply crunch, quality escape, or problem on the NGSA ramp or the A320neo transition. Any new widebody work would then fail outright as a supply or ramp result, which no one overrides, and hold stands.
4. A Joint Venture engine delivery shortfall. Our P&W and RR positions on NGSA both ride on that one engine. I would take it to the safety review and lean on CFM as the backstop. There would be no NGSA re-timing and never a cancel.
5. Boeing launching a 787 Re-engine this round. Rule 3 would then close the A350 Re-engine for 2050, whatever the state of engine readiness.
ops.memo:
My tests come from my role, not from anything I have said on record. Confidence: Very low.

I recommend plan A: NGSA hold, engine code None, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none.

Safety and quality: pass on both options. The brief reports no safety, quality, supply or ramp problem. NGSA flies CFM, P&W and RR. The CFM ducted and Joint Venture engines have been in service since 2036, and no shortfall is reported. Watch items: P&W's first call for its GTF fleet, and our P&W and RR slots both riding on one Joint Venture engine. CFM backstops.

Ramp: pass. Our narrowbody deliveries fall from 1,260 in 2039 to 1,060 from 2049 as share settles. That is the market, not a ramp problem, but supply agreements must be resized to those needs, never held at the peak.

A350 Re-engine: capacity passes, with no overlap, $0 strain and one launch. The A350F and Spirit pass on the game proxy only. The brief is silent, so I cannot confirm either. Readiness fails. The A350 flies Rolls-Royce, which spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine. An UltraFan WB launched this year is ready in 2051, a year after a 2050 entry into service. No other widebody engine is on the record. The engine leads the airframe.

That is a soft veto, binding: the launch is +0.89 / -0.50 against hold, under $1B in both columns, so no override carries it. It moves the window, not the idea. Re-test once an engine is committed that is ready by entry into service.

other_moves.move: Resize the NGSA and A320 supply agreements down to our own needs
other_moves.detail: This is Wagner's finding, and I adopt it. The long-term agreements for engines from all three makers, the wing work packages, titanium forgings and rare earths were sized for the ramp to the 2039 peak of 1,260 narrowbody deliveries. Our own needs fall to 1,140 in 2045 and 1,060 from 2049. The ECSC resizes each agreement to those needs this year. Holding slots at the peak while our needs fall would be over-contracting, and we will not do it. Any agreement committing more than EUR 300m comes to the Board. In public we present this as a more sovereign European supply chain sized to our own programmes [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0331, A-0457].

other_moves.move: Twice-yearly safety review: the NGSA ramp report and the A320neo transition report, taken together
other_moves.detail: Wagner reports the two lines to the Board's safety review as one package [AG-0038, AX-0015]. No widebody engineering is assigned from NGSA in-service support, the NGSA ramp or the A320neo transition. Any quality or supply issue on either line goes to the Board before it reaches the cash line. Wagner flagged one watch item, and the review carries it: our P&W and RR positions on NGSA both depend on the one Joint Venture engine, and P&W's GTF fleet keeps first call on its parts, shops and engineers. CFM is the backstop. A Joint Venture shortfall would lead to a supply response through CFM, never to an NGSA re-timing or a cancel.

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine kept as a staged widebody case, with gates for any re-test
Staged studies outside the board: an NGSA derivative, an A220 variant, and research and technology for the generation after NGSA
ECSC integrity review of supply sizing, hiring and pricing
Capital allocation inside the policy, with buybacks sized after programme cash
other_moves.detail:
These are Toepfer's figures.
- The payout stays within 30-50%.
- Buybacks stay within the 18-month AGM authority and are sized after the year's programme cash.
- With no programme cash in 2045, buyback room after a 50% payout is about $5.1B in the base case and $2.4B in the stress case.
- The EUR 5bn three-year programme, about $1.83B a year, is fundable in every hold case.
- No equity raise, and no dividend cut outside a crisis. State money is upside only [AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0035, A-0348].
The agencies' A+/A1 thresholds are not in our record, so we use Toepfer's proxy: net cash at or above zero every year. On that proxy, hold stays positive through 2049 in both the base and the stress case.

other_moves.move: Open European engineering recruitment continues
other_moves.detail: Ordinary public hiring, sized to NGSA in-service support, the A320neo transition and the staged studies. It never draws on ramp staff and never targets any rival's programme teams. The ECSC reviews it this year [A-0366, A-0485].

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: We continue to press, through the industry coalitions on both sides of the Atlantic, for a tariff-free regime in civil aerospace [AX-0088].

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s, with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We continue its production in a disciplined and controlled way, alongside the A320neo family, and we put fleet safety and operational integrity above all. The people and suppliers who deliver both remain protected.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus. We keep studying the options for its future on our own technology and industrial clock. We will take decisions when the technology and the case are mature, and not before.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain, with long-term agreements sized to our own programmes. We also continue to recruit the engineers who will build the next generations of Airbus aircraft.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in preparing our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
**Decision: the company default.** NGSA hold, engine code None (the only code on the menu), A350 hold, Delay Tactics none.
- Grid: +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2.
- No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item.

**1. Red-line and pillars screen (the team rule's first step)**
Neither option breaks a company red line or the five pillars.
- Rule 1 is met: NGSA entered service in 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year.
- Rules 2 and 7: there is no NGSA cancel on the menu.
- Rule 3 is not binding: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
- Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are closed, and none is the only value.
- Rule 6 is met: a 2045 A350 Re-engine would be one launch with zero overlap with NGSA.
- Wagner confirms safety and quality pass on both options. The brief reports no safety, quality or supply problem and no inject.
Both options therefore go on to the colleagues' tests.

**2. Survivors**
- **Plan A (hold)** passes all of Toepfer's tests: peak cash $0, robustness +23.26 in the worst column, net cash and rating proxy. It passes all of Wagner's: safety and quality, ramp shield, engine code, integrity, rule 1.
- **Plan B (A350 Re-engine, entry into service 2050)** fails two binding soft vetoes:
  1. Toepfer's added-move gate, which is also the company's $1B launch test. The item is +0.89 in S1, $0.11B short of $1B, and -0.50 in S2, negative in the worst plausible column.
  2. Wagner's production-readiness test. No widebody engine on the record is ready by 2050: Rolls-Royce spends on a new widebody engine only with a Re-engine, an UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, and there is no fallback.
  Neither failure is a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch result. Both are soft vetoes.
- **Override.** None is available. B's margin over A, the best passing option, is +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2: under $1B in both columns. The Board's override review would also fail it, as a Qualified Majority item that trails hold in its worst column. The game's single override stays unused. I concur on the merits in any case.

A is the only survivor. It is also the doctrine default: within $1B of the best grid row in my expected column, a $0.89B gap in S1.

**3. Tie-breaks** all point to A: less strain, a later capex start, and fewer Board items (0 against 1).

**4. My read of Boeing, and the expected column**
Expected column: S1, at about 60%. S2 at about 40%, within a 30-50% range.
- For S2: in 2035 Boeing said "We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service". fps has been in service since 2040. Boeing also said the 787 "has room to grow from our Charleston capacity".
- Against S2: "We're not starting a second development alongside this one", "Doing less and doing it better", and debt reduction with a solid investment-grade rating as its priority.
S2 stays the worst plausible column.

At 40%, the launch is worth about +0.33 in expectation (+0.40 at 35%, +0.20 at 50%). It breaks even at 64%. Even at 0% for S2 it is only +0.89, under the $1B test. **The decision rests on our own tests, not on our read of Boeing.** That keeps us on our own clock and ties no widebody step to Boeing.

**5. The staged widebody case the Board asked for in 2035, gate by gate**
| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| Rule 3 | Met. No 787 Re-engine is on the record. |
| A350F in service and Spirit A350 packages at rate | Passes on the game proxy only. The record is silent after 2025 and Wagner has no line data, so the Board's condition that he confirm both is not met. |
| Widebody engine ready by entry into service | Fails. The gap is built into the clocks: an engine launched alongside the airframe is ready at launch + 6, the airframe enters service at launch + 5. |
| Grid gate (at least $1B in the expected column, not negative in the 787 column) | Fails at +0.89 / -0.50. |
| Peak cash | Passes: $1.0B a year over 2045-49, $4.2B under the $5.2B line. |
| Qualified Majority | Required. |

The option to wait: on Toepfer's reconstruction (an inference), a like-for-like 2050 launch is worth about +0.6 in a rivals-hold column. It is still under $1B. A 787 Re-engine in 2045 would close it under rule 3, and the company already named 2035-37 as the last window. The case stays staged and is not launched.

**6. Board-gate line**
There is no Board item this round. For the record, the hold package:
- five pillars: pass;
- Toepfer: pass, with a peak programme cash of $0 against the $5.2B line;
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the ramp shield and integrity;
- grid: +23.37 in S1 and +23.26 in S2.
The Board says hold is never vetoed.

**7. Cost and objective**
- Holding gives up $0.89B in S1, about $0.33B in expectation at 40% for S2. It gains $0.50B against B in S2.
- Plan A's worst column (+23.26) is better than plan B's (+22.76), so it meets the robustness preference.
- No PV is traded for the 60/40 objective, which no order on this menu can move.

**8. Operating actions**
- Supply agreements are resized down to our own falling needs (Wagner).
- The Joint Venture engine is carried as a watch item, with CFM as backstop.
- Buybacks are sized after programme cash (Toepfer).
- Studies stay studies, below EUR 300m each until a Board gate.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer's tests are role-derived (Low confidence), and I weighed them as such. His arithmetic matches the brief.

Plan A: passes everything.
- Peak programme cash $0 against the $5.2B line.
- Robustness +23.37 / +23.26.
- Net-cash proxy positive through 2049 in both the base case (+$43.6B) and the stress case (+$3.7B), with the full buyback.
- No Board items.

Plan B:
- Passes peak cash ($1.0B a year, $4.2B of headroom), rule 6 (zero overlap, one launch) and the plan-level robustness test (positive in both columns).
- Fails his added-move gate, the company's $1B launch test: +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2. Soft veto, binding.
- His expected-value schedule confirms my figures: +0.33 at 40% for S2, break-even at 64%. Even at 0% the item is +0.89, under $1B.
- His override arithmetic confirms that no override can carry B, under the team rule or the Board's review.

Accepted: the veto is binding, no override is allowed, and I agree on the merits. I also adopted:
- his rule that buybacks are sized after programme cash, the trim he would make first under stress;
- his staged sizing of the studies, below EUR 300m each and about EUR 0.9bn in aggregate;
- his option-to-wait estimate (about +0.6 for a 2050 launch, still under $1B);
- his finance line for the public statement.

He uses proxies he labels as inference: operating profit for EBIT Adjusted, an FCF/EBIT ratio of 0.667, and net cash at or above zero standing in for the agency thresholds, which are not in his record. I take them as indicative.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner's tests are role-derived (Very low confidence), and I weighed them as such. Where his record is silent, he says so.

Results:
- Safety and quality: pass on both options. It is a pillars result, but there is no line data after 2025, so it rests on the brief reporting no issue.
- NGSA ramp shield and A320neo transition: pass. A ramp result.
- Supply crunch: not applicable, as none is reported.
- Engineering capacity and rule 6: pass for B, on two conditions: a named widebody team ring-fenced from NGSA and the A320neo, and the studies staying studies.
- A350F and Spirit absorption: pass on the game proxy only. The record is silent, so he cannot confirm the Board's condition from data.
- Production readiness: fail for B. No widebody engine is ready by a 2050 entry into service. UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, and there is no fallback. Soft veto, binding. It is not a safety, quality, ramp or supply result, and it moves the window rather than closing the idea.
- Engine code: None only; the fitted CFM + P&W + RR set stands.
- Integrity and Delay Tactics: pass.
- Rule 1: pass.

Accepted: B's margin over hold (+0.89 / -0.50) is under $1B, so no override is allowed. On the merits, an entry into service without a ready engine is the very discipline we hold NGSA to under rule 1.

I adopted:
- his finding that the supply agreements must be resized down from the 2039 peak (1,260) to our own falling needs (1,140 in 2045, 1,060 from 2049). Holding slots at the peak would be over-contracting;
- his Joint Venture watch item, with CFM as backstop;
- his condition that the studies stay studies and draw on no NGSA or A320neo engineers;
- his request that both ramp reports go together to the safety review.

decision.expected_scenario:
S1 (rivals hold), at about 60%. S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine) is at about 40%, within a 30-50% range, and is the worst plausible column.
- For S2: Boeing said in 2035 it would look at the 787's next step once fps was in service. fps has been in service since 2040, and Boeing has said the 787 has room to grow.
- Against S2: Boeing's one-development-at-a-time discipline and its priority on debt reduction and investment grade.
The decision does not depend on this read: the launch fails the $1B test even at 0% for S2.

boeing.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service since 2040, on the date we gave you. That's five years of airplanes in customers' hands, and we're climbing the ramp the way we said we would. We take one step at a time, on our KPIs, agreed with the FAA, and only after the line has shown it's stable at the rate it's on. We've come a long way. There's still a lot of work in front of us, and we're not going to hurry the last part of the climb.

We're not launching a new program today. We've looked hard at the 787's next step. It's a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll take that next step when the market, the technology and we are ready. Today all three aren't there. So I'm not going to give you a date for something we haven't launched.

Paying down debt is far and away our priority. We're funding the business from our operations, with no new equity. I'm not going to put a year on the rating before the data supports it. You'll see it in the numbers.

We said we wanted to hold half of the single-aisle market. We're at 43% this year, up from 38% when the airplane came into service, and still climbing. That's short of half, and I won't dress it up. We earn the rest one delivery at a time.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our suppliers funded and healthy for the rates in front of us. We'll keep working with CFM, our engine partner, to support those rates.

Others make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. The financials will follow our production performance.

**2. The grid** (from the brief):

- B's item: +0.30 / -1.26. It breaks even at a 19.2% chance of S2.

**3. My tests.**
- **KPI stability: pass.** No live problem in the brief. Pope rightly says delivery counts are not the KPI record, so the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report to Aerospace Safety [BX-1271, BX-1259].
- **Three work streams: not converged** [BX-1296].
  - *Market:* S2 is plausible. If both re-engined airplanes enter service in 2050, share does not move and our 787 margin falls to 15.77%.
  - *Technology:* Pope fails it, as advice. The upgraded GEnx has been on the 787 since 2033, so a Re-engine on it adds no new engine. A GEnx derivative has no durability record. UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051, after a 2050 EIS. My technology risk appetite is low [BX-1298]. This is unpriced, and it is not why I hold, but it means the work stream isn't there.
  - *Boeing:* fundable. About $1.0B a year is 6.1% of the 81.5 of operating profit in 2045-49. Readiness is not the issue; the return is.
- **Debt before the next airplane: B fails.** A second development must beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and B does so in neither column [BX-1305, B-2326].
  - Malave corrects the penalty: +$3.10B undiscounted, which on the grid's pro-rata allocation is about 0.50 PV, not the 0.28 Pope and I used. The grid governs, and nothing is subtracted twice.

  - I'm not holding because of Airbus either. The hold rests on ε, debt-first and readiness.

That is a loss we accept, not a wait. On an item inside ε, with a technology work stream that hasn't converged, I'd rather be a year late than a year early [BX-1322].

- The Re-engine's +0.30 in S1 is inside ε, so doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] take the tie.
- In S2 it loses 1.26. It is a bet that Airbus holds, not a hedge, and I don't time orders to Airbus either way [B-2313].
- Debt first: a second development has to beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and it does in neither column [BX-1305].
- Stability first: the fps is in its ramp, and Pope's results will tell me whether the technology work stream is even ready.

**Expected column, provisional: S1, rivals hold.** My confidence on Airbus is Low.
- Airbus repeated last round's line, "the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus", and it held in both 2030 and 2035.
- Rolls-Royce's line is a condition on its own spending, not an Airbus commitment.
- A move is real only when it is launched (doctrine §7).
- S2 stays plausible: NGSA has been in service since 2037, which frees Airbus engineers, and doctrine expects an A350 Re-engine attempt.
- The orders are the same either way: hold ties in S1 and wins by 1.26 in S2.

**Premium:** 0.30 if S1 (cumulative 0.76 of $2B); 0 if S2. No objective premium and no hard-rule cost this round.

**What would change my lean:** a grid where the Re-engine clears ε in the expected column with no column below -$1B, with Pope's readiness and strain results behind it. A live problem would only make the hold stronger.

**Public line:**
- The fps is in service and climbing, and we're ramping on our KPIs, step by step with the FAA.
- We're not starting a second development today. The 787 grows from Charleston, and we'll look at its next step when it earns its place.
- Debt stays first, with no new equity.
- No date for anything we haven't launched, no order tied to anyone else's clock, and no blame on anyone.
- "the financials will follow our production performance" [BX-1287].

Rebuilt item:

tests.name: Balance sheet first: debt penalty of B (ask 2)

Correction on the PV: the grid behaves as if the combined penalty is spread across the bills pro rata (inference from my rebuild, which ties out):

Phasing against my 2030-39 curve:

Post-EIS debt path (board convention: $105.32B at EIS 2040, 81% of EV):

cfo.memo:
Kelly, the brief labels no risk-case column this year. The fps is in service, so there is no slip leg and my veto has nothing to bind. I still read S2 first, as the Board does. Against its -1.66 floor, Do Nothing passes by 2.00 and the Re-engine row by 0.74. Neither row draws a veto.

Your grid is confirmed: +0.66 / +0.34 against +0.96 / -0.92, an item of +0.30 / -1.26 that breaks even at a 19% chance of S2. One correction: the extra penalty is $3.10B undiscounted, as you said, but the board spreads the combined penalty across both bills, so it costs about 0.50 PV, not 0.28. It is in the grid; we never subtract it again.

The Re-engine is fundable from operations, about $1.0B a year, 6% of operating profit. The issue is the return: +0.30 is inside ε, and in S2 we lose 1.26 for no share. A year of certification slip costs little on the board; the real cost is concessions, rework and carrying cost.

The fps came in on its date and its $60.32B. Debt stays the first call on the $48.0B uplift, with no new equity. We plan on solidly investment grade by 2053, barring a ramp shortfall or a second development, and we'd like to beat it.

I recommend Do Nothing. Holding likely forgoes the Re-engine on this board: a 2050 launch scores about +0.04. That 0.30 premium we accept, cumulative 0.76 of $2B.

tests.name: KPI gate for the 737 Rate Increase: my veto (doctrine; CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, with 2-3 months of stability before the next. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers: The 2045 brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. rate_737 is offered only at hold, so the veto has nothing to bind: I checked it and do not invoke it. On the record for all three lines: narrowbody (fps) deliveries were 760 in 2040 and are 860 in 2045, rising to 940 in 2049; the 787 is flat at 100 a year (58.8%) through 2060. The board carries deliveries, not KPIs. The KPI record (stable months at rate, quality escapes, FAA findings) has to come directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer to Aerospace Safety, and I do not substitute delivery counts for it. Nothing in the board's numbers contradicts stability: no dip, no slip, no flag.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: Do Nothing and the fps in service (record [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? The brief labels no column 'Risk case' this year, because the fps is in service and has no slip leg. So I read each plan's worst column and say how much of its value rests on a nominal date.
tests.numbers: The fps entered service in 2040, on its date. Observed narrowbody share was 38/39/40/41/42% in 2040-44. That is exactly the plan path: NGSA 2037 and fps 2040 give 3 years of lead and a long-run split of 47/53, reached at 1 pp a year. The 2040-44 Delay Tactics window (5 pp for 5 years from EIS, $1.41B a year nominal in my Round-2 memo) closed with no dip on the record. I attribute nothing. Do Nothing's worst column is S2 at +0.34, and none of its value rests on a future EIS. It rests on the ramp holding the path to 47% in 2049. Sensitivity: each point of narrowbody share is 20 fps a year x $55M x 25.64% = $0.28B a year of operating profit, nominal.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: 787 Re-engine with EIS 2050, row B (record [BX-1331] by inference; doctrine slip prior)
tests.threshold: Same test. I add doctrine's slip prior for a major derivative: central +2 years, range +1 to +4 (profile §3, inference). Certifying before building at rate moves the date; it does not let the line build ahead.
tests.numbers: Worst column: B is -0.92 in S2, against A's +0.34, so 1.26 lower. The board fixes EIS at launch + 5 = 2050, with no headroom. Doctrine's central prior is 2052. The record runs both ways: the MAX 8 came early on a conservative date [B-0535], while the 777X and MAX 10 derivatives ran 6-7 years late [B-1498, B-2243]. Each year of slip defers about $0.94B a year of nominal 787 margin uplift (100 airplanes x $180M x 5.21 pp). The $180M is the brief's 2026 revenue of $56.4B, less 800 x $48M, divided by 100. My rough reconstruction does not reproduce the grid exactly. On it, one year of slip costs 0.06-0.08 of the S1 item's +0.30, and the central two years cost 0.12-0.15, so 40-50% of the S1 value rests on the nominal date (inference; Malave costs the slip). In S2 the 787 margin falls from 20% to 15.77%, which is $0.76B a year less, nominal. A slip of ours in S2 also leaves an A350 Re-engine alone, gaining 1.5 pp a year until we enter service.

tests.name: fps ramp stability and supplier readiness (doctrine; CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: Every step KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA: steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, with 2-3 months of stability before the next. Supplier readiness is a hard gate. Fragile suppliers stay funded and hot above our rate. No attribution.
tests.numbers: The ramp goes from 760 deliveries (2040) to 860 (2045) to 940 (2049). That is +20 a year (1 pp of 2,000), or +1.67 a month each year: one step of 5 about every three years. That is about 17% of doctrine's maximum tempo of two steps a year. In relative terms the 2045-49 ramp adds 9.3% over four years, about 2.3% a year. The board's volumes are stylised. On its revenue, every Boeing narrowbody since 2040 is an fps (2045: 860 x $55M + $18.0B of widebody = $65.3B). That puts the line at 72 a month in 2045 and 78 a month in 2049, above the 737's live ladder of 38-42-47-52 [B-2287], so I read the ramp in relative terms. The brief names no supplier problem, so I name categories, not companies. Where supply binds, in order (inference from doctrine): (1) the CFM engine line: sole source, with the code locked (next test); (2) long-lead airframe structures: the step to 52 broke supply [B-1449], and the answer was to embed staff [B-2097]; (3) titanium forgings and (4) rare-earth parts: capacity is shared and finite, and the bulletin shows another airframer's long-term agreements, sized to its own needs, which is an ordinary market move. Beyond 47 a month the 737 supply base bound [B-2340]. Keep all four categories funded and hot above our rate through 2049, not just 2044 [B-2330, BX-1243], and embed staff wherever one falls behind.

tests.name: Engines: CFM ducted durability in service and CFM allocation (doctrine; CEO ask 3; not priced on the board)
tests.threshold: No durability or safety flag in service. Boeing's engine need is tracked against the maker's output across both airframers and the aftermarket.
tests.numbers: The CFM ducted engine was ready in 2036. It has flown on NGSA since 2037 and on the fps since 2040: 9 years in service, 5 of them on the fps. The brief carries no durability or safety flag, and CFM has committed in public that any such flag reaches the Board before the next round's orders. So I can confirm there is no flag on the record, but not that durability is shown; the in-service results are the Chief Engineer's to give Aerospace Safety [BX-1298, B-2304]. Allocation (arithmetic from the bulletin): CFM delivered 53.7% of 4,000 narrowbody engines in 2044, which is 2,148. We needed 1,680 of them (840 x 2), or 78%. Our need is 1,720 in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049 (+160, +9.3%). CFM also supplies NGSA (code 7, with CFM fitted) and the A320neo, and LEAP-1B spares for the 737 fleet are off the board. With a sole source and the code locked, we track allocation by airframer, which is easy to measure [B-1923], and contract delivery commitments for the ramp [BX-1264, BX-1325].

tests.name: Two-front strain (engineering capacity), row B (doctrine; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and a 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps counted from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS. Any derivative certifies before it builds at rate.
tests.numbers: The fps counted 2033-40, and a Re-engine launched in 2045 would count 2045-50. Overlap is 0 years and strain $0, 2 years inside H4. On doctrine, the fps development engineers were released at EIS 2040. Doctrine's 2.5 years from first delivery to design rate puts the handover around 2042-43 (inference). So a Re-engine would feather in on the back side [B-1393, B-0341] without pulling people off the ramp, which is now production, supplier and FAA work. Two things the board does not carry: in-service support for an fps fleet on a new engine, and FAA certification bandwidth (certification has been the pacing item since 2019 [B-2343]). I confirm certify-before-rate on any derivative as a condition, with no concurrency [BX-1263, B-2228]. It moves the date, not the line.

tests.name: Technology readiness for a 787 Re-engine (doctrine; CEO ask 5; not priced on the board)
tests.threshold: A new widebody engine, matured, with durability shown, ready by the Re-engine's EIS of 2050 [BX-1296, BX-1298, B-2304].
tests.numbers: On the public record, the upgraded GEnx has flown on the 787 since 2033. It is the engine the airplane already has, so a Re-engine on it adds no new engine. Doctrine's choice was a GEnx derivative (profile §6), which has no durability record until it is built and tested. CFM calls RISE technology, with no product date. Rolls-Royce will spend nothing new on a widebody engine without a Re-engine. UltraFan WB is ready 6 years after launch (rules), so if launched now it is ready in 2051, a year after a 2050 EIS. No engine on the record meets the threshold, and the technology work stream has not converged. Advice, not a veto ground.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers: No ramp order is offered. The fps has been in service since 2040 on the 10-year ramp, with $60.32B booked at EIS. The board offers fps: hold only.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied to airplanes by inference; CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Solo where Boeing owns the IP. Partner only where the partner adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: A Re-engine would be a Solo airframe derivative with an engine partner, and that is the right split. The 787 airframe IP is Boeing's. Boeing owns no engine IP, so the engine is a partner's in every case. I see no reason to do it otherwise: the board offers no Re-engine Joint Venture, and the 787's own risk-sharing lesson is to wall off critical technology [B-0361, B-0386]. The fps stays Solo, in service on CFM.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: Rate Increase (inference [BX-1329])
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it, in the expected column.
tests.numbers: rate_737 is offered only at hold, and the grid has no Rate Increase row.

tests.name: Widebody capacity at Charleston (inference [BX-1329]; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Add capacity where demand on the grid is visible.
tests.numbers: Without a Re-engine, the board holds the 787 at 100 a year (58.8% of 170), or 8.3 a month, through 2060. The Charleston expansion is built for rates above 10 a month and into the teens [BX-1317, B-2336], which leaves about 20% of headroom at 10 a month. With a Re-engine alone (S1), +1 pp a year from 2050 gives about 119 a year by 2060, or 9.9 a month, still under 10. In S2 nothing moves. So Charleston can grow the 787 with or without a Re-engine. The board shows no demand above 100 a year for it to meet; growth beyond that is commercial and unpriced.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number with a sensitivity per unit.
tests.numbers: A has no new bill. Operating profit runs 15.7 to 16.9 a year in 2045-49: 81.5 in all, 48.0 above the status quo. The fps's $60.32B, booked at EIS 2040, against cumulative operating-profit uplift above the status quo: 40.9 by 2044, 59.2 by 2046 and 68.8 by 2047. So nominal payback on the uplift comes in 2047, seven years after EIS (inference; Malave owns the real phasing and the debt path). B's $5B is booked at EIS 2050; on an even spread it is about $1.0B a year over 2045-49 (inference), which is 6.1% of operating profit and 10.4% of the uplift. Its debt penalty is $3.10B undiscounted on top of the fps's $105.32B of debt: $0.62B per $1B, against $0.6B in all ($0.12B per $1B) for a Re-engine alone. In PV at 2026 that is about 0.46 for the bill and 0.28 for the penalty, both already inside the grid and never subtracted again. B is fundable from operations; whether it moves the investment-grade year is Malave's call. A converts cash best.

tests.name: 737 and 787 results, and keeping customers through the fps ramp (doctrine; CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: KPI and safety results come directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. Deliver on the dates promised, and make every transaction build trust.
tests.numbers: 787: 100 a year at a 20% margin is $3.6B a year of operating profit (100 x $180M x 20%), flat, with no live problem in the brief. 737: the brief's revenue reconciles to every Boeing narrowbody at the fps price from 2040 (2040: 760 x $55M + $18.0B = $59.8B). So on the board the 737 MAX has no new-build deliveries, and its results are fleet and aftermarket, which are off the board. The quality, FAA and safety results belong to the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer; I give the board's delivery record, not a substitute for theirs. Customers: deliver on the dates promised, and quote fps slots only against what the KPI-gated ramp supports, never against an earlier internal number [BX-1273, B-2315]. Track LEAP-1B spares for the 737 fleet with CFM.

vetoes.ground: Not my veto, and no hard-rule breach. H3, second half: not triggered, since no A350 Re-engine is on the public record. H4: 0 years of overlap (fps 2033-40, Re-engine 2045-50), $0 strain. H5: once launched, a Re-engine is never cancelled, so an A350 Re-engine launched in the same sealed round would lock in S2's -1.26 with no exit. Advice only, not binding: technology readiness fails (no new widebody engine with durability shown can be ready by 2050, and UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051); doctrine's derivative prior is central +2 years, which takes roughly 40-50% of the S1 item's +0.30; and the worst column is -0.92 against Do Nothing's +0.34. Recommend hold.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Three things would change my view. (1) A live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, reported in a brief or by the Chief Engineer or the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer. I would invoke the binding KPI veto against any Rate Increase, and ask for the fps ramp to hold at its current rate until the KPIs show 2-3 months of stability, with staff embedded at any supplier that falls behind. (2) A CFM ducted durability or allocation flag. I would hold the next fps rate step and contract engine delivery commitments before resuming. (3) For a 787 Re-engine in the 2050 round, all of the following: the A350 not re-engined (H3); the grid showing an item value above $1B in the expected column with no column below -$1B; a widebody engine with durability shown that can be ready by the Re-engine's EIS (for example a launched UltraFan WB, or a GEnx derivative with test results); and a planning date with headroom against doctrine's +2-year derivative prior. With all four in place, my strain, capacity and IP tests already pass, and I would back it.
ops.memo:
My record is thin: two Global Services events, nothing from BCA. Delivery, cash and IP are my record, applied by inference; the KPI, supplier and strain tests are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time, predictable delivery. The fps entered service in 2040, on its date, and share has run the plan path: 38% to 42% over 2040-44, no dip. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The rate is offered only at hold, so my KPI veto is checked and not invoked.

Second, the ramp. 860 to 940 deliveries is 20 more a year, under 2 a month: one step of 5 every three years, against a doctrine floor of six months. Supply binds first on the CFM line: in 2044 we took 1,680 of CFM's 2,148 narrowbody engines, 78%, sole source with the code locked. Then structures, titanium forgings and rare-earth parts. Keep them funded and hot through 2049.

Third, the Re-engine. Strain is zero; engineering capacity passes. Technology does not: no new widebody engine with durability shown can meet 2050, and a Rolls-Royce one launched now is ready in 2051. Doctrine puts a major derivative two years late, central, which takes 0.12 to 0.15 of its 0.30 in S1. In S2 it loses 1.26.

And finally, cash. The Re-engine is $1.0B a year, 6% of $81.5B operating profit, but each $1B beside the fps carries $0.62B of penalty, against $0.12B alone. Do Nothing converts best.

Orders: fps hold, code null, rate hold, Re-engine hold.

other_moves.move: fps ramp stays KPI-gated, step by step with the FAA
other_moves.detail: The fps goes from 860 deliveries in 2045 to 940 in 2049. Each production step is gated on KPIs and agreed with the FAA, with 2-3 months of stability at a rate before the next step. On Pope's arithmetic that is about one step of 5 a month every three years, about 17% of doctrine's maximum tempo. If a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem goes live, the ramp holds at its current rate until the KPIs show stability again [BX-1271, BX-1259, BX-1322].

other_moves.move: Chief Engineer and Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report directly to the Aerospace Safety Committee each year
other_moves.detail: The report covers fps in-service safety and reliability, CFM ducted durability in service, supplier and quality KPIs through the ramp to 940, and the 737 and 787 results. The board carries deliveries only, so their results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record. The commitment is public; the reports are internal [BG-0043, BX-1298].

other_moves.move: Certify before building at rate on any derivative; no fixed-price development
other_moves.detail: No production-certification concurrency on any derivative, including any future 787 step [BX-1263, B-2228]. Development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Neither is priced on the board.

other_moves.move: Supply base funded and hot through 2049
other_moves.detail: Pope's binding order: (1) the CFM engine line, (2) long-lead airframe structures, (3) titanium forgings, (4) rare-earth parts. All four categories stay funded and hot above our rate through 2049, not just 2044. Staff are embedded at any supplier that falls behind [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2097]. We name categories, not companies, and attribute nothing to anyone.

other_moves.move: CFM allocation tracked by airframer; delivery commitments contracted for the ramp
other_moves.detail: In 2044 we took 1,680 of CFM's 2,148 narrowbody engines (78%). Our need rises to 1,720 in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049. CFM is sole source and the code is locked, so we track allocation across the fps, NGSA, the A320neo and 737 LEAP-1B spares, and contract delivery commitments for each ramp step [BX-1264, BX-1325, B-1923]. A durability or allocation flag holds the next fps step.

other_moves.move: Yearly funding report to the Finance Committee; debt first, no new equity
other_moves.detail: Malave's report is the baseline. Debt was $105.32B at EIS 2040 (81% of EV) and is the first call on the $48.0B of operating-profit uplift over 2045-49. Planning case: solidly investment grade (debt back to $45B) by 2053, with 2047 held as upside. It is restated once, before any commitment, if deliveries or operating profit fall below the brief's path, a live problem appears, or a second development is proposed. No new equity. No dividend or buyback proposal: that is reserved to the Board, and only once the rating is solid [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Publicly we say debt first and give no rating year.

other_moves.move: 787 grows from Charleston; no Re-engine launch this round
other_moves.detail: The 787 holds 100 a year on the board. Charleston has headroom above that [BX-1317, B-2336]. We give no Re-engine date. Internally, readiness work on the 787's next step continues without a launch: engine durability data and customer requirements. Pope finds no matured widebody engine for a 2050 EIS [BX-1296].

other_moves.move: Independent estimate check and early-warning rule continue
other_moves.detail: Malave stays the independent check on every programme estimate [BX-1316]. Any reset is planned once and reported early, with the mitigation attached [BX-1318, BX-1306].

other_moves.move: Customer slots quoted only against the KPI-gated ramp
other_moves.detail: fps delivery slots are offered only against what the gated ramp supports, never against an earlier internal number. Every transaction should build trust [BX-1273, B-2315].

decision.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service since 2040, on the date we gave you. That's five years of airplanes in customers' hands, and we're climbing the ramp the way we said we would. We take one step at a time, on our KPIs, agreed with the FAA, and only after the line has shown it's stable at the rate it's on. We've come a long way. There's still a lot of work in front of us, and we're not going to hurry the last part of the climb.

We're not launching a new program today. We've looked hard at the 787's next step. It's a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll take that next step when the market, the technology and we are ready. Today all three aren't there. So I'm not going to give you a date for something we haven't launched.

Paying down debt is far and away our priority. We're funding the business from our operations, with no new equity. I'm not going to put a year on the rating before the data supports it. You'll see it in the numbers.

We said we wanted to hold half of the single-aisle market. We're at 43% this year, up from 38% when the airplane came into service, and still climbing. That's short of half, and I won't dress it up. We earn the rest one delivery at a time.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our suppliers funded and healthy for the rates in front of us. We'll keep working with CFM, our engine partner, to support those rates.

Others make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. The financials will follow our production performance.
decision.rationale:
**Decision: Do Nothing.** The orders are fps hold, fps_engine_code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold. The row is +0.66 / +0.34 (S1 / S2). Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board.

**1. Team rule, applied.**
- **Malave's buffer test** is not applicable. The brief labels no column 'Risk case', and the fps has been in service since 2040, so it has no slip leg. He confirms he holds no veto this round, and no plan is out on this ground.
- **Board proxy on S2** (floor 0.34 - 2.00 = -1.66): A passes by 2.00 and B by 0.74.
- **KPI doctrine (Pope's seat):** not in play. rate_737 is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. She checked the veto and did not invoke it.
- No colleague flagged a red line, and I override nothing. The rest is my call.

**2. The grid** (from the brief):
- A, Do Nothing: +0.66 / +0.34.
- B, fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +0.96 / -0.92.
- B's item: +0.30 / -1.26. It breaks even at a 19.2% chance of S2.
- Malave rebuilt the item from the rules and tied out to rounding (+0.29 / -1.27).

**3. My tests.**
- **KPI stability: pass.** No live problem in the brief. Pope rightly says delivery counts are not the KPI record, so the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report to Aerospace Safety [BX-1271, BX-1259].
- **Three work streams: not converged** [BX-1296].
  - *Market:* S2 is plausible. If both re-engined airplanes enter service in 2050, share does not move and our 787 margin falls to 15.77%.
  - *Technology:* Pope fails it, as advice. The upgraded GEnx has been on the 787 since 2033, so a Re-engine on it adds no new engine. A GEnx derivative has no durability record. UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2051, after a 2050 EIS. My technology risk appetite is low [BX-1298]. This is unpriced, and it is not why I hold, but it means the work stream isn't there.
  - *Boeing:* fundable. About $1.0B a year is 6.1% of the 81.5 of operating profit in 2045-49. Readiness is not the issue; the return is.
- **Debt before the next airplane: B fails.** A second development must beat Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column, and B does so in neither column [BX-1305, B-2326].
  - Malave corrects the penalty: +$3.10B undiscounted, which on the grid's pro-rata allocation is about 0.50 PV, not the 0.28 Pope and I used. The grid governs, and nothing is subtracted twice.
  - B would also move his conservative investment-grade year from 2053 to 2054.
- **Certification slip:** there is no risk-case column, so this is for scale only.
  - Malave: one year of slip costs about 0.15 all-in in S1.
  - Pope: doctrine's central +2-year prior takes 40-50% of the S1 item.
  - So B's +0.30 rests partly on a nominal date with no headroom. I won't plan that way [BX-1318, BX-1319].
- **Doing less, better:** +0.30 in S1 is inside ε, so the plan with less to execute wins [BX-1239]. It is also the higher-confidence plan, with a worst column higher by 1.26 [BX-0548]. In S2, A leads by 1.26, outside ε. A wins whichever column I expect.
- **Airbus does not set the date:** both directions apply.
  - I'm not launching to pre-empt an A350 Re-engine. That is doctrine's Chicken-game reading, which I did not use [B-2313].
  - I'm not holding because of Airbus either. The hold rests on ε, debt-first and readiness.

**4. Hard rules.**
- H1, H2, H6 and H7: not at issue.
- H3, second half: not triggered, since no A350 Re-engine is on the record. If Airbus launches one this round, it bars a 787 Re-engine from then on, and I accept that.
- H4: 0 years of overlap (the fps counted 2033-40).
- H5: the fps is in service and cannot be cancelled.
- H8: the premium below.

**5. The 2050 window.** Malave estimates that a 2050 launch scores about +0.04 in S1, about $0.96B short of the Board's bar. So holding now very likely forgoes the 787 Re-engine on this board. That is a loss we accept, not a wait. On an item inside ε, with a technology work stream that hasn't converged, I'd rather be a year late than a year early [BX-1322].

**6. The Board.** It would veto re787: launch on business case (+0.30 / -1.26 clears $1B in neither column) and on downside (-1.26 against its -$1B limit). It approves Do Nothing. Weighed: no conflict.

**7. Record versus doctrine.**
- My record drove: the tie-break [BX-1239, BX-0548], debt-first [BX-1305], the three work streams [BX-1296] and under-disclosure of the rating year [BX-1268].
- Doctrine drove: Pope's supplier binding order, the slip prior and the reading that the engine code is locked.
- Malave's investment-grade year is his inference (debt back to $45B). I keep it internal.

- From EIS it ran 38% in 2040 (the worst year), then 39, 40, 41 and 42% through 2044.

Both objectives are recorded as not met:
- 50/50: below 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Incumbency (40% or more in 2030-50): the worst year is 38%.

No order on offer this round moves that path. The 787 Re-engine is widebody only. So the objective premium is 0.
