cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: both new single-aisle airplanes are in service, and there's a CFM engine on both. The ducted engine CFM and Safran launched in 2030 has been in service since 2036. Our work with Embraer has been in service since 2037, and the upgraded GEnx on the 787 since 2033. Those are dates on the record, not on slides. We didn't take those positions for granted then, and we don't now. We don't have a birthright on the next order, so we earn it the way we earned the last one: by delivering. That means LEAP and the new engine, and the spares behind them, on time to every customer we serve. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

What we don't know yet is how these new engines hold up over years of service, especially in the hot and harsh places where engines work hardest. So we'll measure time on wing on the fleet, in cycles, against the yardstick our customers know, and we'll report it on field data, not on analysis. Where we find something, we fix it with Safran, the airframers and the regulators. We don't trade durability for delivery.

The ducted engine is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

We're not starting anything new this year. We plan on the low case and keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. Any commitment on CFM capacity, we make together with Safran. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every field. There is no Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain and a premium of $0.

THE FRAME [CX-0467]. The narrowbody contest is decided. NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM, P&W and RR (code 7), and fps since 2040 with CFM alone (code 3). The Joint Venture engine has been in service since 2036. No code can move, no slot is open, and the brief has one column, S1. The game is the installed base we already hold [CX-0422]: LEAP on the 737 and A320neo, the Ducted on fps, NGSA and Embraer, and the GEnx on the 787. We win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658].

THE GRID (brief §3, S1 at weight 1.0, so the expected column is also the worst). Ghai reproduced every row.
- Hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%). This is the best row: engine value -32.29, R&D -4.00 and strain -2.00, the 2030 package, all booked.
- Open Fan: -68.85, or -30.56 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus $22.56B of 35 pp wait penalty from 2045.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -60.18, or -21.89 against hold. That is the $9B bill plus $12.89B of 20 pp penalty.
- Lobby beside an Open Fan: +8.67. Lobby alone: about -1.00 (not a grid row; it has no board effect on its own).
Nothing is positive against hold. Every alternative loses more than its own bill (3.8x and 2.4x).

CORRECTIONS TO MY FRAME, accepted:
- Ali: 2055 is 18 years after NGSA's entry and 15 after fps's, not 'eight and five'. That was my arithmetic slip. It never reached a statement or a move.
- Ghai: the penalty starts in 2045. He reproduces it within $0.03B on a 2045 start, and a 2046 start does not match. $0.645B per raw point and $0.678B per point of share are the same rate.
- Ghai: no new strain arises because the $2B is a one-time charge already in hold, not because it is 'one project'. Open Fan + Lobby would be two projects.
- Ghai: on renormalised shares, Dominate falls to 21.0% (2045) and 23.5% (2050) with the Open Fan alone, and to 35.2% and 37.8% with Lobby. My rough figures ran 1-2 points low; the conclusion stands.

MY TESTS.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]. The new NBs are on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect, and it is all cost: the board gives the Open Fan no share gain. Nothing is ordered.
- H2. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 at the earliest (launch + 10), 18 and 15 years after the two entries. Every route waits, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route is $21.89B against $15B, $4.89B above the allowance plus the round cap and $2.89B above the allowance plus the full game cap.
- H3. The Ducted stands as the defence, triggered on the record and in service. It is never the next generation.
- H5. RISE continues whole; holding the Open Fan is not a cancel.
- My 20% and durability lines are unaffected. The Ducted is not called the next generation, and no durability margin is traded.
- Strain: no new project.
- Tie-break: not needed. The nearest alternative is $21.89B behind, far outside ε.

OBJECTIVE. Dominate is met (51.1% worst year, 2040; 54.3% in 2045; 56.8% in 2050). Introduce is unreachable. Launching an Open Fan would give up an objective we meet for one we can't reach. That is a net objective loss, not a premium.

LOW CASE FIRST [CX-0248, CX-0536]. I book -39.60: S1's -38.29 less $1.31B, the larger of the two exclusive widebody risks named by the Board and Ghai. Those risks are not put into any grid row or column. On Ghai's advice I go no lower: the narrowbody is locked, and booking below the low case misinforms too. I raise toward -38.29 only if the next bulletin shows no widebody move.

THE JOINT VENTURE LESSON. The record moved from -31.20 to -38.29, which is -$7.09B. The board took 20 raw points off us, not 15: the Joint Venture's 10 stacked on one solo-sized 10. That sits between Ghai's two readings (+$7.1B fold, -$14.2B stack), on the stacked side at half the size. My -56.00 booking covered it by $17.71B, so guiding low worked. But we named the risk and didn't book it, and we discounted a rival's stated sequencing. The lesson, adopted: a named risk with a negative midpoint gets its midpoint booked in the round we find it, and a rival's stated sequencing is not data.

SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold orders no new CFM narrowbody move, so there is nothing to gate. RISE continues as a 50-50 decision [CX-0166]. An Open Fan with no airframer path would need a reason why Safran would agree, and there is none: a 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base. Lobby serves RISE, so consent is assumed, but the point is moot. Any CFM price, terms or capacity is joint [CX-0184], including any answer to the airframer's backstop rate request. GEnx is GE alone.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, drove these parts:
- Lobby only beside a live Open Fan (no lobbying evidence in my record).
- Embraer held (my record is silent on it).
- No reaction to the Joint Venture (profile.md §5, §7).
- Supply and raw materials: Ali's supply record is my own description of his job, so I checked it against doctrine (OE first, spares never crowding out OE).

BIAS NAMED. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) pulls toward an Open Fan for the objective. But admission buys a seat, and both airframes are flying. There is no seat until an airframer wants one [CX-0469, CX-0205]. My ramp optimism [CX-0590, CX-0592] is checked by publishing no rate, and no capacity commitment on the backstop request without field data and Safran.

WHAT CHANGES MY MIND:
- A durability or safety flag. That means fleet action and a reserve in the round it is found; it lowers the booking, not the orders.
- A widebody move on the record. I re-price it in 2050.
- A firm airframer launch that wants RISE [CX-0469]. None is possible in the NB window.
Investors asking does not move me [CX-0444].

No veto stands. Ghai's binding vetoes and Ali's advice all fall on orders I don't make, so there are no overrides.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467, CX-0319] For this horizon the narrowbody contest is decided. Both new airframes are in service: NGSA since 2037 with CFM, P&W and RR on it, and fps since 2040 with CFM alone. The P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035 and its engine is fitted on NGSA. No code can move, no narrowbody slot is open, and the brief has one column, S1. In that column no rival selection takes our slot.

So the game now is the installed base we already hold [CX-0422]: LEAP on the 737 and A320neo, the Ducted on fps, NGSA and Embraer, and the GEnx on the 787. We win it the way we always have: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. That means durable engines in service, OE engines and spares on time to every airframer, and the balance sheet and payout kept whole.

The only real question on the menu is the Open Fan. A 2045 launch could not be ready before 2055. That is eight years after NGSA's entry, five after fps's, and outside the objective's 2050 date. On the grid it loses $30.56B against hold on its own and $21.89B with Lobby. It would also trade an objective we meet today (Dominate NB, 54.3% in 2045) for one we can no longer reach (Introduce the Open Fan by 2050).

My aim is to say that plainly, keep RISE whole as technology with Safran, and book low. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD, 2045 (bulletin).
- fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on a 10-year ramp, in service since 2040, selection CFM (code 3), fitted CFM. Boeing: 'Our engine partner stays CFM.'
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, in service since 2037, selection RR, PW and CFM (code 7), all three fitted.
- P&W GTF2 (Solo, ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (Solo, ready 2037) both folded into the P&W-RR Joint Venture in 2035. The Joint Venture NB engine launched in 2035 and has been ready and in service since 2036, carrying a folded solo's schedule.
- Ours: Ducted launched 2030, in service since 2036. Embraer partnership launched 2030, in service since 2037. GEnx upgrade launched 2030, in service since 2033, counting from 2042.
- Observed NB engine shares: CFM 76.0% to 2036, then 51.7% (2037), 50.5% (2039, the low), 51.1% (2040) and 53.7% (2044). P&W and RR are equal at about 23%.
- Observed WB engine shares: GEnx 42.0% to 2041, then 44.8% from 2042.
- NB airframes: Boeing troughed at 37% in 2039 and is climbing 1 pp a year from fps's entry (42% in 2044). That pulls our share up, because fps and the 737 are CFM.
- No Delay Tactics effect is visible on the fps path.

WIDEBODY SIGNALS (nothing on our menu answers them).
- Boeing will 'look at [the 787's] next step once this airplane is in service', and fps now is.
- RR: 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine.'
- Airbus: the A350 family stays its focus. It is locking up titanium forgings and rare earths for NGSA and A320 needs.

OUR POSITION (brief §1). If nobody moves again: ΔPV -38.29 (yield 76.07%). That is engine value -32.29, R&D -4.00 and strain -2.00, the 2030 package, all booked. The path is NB 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% from 2049 to 2056; WB 44.8%.

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T [CX-0436].
- Last round's S1 row (the record) was -31.20. Today's hold is -38.29, a move of $7.09B. Codes and dates did not change; the Joint Venture is the only new fact on the record.
- My arithmetic (inference): about -4.8 pp of NB share every year from 2037 (2037: 56.5% to 51.7%; 2040: 55.9% to 51.1%; 2045: 59.0% to 54.3%; 2050: 61.6% to 56.8%), at about $1.47B PV per point over 2037-56.
- That lies between Ghai's round-2 readings: +$7.1B if the Joint Venture folded both solos, -$14.2B if it stacked on top. The sign was on the stacked side, at about half the size.
- I booked -56.00 last round. The switch columns did not happen; the backlog held. The hit came from a risk we named but did not book.

OBJECTIVE (brief §2; it never changes the payoff).
- Dominate NB engines: MET. 51.1% in 2040 (the worst year, now locked), 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% in 2050.
- Introduce the Open Fan: NOT MET, and unreachable in this game. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 at the earliest (launch + 10). A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, after the narrowbody count ends in 2056.
- An Open Fan launch would also break Dominate. My arithmetic, inference, ignoring renormalisation: about 19% in 2045 and 22% in 2050 on its own, and about 34% and 37% with Lobby. That holds if the penalty starts in the decision year; 2050 fails either way.

THE GRID (brief §3, one column, S1: rivals hold). Hold everything is -38.29 (76.1%), the best row.
- Open Fan: -68.85 (57.0%).
- Open Fan + Lobby: -60.18 (62.4%).
- No row is positive against hold.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision).
It WOULD VETO:
- open_fan: launch, alone. It is -30.56 against hold: the $8B bill plus about $22.56B of wait penalty. It fails the airframer-path test, and the RISE allowance cannot cover it ($30.56B against $15B). With no airframer path it would need a stated reason why Safran would agree.

- Any premium above $0 not tied to a grid plan. Any RISE allowance used outside the airframer-path test; it says that cannot happen in this round or in 2050.
It WOULD APPROVE:

- unpriced moves: in-service durability reporting with Safran's engineers; LEAP and Ducted OE and spares on time; RISE whole, 50-50, with no date; a private CFM offer on standard terms set with Safran; no reaction or price cut on Joint Venture news.

- So the penalty starts in 2045. Culp's two rates are the same thing on two bases: $0.645B per raw point (before renormalisation, /105) and $0.678B per point of share after it.

Strain: the residuals after bill and penalty are +0.03 and +0.02, so neither Open Fan row adds strain. One correction to Culp's reason. It is not 'one project, not two': Open Fan + Lobby would be two new projects. The $2B is a one-time charge already in hold's -2.00, so no new strain arises.

tests.name: Pays for itself: hold everything (Culp's lean)
tests.threshold: Each order beats its default in the expected column, with the grid charging every bill in full (inference: price/cost rule in PV form). A plan with no Board item passes if no alternative beats it.
tests.numbers:
Hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%) in S1 at weight 1.0, the best row (brief §3).
- It has no Board item, so there is no item value to test.
- The best alternative, Open Fan + Lobby, is $21.89B behind it, far beyond the $1B epsilon.
- Components: engine value -32.29, R&D -4.00 and strain -2.00 (the 2030 package, all booked).

tests.name: Pays for itself: alternatives (Open Fan, Open Fan + Lobby, Lobby alone)
tests.threshold: The change from default beats hold in the expected column (S1), net of its bill
tests.numbers:
Item values in S1 (expected, only and worst column):
- open_fan: launch: -30.56. That is -$8B bill and -$22.56B penalty: it loses 3.8x its bill.
- open_fan + lobby_emissions: launch: -21.89. That is -$9B bill and -$12.89B penalty: 2.4x its bill.
- lobby_emissions alone: -1.00.
All three lose more than their bill, so each fails the Board's bounded-downside test as well. On this board the Open Fan has no share gain: it is all cost.

tests.name: Volumes first
tests.threshold: Judge a launch in the columns consistent with the public record (selections and rival engines announced). A launch that beats hold only by assuming a selection not on the record fails (inference: disclosure habit applied as a capital test)

tests.name: No overcapitalization (new R&D and strain per year against payout room)
tests.threshold: New R&D and strain committed this round, spread over their development years, within about $2.5B a year: 30% of about $8.5B of 2028 free cash flow left after returning more than 70% (inference: analogy from capex to R&D)
tests.numbers:
This round: $0.00 of new R&D and $0.00 of new strain.
- The 2030 package ($4B Ducted R&D + $2B strain) ran $1.00B a year over 2030-35. It is complete, with the Ducted in service since 2036.
- Room: 0.30 x $8.5B = $2.55B a year, all of it free. No debt, no rating effect; the >70% return holds.
- For the record: an Open Fan would run $0.80B a year ($8B/10), or $1.80B in its first year with Lobby. Both fit the room, so this test is not why it fails. Pays-for-itself is.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (ask 3)
tests.threshold: Doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game; one RISE allowance up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan (company doctrine, hard rule 9)
tests.numbers:
Premium this round $0.00. Game to date $0.00 of $4.0B. RISE allowance $0 of $15B, unused.

Objective premium declined, against hold:
- $21.89B for the cheapest route (Open Fan + Lobby);
- $30.56B for the Open Fan alone.

The cheapest route is $4.89B above the allowance plus the round cap ($17.0B), and $2.89B above the allowance plus the full game cap ($19.0B).

It buys nothing toward 'Introduce'. The Open Fan is ready in 2055 at the earliest, after the 2050 test. It would also cost 'Dominate', which is met today. That is a net objective loss, not a premium.

tests.name: Joint Venture reconciliation (ask 4, Board item 4)
tests.threshold: Reproduce the record's move from round 2's S1 (-31.20) to today's hold (-38.29) from the public rules, and score it against my round-2 readings (inference)
tests.numbers:
Reproduced exactly: -$7.09B.

The rule the board applied (my reading):
- CFM's raw NB hit is -20 pp, against -15 pp with the two solos.
- That is the Joint Venture's -10 pp stacked on one solo-sized -10 pp (the size of the UltraFan NB solo's hit). GTF2's -5 pp dropped out when it folded.
- P&W and RR were then equalised.
- Check, 2037: (39 + 61/3 + 15 - 20)/105 = 51.7%. 2040: 51.1%. 2045: 54.3%. 2050: 56.8%. All match the brief.
- I can't tell from our share alone whether the second -10 is UltraFan's or a second Joint Venture count.

Score against round 2. Each 5 raw points is $7.09B: $1.419B per raw point, or $1.49B per point of share over 2037-56. Culp's $1.47B is close.
- Fold-both reading (-10 pp): +$7.09B. Wrong.
- Stack-on-both reading (-25 pp): -$14.19B. Wrong.
- The record is -$7.09B, half the stacked case and on the stacked side.

The booking: -56.00, which sat $17.71B under the record, so guide-low covered it.

The miss: I discounted formation because one partner said it would wait for the other's commitment. Both committed in the same sealed round.

The lesson: a rival's stated sequencing is not data. A named risk whose readings straddle zero with a negative midpoint (here -$3.55B) gets its midpoint booked in the round we find it.

tests.name: Objective share check under an Open Fan (ask 2)
tests.threshold: CFM NB share >= 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050, with the penalty from 2045 and shares renormalised to 105 raw points (inference)
tests.numbers:
Hold: 51.1% (2040, locked), 54.3% (2045), 56.8% (2050). Met.

Open Fan alone:
- 2045: (57 - 35)/105 = 21.0%;
- 2050: (59.67 - 35)/105 = 23.5%.

Open Fan + Lobby:
- 2045: 35.2%;
- 2050: 37.8%.

Both routes fail Dominate in 2045 and 2050. Culp's rough 19%/22% and 34%/37% ignore renormalisation and run about 1-2 points low; the conclusion stands.

This result is for the alternatives. Hold passes.

tests.name: Terms (ask 6)
tests.threshold: No launch-era pricing, no price concession, and no CFM narrowbody price talk without Safran in any public statement or other move
tests.numbers:
There is no price lever on the board.

Culp's statement plan passes as described: safety first, engines on time, the Ducted not called the next generation, RISE with Safran, and no rival, price, rate or date.

The other moves pass:
- the private CFM offer on standard terms, price set jointly with Safran;
- no reaction and no price cut on Joint Venture news;
- 'paid in dollars, not in percentages' is about returns, not price.

One flag. Airbus's public supply move seeks engine rate commitments from all three makers, with CFM as backstop. Any CFM answer is NB capacity, so it is joint with Safran (hard rule 7). It goes on standard terms, with no price concession attached and no rate published. I re-test the exact text at the veto check.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (ask 7)
tests.threshold: Name the worst column for the recommended plan, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores
tests.numbers:
Worst column: S1 at -38.29, a $0 gap, because it is the only column. The narrowbody is locked: codes fixed, both airframes in service, the Joint Venture formed, and Delay Tactics closed after fps's 2040 entry.

Left out (my own arithmetic, inference):
(a) RR Trent 1000 upgrade, +5 pp WB from 2048: -$0.76B. The Board says -$0.8B.
(b) UltraFan WB, +10 pp. It counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service; a 2045 launch is ready in 2051: -$1.08B. From 2050 it is -$1.22B. The Board says -$1.3B.
(c) (a) and (b) are exclusive, so the board's downside is at most about -$1.3B. A 2050 launch would cost only -$0.41B or -$0.50B.
(d) A 787 or A350 re-engine shifting WB airframe share. I can't price an engine-share link, and it could cut either way for GEnx.
(e) Ducted in-service durability. On LEAP, time-on-wing shortfalls became reserves in the quarter found.
(f) Raw materials: titanium forgings and rare earths, with Airbus locking up its own needs.
(g) Supplier-dependent volumes, which have slipped on us before.
(h) Macro (recession, tariffs, airframer slowdowns): the board's fixed 2,000 NB a year leaves it out.

tests.name: Dated profit sequence
tests.threshold: For each programme: bill year, ready year (Ducted launch + 6; Open Fan launch + 10, not before 2045; Embraer 7 years after; GEnx 3 years after) and first year of share gain, inside the board's horizon (NB to 2056, WB to 2061 per the brief) (inference)

tests.name: No second stack of projects (advice)
tests.threshold: Flag any plan that adds a project or stacks two or more; add-ons pass only net of the $2B strain (inference)
tests.numbers: Nothing is added. The $2B strain is a one-time charge already booked in hold. The real load is operating: LEAP OE and spares on the 737 and A320neo, and Ducted OE and spares on fps, NGSA and Embraer, through one base. That is Ali's ground. GE9X losses are not treated as live.

tests.name: Guide low (ask 7, advice on expected_pv_b)
tests.threshold: Book the low end of the expected column, with no upside before it is confirmed (inference)
tests.numbers:
Book -39.60: S1's -38.29 less about $1.3B, the Board's figure for the larger of the two exclusive widebody risks. My own figure is $1.08-1.22B, so -39.60 is the conservative end.

I would not go lower. The narrowbody is locked and no other board line can move against us; booking below the low case misinforms as much as booking above it.

I would not hold at -38.29 either. Round 2 taught us that a named one-sided risk gets booked.

Range: -38.29 to -39.60. Raise toward -38.29 only after a bulletin shows no widebody move.

tests.name: Board package check (ask 8)
tests.threshold: No Board item vetoed: no Open Fan, no Lobby, no premium above $0 untied to a grid plan, no RISE allowance outside the airframer-path test, new R&D and strain within about $2.5B a year, and no item that loses more than its bill in any plausible column

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch (alone)
vetoes.ground:
capex (pays for itself; volumes first; premium cap, hard rule 9).
- Item value in S1 (expected, only and worst column) is -30.56: the $8B bill plus $22.56B of 35 pp wait penalty from 2045. It loses 3.8x its bill.
- No airframer has selected or asked for an Open Fan, and both new NBs are in service.
- The $30.56B premium exceeds the $15B RISE allowance plus the $2.0B round cap ($17.0B).
My veto right is an inference (teams.md §1): it binds unless Culp answers the failed test with evidence. Holding is not a RISE cancel (H5).

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch with lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground:
capex (pays for itself; premium cap, hard rule 9).
- Item value in S1 is -21.89: the $9B bill plus $12.89B of 20 pp penalty, with no added strain.
- That is $4.89B above the allowance plus the round cap ($17.0B), and $2.89B above the allowance plus the full game cap ($19.0B).
- Lobby's +8.67 exists only beside a live Open Fan, so it falls with it.
My veto right is an inference (teams.md §1): it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch with no live Open Fan
vetoes.ground: capex (pays for itself). It costs $1B and has no board effect on its own: about -1.00 in S1. My veto right is an inference (teams.md §1): it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing or a price concession, or talks CFM narrowbody price or terms without Safran. This includes a price cut on Joint Venture news and any price attached to a CFM backstop rate commitment for Airbus.
vetoes.ground: terms. No launch-era pricing or concessions, and CFM narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran. My veto right is an inference (teams.md §1). On a statement alone, the Board reads it as a recommendation, not an item veto. Culp's plan as described passes.

vetoes.plan: Culp's lean: hold on every field
vetoes.ground:
No veto; advice only.
(a) Book -39.60, not lower and not -38.29.
(b) Correct the record:
- the Open Fan penalty starts in 2045;
- no strain is added because the $2B is a one-time charge already in hold, not because it is 'one project';
- the Dominate figures renormalised are 21.0%/23.5% alone and 35.2%/37.8% with Lobby.
(c) A CFM rate or capacity backstop for Airbus without Safran would breach hard rule 7. That is a red line for Culp to strike, not my veto.
(d) The Joint Venture lesson goes into the rationale: a named risk with a negative midpoint gets its midpoint booked.
(e) Durability and supply are Ali's ground.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
(1) A grid I've misread, meaning any row that beats hold in S1. There is none on this brief.
(2) A firm airframer launch that wants an Open Fan, with entry after a 2055 ready year and Safran agreeing. None is on the record, and none is possible in the NB window with the codes locked.
(3) A safety or durability flag from Ali on the Ducted, Embraer, LEAP or GEnx fleets. That means fleet action and a reserve in the round it is found. It lowers the booking, not the orders.
(4) A widebody move on the record (Trent 1000 upgrade, UltraFan WB, or a 787 or A350 re-engine). I'd re-price the booking: -$0.76B, or -$1.08B to -$1.22B. With no such move at the next bulletin, I'd raise toward -38.29, and not before.
(5) Any price, concession or terms wording, or a CFM NB capacity or rate commitment without Safran. That is a terms veto, or hard rule 7.
cfo.memo:
Larry, your arithmetic holds. Hold is -38.29, the best row. The Open Fan is -30.56 against hold: the $8B bill plus $22.56B of penalty. I reproduce that penalty within $0.03B only if it starts in 2045, at $0.645B a raw point. Open Fan + Lobby is -21.89. Neither row adds strain, but not because it's one project: the $2B is a one-time charge already in hold. Either route takes Dominate to about 21% (35% with Lobby) in 2045 and 23.5% (38%) in 2050. We'd give up an objective we meet for one we can't reach.

On the Joint Venture, we've been proven wrong on that one before. The board took 20 raw points off us, not 15: the Joint Venture's 10 on top of one solo-sized 10. That's -$7.09B, half my stacked case. My readings straddled zero with a negative midpoint, and I booked neither. The good news: our -56.00 booking sat $17.71B under the record. The lesson: when a named risk's midpoint is negative, book the midpoint when we find it.

Capex: $0 new R&D, $0 new strain, premium $0 ($0 of $4.0B), RISE allowance unused, payout whole within about $2.5B a year of room.

Terms: clean. One flag: Airbus wants CFM as its rate backstop. Any answer is joint with Safran, on standard terms, with no price attached and no rate published.

Book -39.60, not lower: the narrowbody is locked, and the widebody risks are exclusive, about -$0.8B or -$1.1-1.3B. I concur with hold.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (date veto ground 1): the ready year of every order and every grid row
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time. Ducted: launch + 6. Open Fan: launch + 10, and not before 2045. Partner Embraer: counts 7 years after launch. GEnx: counts 3 years after launch, not before 2035, and from 2042 if nobody re-engines. An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails. This is an inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times.
tests.numbers: Reporting back against last round's promise. We said 'not before 2036'. The Ducted was 2030 + 6 = 2036 and has been in service since 2036 (bulletin). Embraer was 2030 + 7 = 2037 and has been in service since 2037. Both dates were met, and neither came early. GEnx upgrade: 2030 + 3 = 2033, in service. The board counts its +5 pp WB from 2042: WB share went from 42.0% to 44.8% in 2042, which is after the 2035 floor. The hold row, -38.29 (76.07%) in S1, is priced on those years and no earlier. If the Open Fan is launched now, 2045 + 10 = 2055. The 2045 floor is not the binding limit; launch + 10 is. The Open Fan row (-68.85, which is -30.56 against hold) and the Open Fan + Lobby row (-60.18, which is -21.89) are both priced on a 2055 ready year with the wait penalty, and neither rests on an earlier year. A 2050 launch: 2050 + 10 = 2060. Nothing in Culp's lean depends on a year earlier than launch plus development years. Ask (2) confirmed: a 2045 launch is ready no earlier than 2055, and a 2050 launch no earlier than 2060.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (date veto ground 2): dates in the frame, the statement plan and the other moves
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back. No Open Fan entry before 2045 and none before launch + 10. No RISE fly-demo, ground-test or flight-test date. No ramp rate. In-service years already on the record are facts, not promises.
tests.numbers: Ask (5). The statement plan gives no Open Fan or RISE date and no ramp rate. It cites only in-service years on the record: Ducted 2036, Embraer 2037, GEnx 2033, NGSA 2037, fps 2040 and the Joint Venture engine 2036. That passes. The record carries no RISE demo, ground-test or flight-test date: the round-2 public move gave none. One correction to the frame, which is not yet in the statement. The frame's 'question' says 2055 is 'eight years after NGSA's entry, five after fps's'. In fact 2055 - 2037 = 18 years and 2055 - 2040 = 15 years. 'Eight and five' would place an Open Fan ready in 2045 from a 2045 launch, below launch + 10. Correct it before it reaches the Board's papers. If it reaches the statement or other moves, it fails at step 4. 'Durable engines in service' is a claim, not a date: see the durability test.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted and Partner Embraer (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted ready 2036: 1 year before NGSA's 2037 entry and 4 years before fps's 2040. Embraer counted from 2037: the same year as NGSA's entry and 3 years before fps's. Both are in service on the record, so no gap remains open. Neither field offers anything but hold.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan, if launched (advice)
tests.threshold: An Open Fan ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry avoids the board's loss. Ready after it, the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with lobbying). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Launched in 2045, it is ready in 2055. That is 18 years after NGSA (2037) and 15 years after fps (2040). It is also 5 years after the objective's 2050 date and 1 year before the NB count ends in 2056. The 35 pp wait applies, or 20 pp with Lobby. Against hold in S1 that is -30.56 alone and -21.89 with Lobby (grid). Launched in 2050, it is ready in 2060, 4 years after the count closes. 'Introduce the Open Fan' is unreachable on any order. The last launch that could have been ready by 2050 was in 2035 (+10 = 2045). Culp holds the Open Fan, so his plan does not fail this test; only the launch option does. Ask (2) on real testing: my evidence ends in October 2025. It shows over 350 RISE tests with an early durability focus, compact-core HPT blades in dust testing (the earliest we have ever started that test), and open-fan noise tested with Airbus, lower than today's LEAP. It shows no open durability failure in compact-core or hot-section testing. Ground and flight test was set for 'this decade', after a mid-decade fly demo slipped, and the outcome is not in my evidence. I do not infer progress past October 2025.

tests.name: Physics: the 20% line and the Ducted's wording
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A Ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so it is never called the next generation. That it is a defence only is company doctrine (hard rule 3). This is a wording check unless a fuel-burn claim is made (inference).
tests.numbers: Ask (4): nothing has changed. Neither the brief nor the frame makes a fuel-burn claim. The frame keeps the 20% line on RISE. The statement plan says the Ducted is 'the right engine for the airplanes in front of us, not the next generation'. RISE is 'more than 20%'. 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan', and a ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain. I recheck the statement's wording at step 4.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn, schedule or delivery (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: Hold trades nothing. The frame puts safety and quality ahead of delivery and states that durability is not traded for delivery or fuel burn. The evidence gap, said plainly: the brief carries shares, not cycles. It has no time-on-wing, shop-visit, removal or inspection data on the Ducted (in service 2036), Embraer (2037), the GEnx upgrade (2033) or the LEAP fleet. My last field data is LEAP. In 2023, fleet leaders ran 9,882 cycles against about 17,000 for the CFM56 in benign service, and about 4,800 against 7,000-8,000 in harsh service. The LEAP-1A HPT hardware was certified in December 2024. By July 2025 it was in all LEAP-1A deliveries and shop visits, with more than twice the time on wing, and by November 2025 new LEAP-1A engines performed at CFM56 levels. The LEAP-1B kit was in certification for 1H 2026, and its outcome is not in my evidence. Retrofit runs through shop visits: 'years, not months'. Advice for the statement: report time on wing in cycles against the CFM56 yardstick, or not at all. Do not claim a durable fleet that field data in hand cannot show.

tests.name: In-service safety and durability report: Ducted, Embraer, GEnx, LEAP (Culp's ask 1; Board recommendation 1)
tests.threshold: Report only what has been turned on and turned off, in test or in the field, not analysis. Say where the evidence stops. Give any flag with its cross-functional answer, made with Safran's engineers, and its fleet action (inspection, shop visit, spares).
tests.numbers:
No field data is in the brief, so no flag can be raised on evidence and none can be cleared on evidence. I raise none, and I do not certify that none exists.
- Ducted, in service since 2036 on fps and NGSA: no core or hot-section test result and no field result in my record.
- Embraer, since 2037: it rides on the same engine, so the Ducted's answer covers it.
- GEnx upgrade, since 2033: no field data. Its lineage is GE90/GEnx hot-section experience.
- LEAP: as in the durability test. Its post-2026 state is not in my evidence.
Where I look first (inference from the LEAP history, not a flag): the Ducted fleet in hot and harsh service, because that is where LEAP first fell short, through 'a small, handful of parts', in the Middle East and India. If a shortfall is found, the answer is the LEAP answer: root cause, inspection and a parts fix accepted by the airframer and the regulator, targeted or fleet-wide, with no redesign of the engine. Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts stays in new-make shops and MRO. Any flag reaches the Board before orders.

tests.name: Supply load
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain. This is inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only. No evidence: following doctrine.
tests.numbers:
No new project: hold adds $0 of R&D and $0 of strain. The $2B strain and the $4B of Ducted R&D are the 2030 package, already in the hold row. An Open Fan would be one new project; Ducted, Embraer and GEnx are all in service. Ask (3), No evidence: following doctrine and Culp.
- The only data I have is Culp's 2024 count: 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites. I have no field data from them after 2024.
- The load runs through that same base: LEAP OE and spares on the 737 and A320neo, Ducted OE and spares on fps, NGSA and Embraer, GEnx support, and the shop-visit kit flow.
- Doctrine order: OE on time to every airframer, spares never crowding out OE, no rate published.
- Raw materials, unpriced and unquantified: Airbus's long-term agreements on titanium forgings and rare earths are 'sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs' (bulletin). Our exposure is not in my evidence.
- Its public other move also asks all three makers for engine rate commitments, 'with CFM as backstop'. That is a possible capacity call on the same base. Any such commitment is joint with Safran (H7), and it does not go ahead of OE on time to every airframer.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into the fleet while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: genx: hold, the only value offered. The upgrade on the GE90/GEnx hot-section lineage has been in service since 2033 and counts +5 pp WB from 2042 (44.8%). The widebody signals in the bulletin (Boeing on the 787's next step, RR's 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine') are not on this menu, and their dates are not ours to give. RISE technology keeps flowing into the LEAP and Ducted fleets.

tests.name: Safety call
tests.threshold: If a problem in the brief or an order touches safety or durability, it needs a cross-functional team, not one person.
tests.numbers: The brief raises no safety problem. The frame's red line puts in-service safety and durability calls with one cross-functional supply, engineering and quality team, with Safran's engineers on CFM engines. Any flag is answered on the fleet, not traded against delivery. Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts stays in new-make shops and the MRO network.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch (options 2 and 3)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto. This is not my date ground: the grid prices the Open Fan at 2045 + 10 = 2055, and its value rests on no earlier year. It fails readiness against the airframe. 2055 is 18 years after NGSA's 2037 entry and 15 years after fps's 2040, 5 years after the 2050 objective date and 1 year before the NB count ends in 2056. Against hold in S1 it is -30.56 alone and -21.89 with Lobby. Physics conviction is not a calendar: my own fly-demo date slipped from mid-decade to 'this decade'. Culp holds, and I agree. On Lobby alone, No evidence: following Culp and doctrine.

vetoes.plan: Frame wording: 2055 is 'eight years after NGSA's entry, five after fps's'
vetoes.ground: No veto now; it is in the frame, not in the statement or other moves. The correct gaps are 2055 - 2037 = 18 years and 2055 - 2040 = 15 years. 'Eight and five' would imply an Open Fan ready in 2045 from a 2045 launch, earlier than launch + 10. If that wording, or any Open Fan or RISE date, reaches the public statement or other moves, I veto it at step 4 on binding ground 2: a date no test backs. My veto right over programme dates is an inference from my 2024 standard for believing durability-fix results [CX-0009, CX-0008]. The team rule makes a failed date test bind unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Public statement: durability and RISE wording (checked at step 4)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding. Do not claim the Ducted, Embraer or LEAP fleets are durable in service: the brief carries no field data. Say we report time on wing on field data, against the CFM56 yardstick. Give no RISE demo, ground-test or flight-test date, no ramp rate and no word implying RISE progress past October 2025, because my evidence ends there. Never call the Ducted the next generation.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Only test or field data changes my mind, never analysis or a forecast.
(a) Field data from the Ducted or Embraer fleet shows a time-on-wing shortfall against the LEAP-1A post-kit or CFM56 yardstick, especially in hot and harsh service. Or a fleet inspection finds a safety-critical-part problem. Then I raise a flag. It goes to the cross-functional team with Safran's engineers and reaches the Board before orders. The answer is fleet action: root cause, inspection, a parts fix turned on and turned off in test, shop visits and spares. It is never traded for delivery.
(b) Field data from the 9 suppliers and 15 sites shows spares crowding out OE, or a backstop rate call outrunning the base. Then OE on time to every airframer comes first, and any capacity commitment is joint with Safran.
(c) A durability failure is reproduced in RISE compact-core or hot-section testing. Then I raise a flag, and no product builds on that hardware until the failure is turned off in test.
(d) An airframer firmly launches an airplane that wants RISE, with an entry year no earlier than launch + 10. Then the Open Fan's date test could pass, and the timing is Culp's call. None is on the record, and the NB count ends in 2056.
Nothing on this grid moves me off hold. Weights and booking are Culp's and Ghai's ground.
ops.memo:
I report back against last year's promise. We said the Ducted would not be ready before 2036, launch plus six. It entered service in 2036. Embraer counted from 2037, launch plus seven. The GEnx upgrade has been in service since 2033 and counts from 2042. Those dates are on the record, not on slides.

What I can't show you is field data. The brief carries shares, not cycles: no time on wing, no shop-visit findings, no inspection results on the Ducted, Embraer, LEAP or GEnx fleets. So I raise no safety or durability flag, and I don't claim there is none. My last real data is 2025: LEAP-1A HPT hardware certified, in every delivery and shop visit, at CFM56 levels. The LEAP-1B kit was in certification for 1H 2026; its outcome is not in my evidence. LEAP first fell short in hot and harsh service. That is where I look first on the Ducted. The yardstick stays the CFM56.

Open Fan: launched in 2045, ready in 2055 at the earliest. Correct the frame: that is eighteen years after NGSA and fifteen after fps, not eight and five. Launched in 2050, ready in 2060, after the count ends. Hold. No RISE date of any kind; mine slipped.

Physics unchanged: a ducted engine gets less than half the gain. Not our next generation.

Supply: no new project, no new strain. On suppliers and raw materials after 2024, no evidence: following doctrine.

No single person can make a safety decision.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: both new single-aisle airplanes are in service, and there's a CFM engine on both. The ducted engine CFM and Safran launched in 2030 has been in service since 2036. Our work with Embraer has been in service since 2037, and the upgraded GEnx on the 787 since 2033. Those are dates on the record, not on slides. We didn't take those positions for granted then, and we don't now. We don't have a birthright on the next order, so we earn it the way we earned the last one: by delivering. That means LEAP and the new engine, and the spares behind them, on time to every customer we serve. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

What we don't know yet is how these new engines hold up over years of service, especially in the hot and harsh places where engines work hardest. So we'll measure time on wing on the fleet, in cycles, against the yardstick our customers know, and we'll report it on field data, not on analysis. Where we find something, we fix it with Safran, the airframers and the regulators. We don't trade durability for delivery.

The ducted engine is the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

We're not starting anything new this year. We plan on the low case and keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole. Any commitment on CFM capacity, we make together with Safran. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every field. There is no Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain and a premium of $0.

THE FRAME [CX-0467]. The narrowbody contest is decided. NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM, P&W and RR (code 7), and fps since 2040 with CFM alone (code 3). The Joint Venture engine has been in service since 2036. No code can move, no slot is open, and the brief has one column, S1. The game is the installed base we already hold [CX-0422]: LEAP on the 737 and A320neo, the Ducted on fps, NGSA and Embraer, and the GEnx on the 787. We win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658].

THE GRID (brief §3, S1 at weight 1.0, so the expected column is also the worst). Ghai reproduced every row.
- Hold everything: -38.29 (76.1%). This is the best row: engine value -32.29, R&D -4.00 and strain -2.00, the 2030 package, all booked.
- Open Fan: -68.85, or -30.56 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus $22.56B of 35 pp wait penalty from 2045.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -60.18, or -21.89 against hold. That is the $9B bill plus $12.89B of 20 pp penalty.
- Lobby beside an Open Fan: +8.67. Lobby alone: about -1.00 (not a grid row; it has no board effect on its own).
Nothing is positive against hold. Every alternative loses more than its own bill (3.8x and 2.4x).

CORRECTIONS TO MY FRAME, accepted:
- Ali: 2055 is 18 years after NGSA's entry and 15 after fps's, not 'eight and five'. That was my arithmetic slip. It never reached a statement or a move.
- Ghai: the penalty starts in 2045. He reproduces it within $0.03B on a 2045 start, and a 2046 start does not match. $0.645B per raw point and $0.678B per point of share are the same rate.
- Ghai: no new strain arises because the $2B is a one-time charge already in hold, not because it is 'one project'. Open Fan + Lobby would be two projects.
- Ghai: on renormalised shares, Dominate falls to 21.0% (2045) and 23.5% (2050) with the Open Fan alone, and to 35.2% and 37.8% with Lobby. My rough figures ran 1-2 points low; the conclusion stands.

MY TESTS.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]. The new NBs are on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect, and it is all cost: the board gives the Open Fan no share gain. Nothing is ordered.
- H2. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055 at the earliest (launch + 10), 18 and 15 years after the two entries. Every route waits, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route is $21.89B against $15B, $4.89B above the allowance plus the round cap and $2.89B above the allowance plus the full game cap.
- H3. The Ducted stands as the defence, triggered on the record and in service. It is never the next generation.
- H5. RISE continues whole; holding the Open Fan is not a cancel.
- My 20% and durability lines are unaffected. The Ducted is not called the next generation, and no durability margin is traded.
- Strain: no new project.
- Tie-break: not needed. The nearest alternative is $21.89B behind, far outside ε.

OBJECTIVE. Dominate is met (51.1% worst year, 2040; 54.3% in 2045; 56.8% in 2050). Introduce is unreachable. Launching an Open Fan would give up an objective we meet for one we can't reach. That is a net objective loss, not a premium.

LOW CASE FIRST [CX-0248, CX-0536]. I book -39.60: S1's -38.29 less $1.31B, the larger of the two exclusive widebody risks named by the Board and Ghai. Those risks are not put into any grid row or column. On Ghai's advice I go no lower: the narrowbody is locked, and booking below the low case misinforms too. I raise toward -38.29 only if the next bulletin shows no widebody move.

THE JOINT VENTURE LESSON. The record moved from -31.20 to -38.29, which is -$7.09B. The board took 20 raw points off us, not 15: the Joint Venture's 10 stacked on one solo-sized 10. That sits between Ghai's two readings (+$7.1B fold, -$14.2B stack), on the stacked side at half the size. My -56.00 booking covered it by $17.71B, so guiding low worked. But we named the risk and didn't book it, and we discounted a rival's stated sequencing. The lesson, adopted: a named risk with a negative midpoint gets its midpoint booked in the round we find it, and a rival's stated sequencing is not data.

SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold orders no new CFM narrowbody move, so there is nothing to gate. RISE continues as a 50-50 decision [CX-0166]. An Open Fan with no airframer path would need a reason why Safran would agree, and there is none: a 35 pp loss cuts Safran's half of the same base. Lobby serves RISE, so consent is assumed, but the point is moot. Any CFM price, terms or capacity is joint [CX-0184], including any answer to the airframer's backstop rate request. GEnx is GE alone.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, drove these parts:
- Lobby only beside a live Open Fan (no lobbying evidence in my record).
- Embraer held (my record is silent on it).
- No reaction to the Joint Venture (profile.md §5, §7).
- Supply and raw materials: Ali's supply record is my own description of his job, so I checked it against doctrine (OE first, spares never crowding out OE).

BIAS NAMED. The installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) pulls toward an Open Fan for the objective. But admission buys a seat, and both airframes are flying. There is no seat until an airframer wants one [CX-0469, CX-0205]. My ramp optimism [CX-0590, CX-0592] is checked by publishing no rate, and no capacity commitment on the backstop request without field data and Safran.

WHAT CHANGES MY MIND:
- A durability or safety flag. That means fleet action and a reserve in the round it is found; it lowers the booking, not the orders.
- A widebody move on the record. I re-price it in 2050.
- A firm airframer launch that wants RISE [CX-0469]. None is possible in the NB window.
Investors asking does not move me [CX-0444].

No veto stands. Ghai's binding vetoes and Ali's advice all fall on orders I don't make, so there are no overrides.

memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed as a thin record. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only, so he is Medium confidence on durability, test standard and RISE physics. On supply his record is only my description of his job [CX-0633], so I weighed that part against doctrine.

On dates I deferred fully:
- The Ducted's launch + 6 = 2036 and Embraer's 2037 were met, neither early.
- GEnx: 2033, counted from 2042.
- An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055, and one launched in 2050 in 2060.
I accepted his correction of my frame: 18 and 15 years, not eight and five. It appears in no statement or move.

He is candid that the brief carries shares, not cycles. He raises no flag and does not certify that none exists. I took his wording advice:
- the statement claims no durable fleet;
- time on wing is reported in cycles on field data against the CFM56 yardstick, hot and harsh service first;
- no RISE date and no progress claimed past his evidence;
- the Ducted is never called the next generation.
My statement promise of 'durable engines in service' from the frame was dropped for that reason.

On supply he has no evidence after 2024 and follows doctrine. I carried his raw-materials flag and the backstop capacity call into private other moves, with OE first and the call joint with Safran. He concurs with hold.

The Joint Venture engine has been in service since 2036. Codes are locked, and the Delay Tactics window on fps closed at its 2040 entry.

decision.premium_reason:
Premium this round: $0.00. Game to date: $0.00 of the $4.0B cap. The submitted plan is the best grid plan in the only column, so no doctrine or objective premium arises.

RISE allowance, stated apart: $0 of $15B, unused. It cannot be used this round. Every Open Fan route waits on an airframe already in service, so it fails the airframer-path test.

Objective premium declined for 'Introduce the Open Fan', against the best non-RISE plan (hold):
- $21.89B for the cheapest route (Open Fan + Lobby), which is $4.89B above the allowance plus the round cap and $2.89B above the allowance plus the full game cap;
- $30.56B for the Open Fan alone.
Neither buys anything toward the objective, since the engine is ready in 2055, after the 2050 test. Both would also break 'Dominate', so this is a net objective loss, not a premium.
decision.objective_note:
PD-briefing objective: dominate narrowbody engines and introduce the Open Fan. It never changes the payoff.

(1) Dominate NB engines (CFM at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is MET on the brief. The shares are 51.1% in 2040 (the worst year, now locked), 54.3% in 2045 and 56.8% in 2050. An Open Fan launch would break it. On Ghai's renormalised reading (inference) the shares would be 21.0% (2045) and 23.5% (2050) with the Open Fan alone, and 35.2% and 37.8% with Lobby.

(2) Introduce the Open Fan (launched and ready by 2050) is UNREACHABLE in this game on any order.
- A 2045 launch is ready no earlier than 2055 (launch + 10).
- A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, after the narrowbody count ends in 2056.
- The last launch that could have been ready by 2050 was in 2035, and it would have waited on both airframes.

RISE is not given up. It continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, all in on the physics [CX-0214]. It goes into a product when an airframer and its airlines want it [CX-0469, CX-0205].
decision.predictions:
COLUMN WEIGHTS: S1 1.0, the only column. Hold is -38.29 there. I book -39.60.

What I expect on the record: nothing moves on the narrowbody. The codes are locked, both airframes and the Joint Venture engine are in service, and our NB share follows the brief: 54.3% in 2045, rising to 56.8% from 2049. WB stays at 44.8% unless someone moves.

RISKS OUTSIDE THE COLUMN (named; in no grid row; only the largest sets the $1.31B guide-low cushion in my booking):
(a) Widebody, against GEnx's 44.8%. The two cases are exclusive.
- An RR Trent 1000 upgrade (+5 pp WB from 2048): about -$0.76B (Ghai) or -$0.8B (Board).
- An UltraFan WB re-engine (+10 pp once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service): -$1.08B from a 2045 launch, -$1.22B from 2050 (Ghai), or about -$1.3B (Board).
The signals: Boeing will look at the 787's next step once fps is in service, and it now is; RR does no widebody spend without a Re-engine; Airbus's focus is the A350. I can't put a probability on it, because looking is not moving.
(b) A 787 or A350 re-engine shifting WB airframe share. Unpriced, and it could cut either way for GEnx.
(c) Ducted and Embraer in-service durability, hot and harsh service first. On LEAP, time-on-wing shortfalls became reserves in the quarter they were found. This lowers the booking, not the orders.
(d) Raw materials: titanium forgings and rare earths. Unquantified.
(e) The airframer's backstop rate call on the same supplier base. Any answer is joint with Safran, and OE comes first.
(f) Supplier-dependent volumes, and macro (recession, tariffs) that the board's fixed narrowbody market leaves out.

Upside is not booked. If the 2050 bulletin shows no widebody move, I raise toward -38.29, and not before.

cfo.note:
I concur with hold on every field. I re-tested terms and capex on the exact plan ordered, using brief §1 and §3.

TESTS
- Pays for itself: PASS. Hold everything is -38.29 (76.1%) in S1. That is the only column, so it is both the expected and the worst column, and hold is the best row in it. The plan carries no Board item, so no item value needs testing. The alternatives, measured against hold: Open Fan -30.56 (the $8B bill plus a $22.56B penalty) and Open Fan + Lobby -21.89 (the $9B bill plus a $12.89B penalty). Both lose more than their bill, and neither is ordered.
- Volumes first: PASS. Nothing is launched. The standing Ducted and Embraer rest on the record: fps code 3 in service since 2040, NGSA code 7 in service since 2037, and the Joint Venture engine in service since 2036.
- No overcapitalization: PASS. New R&D is $0.00 and new strain is $0.00, against about $2.55B a year of room (30% of about $8.5B). The 2030 package is complete. There is no debt and no effect on the rating, and the more-than-70% return holds.
- Premium: PASS. The premium is $0.00 this round and $0.00 of $4.0B for the game. The RISE allowance ($15B) is unused.
- Terms: PASS. The statement names no rival and contains no price, concession or launch-era pricing. 'Any commitment on CFM capacity, we make together with Safran' is about the gate, not about price. 'Paid in dollars, not in percentages' is about returns. In the other moves, the Airbus backstop answer and the private offer are joint with Safran, on standard terms, with no price attached and no rate published. 'No price cut' on Joint Venture news is consistent with this test.

RED LINES: none breached. H4 and H7 hold: standard terms, with Safran on price and capacity. H5 holds: RISE continues whole. H9 holds: no premium. Under H3, the Ducted is never called the next generation.

ADVICE (not binding)
(a) The -39.60 booking matches my guide-low number: S1 less about $1.3B, the larger of the two exclusive widebody risks. Don't go lower. Raise it toward -38.29 only after a bulletin shows no widebody move.
(b) What the case leaves out: the gap between the worst and expected columns is $0, because S1 is the only column. ops.red_line: None. H1: every airframer is offered a CFM engine on standard terms, and nobody is locked out (private offer). H2: open_fan is held, so no airframer is pressed into the wait. H3: the statement says the Ducted 'isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE.' H4: standard terms, no concession. H5: RISE continues whole, 50-50 with Safran, and holding the Open Fan is not a cancel. H6: no date without test evidence, and durability is not traded for delivery or fuel burn. H7: no new CFM narrowbody order; any capacity answer on the backstop request is joint with Safran. H8: no rival named, no blame. H9: premium $0.00.

veto.ground: No veto. Neither of my two date grounds fails. (1) No order's value rests on a ready year earlier than launch plus development years, or on an Open Fan ready before 2045. Every field is hold. Ducted: 2030 + 6 = 2036, in service since 2036. Partner Embraer: 2030 + 7 = 2037, in service since 2037. GEnx upgrade: 2030 + 3 = 2033, in service and counted from 2042 (WB 42.0% to 44.8%). Open Fan: held. Launched now, it would be ready in 2045 + 10 = 2055, and launched in 2050, in 2060. (2) The statement and other moves give no date that a test cannot back. The statement has three dates: launched 2030, in service since 2036, Embraer since 2037, GEnx since 2033. All are in-service years on the public record, which are facts, not promises. There is no Open Fan entry date and no RISE fly-demo, ground-test, flight-test or ramp date; RISE's entry 'is really not for us to say'. 'Before the 2050 orders' is a reporting deadline, not a programme date. The frame's 'eight and five years' slip appears nowhere public; the rationale carries the corrected 18 and 15. My veto right over programme dates is an inference from my 2024 standard for believing durability-fix results [CX-0009, CX-0008]. The team rule makes a failed date test bind unless Culp answers it with evidence. Here nothing fails.

ops.note:
I concur. I recomputed every ready year and read every date in the statement, the other moves and the rationale.

REPORT BACK. We said the Ducted would not be ready before 2036 and Embraer before 2037. Both entered service on those years, neither one early. The GEnx upgrade has been in service since 2033 and counted from 2042. Open Fan held: 2055 at the earliest from 2045, 2060 from 2050. The rationale and the objective note carry 18 and 15 years, and 2035 as the last launch that could have made 2050. Both date tests pass.

PHYSICS. The statement never calls the Ducted the next generation and makes no fuel-burn claim. Pass [CX-0183, CX-0180].

DURABILITY. The statement claims no durable fleet: 'What we don't know yet is how these new engines hold up.' Time on wing is reported in cycles on field data against the CFM56 yardstick, or not at all. Pass [CX-0006, CX-0208].

FLAGS FOR THE BOARD (not vetoes)
1. Safety and durability: no flag raised, and none cleared. The brief carries shares, not cycles. I have no time-on-wing, shop-visit, removal or inspection data on the Ducted, Embraer, GEnx or post-2026 LEAP fleets. I do not certify that there is no problem. I look first at hot and harsh service, where LEAP first fell short [CX-0161]. Gate calls stay cross-functional, with Safran's engineers [CX-0012].
2. A wording fix, and I made the same slip in my own memo. The public reporting move says the Ducted has been 'in service since 2036 on fps and NGSA'. The engine was ready and in service in 2036, but it has been on NGSA only since 2037 and on fps since 2040. Tighten the wording. It is a fact on the record, not a forward date, so it is not a veto.
3. Supply (No evidence: following doctrine). I accept both tasks: the field-data check before any backstop capacity commitment, and the titanium and rare-earths review. I hold no supplier data after 2024 [CX-0613]. No capacity commitment goes ahead on analysis, ahead of OE on time to every airframer, or without Safran.

We find problems before problems find us.

DERIVATIVE RULE. Rolls-Royce's technology, or any merged Joint Venture or UltraFan content, reaches the engine only as a derivative of the certified engine:
- with its own full test programme, severe-environment testing included, and all LLPs at full life at its own entry into service;
- as a new build standard or a certified kit at shop visits;
- never through a licence, and never into the gear and core.

A derivative that crosses the gear-and-core boundary is opposed under red line P-1233 and flagged to the Board.

Risk, investment and revenue stay shared on the 49% partner model [P-1563]. Rolls-Royce's technology is protected on the same terms as ours, and we keep the partner whole [PX-0038]. No derivative spend goes out without a live airframer need.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 23.2% in 2044, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them.

What is done: our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design, has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. It shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected.

Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection. It will be ready six years from launch, with durability proven before entry into service. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
THE DECISION: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr hold. premium_b 0. predictions S1 1.00. expected_pv_b -2.93. overrides empty. No Board item.

1. START FROM EDDY'S PROPOSAL. Eddy proposed hold/hold. It is the only row in brief §3.
- A cancel is gone: GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 and has been ready since 2036, and the rules allow a cancel only until an engine is ready.
- A withdraw is gone: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and the rules allow a withdraw only before formation.
- launch and launch_if_selected are not offered, and no live airframe is outside service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040).
I adopt the proposal unchanged.

2. STRIKE WHAT FAILS A BINDING VETO.
- Mitchill invoked one binding veto, on ground 3 (aggressive terms): any share-recovery or pricing campaign to close the Capitalise gap. I had already struck it in my frame, and it stays struck. It also fails my own rule, value not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The board does not price it, and it cannot reach the gap, which comes from the airframe split.
- Mitchill's ground 2 (on a 2050 launch) and ground 4 (on the final text) are standing conditions, not invoked. I checked the final statement against ground 4. It carries no share forecast, no dated recovery, no durability claim, no partner money, no look-back figure and no programme cost figure.
- Eddy invoked neither ground. Ground 1 passes: no order puts an engine on an airframe or compresses a programme, and the engine was ready in 2036 for NGSA's 2037 entry into service. Ground 2 passes: the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem.
- No colleague flagged a company red-line breach.

3. CONSTRAINT FIRST, THEN OPTIMISE [PX-0035].
- The safety and durability constraint now applies to the fleet, not to a launch. We claim no durability that the fleet record does not show, and the brief holds no record. Any finding goes to Governance and Public Policy and the full Board before the 2050 orders.
- Inside the constraint there is one row, so the optimum is hold/hold: -2.93 in S1, worst column -2.93, nothing against hold.

4. TIE-BREAKS.
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080], so I adopt Eddy's order of call. Steps 2 to 4 are weighed jointly with Airbus [PX-0099].
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] asks for nothing. The cycle was answered in 2030 and 2035, and no live airframe can still select us.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer.

5. PREMIUM AND OBJECTIVE.
- premium_b 0. No row differs from hold, so no doctrine or objective premium can arise, and the $1B cap is unused.
- Restore credibility: MET. The Joint Venture engine has been in service on NGSA, a new airframe, since 2037.
- Capitalise: NOT MET at -2.93. No order on the grid reaches it, and I will not chase it with price or terms.
- PV given up for either: $0.

6. ANNUAL PROGRAMME NPV REVIEW (Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own operating dates).
- ΔPV -2.93 = engine value -0.93 + R&D -2.00. The R&D is undiscounted, booked once in 2035, with no fresh share and no write-off since.
- Engine value against the status quo: small gains in 2038-40 (7.6 against 7.5, 7.9 against 7.6, 7.9 against 7.8), worth +0.15 PV. Losses from 2043 (8.1 against 8.3), reaching -1.0 a year by 2049-53, worth -1.12 PV. Net -0.97 on rounded figures against -0.93.
- The drift tracks Airbus's NB share at 0.317 pp per point. That attribution stays private; in public we speak for no airframer [PX-0062].
- Look-backs, inference and private. About +24.8 against being left off NGSA, which is the top of the range, not a point estimate. +5.51 for the 2035 commit, for $0 of new R&D.
- Answer to the shareowner: the $2B defended the franchise, and the residual gap is the airframe split.

7. WHAT CHANGED FROM MY FRAME. Two wording fixes to the statement, both advice and both taken:
- Eddy's and Mitchill's: 'our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design', in place of 'the engine we developed with Rolls-Royce'. It keeps point (c) exact while the derivative suits are open [PG-0039].
- Mitchill's: 'formed on the terms we published' is printed only now that Eddy has confirmed points (a) to (c).
I also added the conditional, dated offer for any future engine: after an airframer's selection, ready six years from launch, durability proven before entry into service.

8. BIASES NAMED.
- Optimism on operating dates: the statement and the fleet report carry no dated recovery.
- Architecture loyalty: the airframe-split reading is supported by the bulletin, but we hold no fleet data, so I do not use it to say the fleet is fine.
- Partner discipline: Rolls-Royce is now a partner under strain, and its technology is protected on the same terms as ours [PX-0038].

9. RECORD VERSUS DOCTRINE.
- My own record grounds fleet first, value not share, the capital order and fast disclosure.
- The Joint Venture close-out and the derivative rule rest on company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1563] and on Eddy's engineering, not on my record (Low).

10. 2050. The standing rule is in other_moves. A 2050 unconditional launch would be ready in 2056 and fails Mitchill's ground 2 and the Board's tests. My 2050 default is hold unless a live airframe not yet in service selects P&W.

The engine is in service, and the public record shows 23.2% in 2044. Report both plainly. Claim no durability the fleet record does not show, and say nothing on airframers' rates or shares. frame.initial_lean:
MY LEAN: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr hold. premium_b 0; predictions S1 1.00; expected_pv_b -2.93; overrides empty. No Board item.

WHY
- It is the brief's only legal row, and it is right.
- Safety and the fleet come first now that the engine is in service [PX-0035][PX-0080].
- No live airframe can still select us, so 'miss a cycle' [PX-0071] asks for nothing. This cycle was answered in 2030 and 2035.
- The Capitalise gap (-2.93) comes from the airframe split, which no P&W order reaches. I will not chase it with price or terms [PX-0055].

BIASES I NAME
- Optimism on operating dates: the fleet report and the statement carry no dated recovery.
- Architecture loyalty. The 'it's the airframe split, not our engine' reading is supported by the bulletin, but we hold no fleet data. I will not use it to imply the fleet record is good.
- Partner discipline: Rolls-Royce is now a partner under strain too [PX-0038], and its technology is protected on the same terms as ours.

PROPOSED OTHER MOVES
1. Public: the GTF Hot Section kit at shop visits, sold on standard terms, with no dated AOG recovery [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106].
2. Private: the fleet report to the Board each round, on measured data or a plain 'none in the brief'. Findings go to Governance and Public Policy and the full Board before the next orders.
3. Private: the order of call. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo deliveries come first [PX-0099].
4. Private: the Joint Venture close-out (Shane's four points), plus the rule that merged content comes only as a tested derivative, off the gear and core, with no licence.
5. Private: Neil's annual programme NPV review, with both look-backs labelled as inference.
6. Private: the 2050 rule. No engine order without a live airframe not yet in service selecting P&W, ready by its entry into service.

BOARD
I will answer each round-2 recommendation and each round-3 recommendation in board_response. These are closed as moot:
- the Joint Venture ready-date question (the bulletin shows 2036);
- the 2045 withdraw test (formed 2035);
- the same-round sequencing question;
- the S2 exposure (code 7, in service).

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public_statement), for Shane and Neil to check
'Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 23.2% in 2044, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with deliveries when we promised them.

What is done: the engine we developed with Rolls-Royce in our Joint Venture has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed on the terms we published. It shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence.

Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

We are not starting a new engine programme today. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.'

WHAT COULD CHANGE THIS
- Hold/hold cannot change.
- The statement and other moves change if any of these comes in:
  - Shane reports a fleet or safety-critical-part finding; it then leads the statement, with the plan;
  - Neil finds a line that books upside;
  - the Board flags a figure.
