ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo = hold; jv_with_rr = hold. premium_b is not my field; I expect 0. No Board item can arise.

(1) WHY
- gtf2_solo hold. It is the only value in brief §3.
  - GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 and has been ready since 2036. A cancel exists only until an engine is ready (rules), so it is gone.
  - launch and launch_if_selected are not offered. No live airframe is outside service: NGSA has been in service since 2037 and fps since 2040, so there is no EIS for a new engine to be ready by.
- jv_with_rr hold. The commitment stands. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw exists only before formation, so it is gone. From here the published terms, not an order, protect the gear and core.
- Grid: hold/hold in S1 (rivals hold) = -2.93 (97.3%). It is the only row and the only column, so nothing is weighed against hold.
- My cancel lever rule (report readiness, default hold) does not apply: cancel is not legal.

(2) JOINT VENTURE CLOSE-OUT, a private note to the Board (the round-2 four points)
(a) Gear and core stay one P&W module with P&W design authority: CONFIRMED on the record.
- The 2035 published terms say one P&W module, run by one P&W team, with design authority for the engine through certification [P-1233][P-1240].
- Rolls-Royce's public terms ('each side's technology protected') mirror ours.
- Nothing in the 2045 bulletin shows a hand-over. The brief holds no Joint Venture design file, so this rests on the terms and on the seat's own control of the module.
(b) No technology licence: CONFIRMED. The published terms say so, Rolls-Royce's terms mirror them, and no licence is on the record.
(c) GTF2's certification baseline was left untouched by the fold: CONFIRMED, on the private configuration freeze adopted in 2035 and on the schedule.
- The Joint Venture engine's ready year equals GTF2's own launch + 6 = 2036. It was not reset to formation + 6 = 2041 and not compressed below 2036.
- The brief holds no certification file, so this point is inference from the freeze and the date, not from a document.
(d) Ready in 2036: CONFIRMED by the bulletin ('formed 2035; engine ready 2036', 'inherits a folded solo programme's schedule').
- Accuracy note: the bulletin tags the engine 'in service since 2036'. On the board that is its ready year. It flew from NGSA's 2037 EIS, and P&W's NB share is unchanged at 24.0% in 2036. Public text should say 'ready since 2036, in service on NGSA since 2037', as Calio's draft does.
NOT CONFIRMED: that all life-limited parts were at full life at NGSA's 2037 EIS. That is my own standard [PX-0128]. The brief holds no LLP data, and I will not claim it.

How Rolls-Royce's technology ('we are actually bringing a technology') reaches the engine:
- Only as a derivative of the certified engine, on its own full test programme, severe-environment testing included, with all LLPs at full life at its own EIS.
- It enters either as a new build standard or as a certified kit at shop visits. That is the route the Hot Section kit took from the Advantage [PX-0088][PX-0106].
- Never through a licence, and never into the gear and core. Rolls-Royce holds its own geared IP [P-2004]. The two gear systems are not merged, and neither side's IP crosses into the other's module.
- No derivative spend without a live airframer need (Calio's 2050 rule). This board has no derivative order. Any such work is unpriced and stays off fleet engineers.
- The integrated-team rule [P-1240] still holds with two partners' content, but only if team boundaries follow module boundaries:
  - the gear-and-core integrated system stays one P&W team, with design authority;
  - Rolls-Royce's content sits in modules it owns, behind controlled interfaces;
  - one engine-level authority runs certification.
  If a derivative needs content across the gear-and-core boundary, the rule fails and I oppose that derivative (red line P-1233).
- Alignment: both partners are on the same engine. That is the condition Rolls-Royce named when it left IAE [P-1875].
- Risk, investment and revenue stay shared on the 49% partner model [P-1563]. Partner shops carry MRO capital [PX-0118][PX-0170] (seat doctrine).

(3) FLEET REPORT
- Plainly: the brief and bulletin hold no measured data for either fleet. There is no time on wing, no LLP life, no shop-visit count and no AOG count. I give no figure.
- What the brief does hold is delivery counts and shares. The board sets those from the airframe split and the engine moves, not from fleet performance; Rolls-Royce has matched us every year since 2037 under the equal-shares rule. So the share drift says nothing about durability, good or bad.
- I will not use 'it's the airframe split' to imply the fleet is fine. My bias is industrial-not-design [PX-0120], and the counter to it is that I have no data.
- No durability or safety-critical-part finding is in the brief, so nothing goes to Governance and Public Policy now. Any finding goes to that committee and the full Board before the 2050 orders, with the plan, and is disclosed early.
- The next report should carry, from measured data:
  - time on wing and shop-visit intervals split by environment, hot-and-harsh against cooler, because that is where GTF time on wing fell short [PX-0122];
  - LLP life against the full-life standard;
  - the AOG count;
  - fleet configuration, the share on the latest standard including the Hot Section kit [PX-0116].
- No dated recovery. Mine have slipped [PX-0115][PX-0128][P-0785], and so have Calio's [PX-0098][PX-0104].

(4) PACING PARTS AND CAPACITY: THE ORDER OF CALL
My bias is fleet lift first [PX-0123]. The company's 2024 practice put Airbus's OE needs first and sent the rest to the fleet [P-0162]. Calio balances the two with Airbus [PX-0099].
1. Safety-critical parts and any airworthiness action, on any fleet [PX-0035].
2. Lift for the in-service fleets: GTF fleet MRO, and support for the Joint Venture engine fleet on NGSA.
3. A320neo engine deliveries.
4. Joint Venture new-engine production for NGSA.
5. Derivative or development hardware: none live, so last.
Steps 2 to 4 are weighed daily and reviewed with Airbus on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0123][PX-0131]. The order is the tie-break ('the fleet beats a new engine'), not a starvation rule; NGSA new builds are still an Airbus commitment.
- Powder metal: capacity is added only with records discipline. The 2015 ramp is where the contaminant came in [P-1040][PX-0039].
- Castings: built up in steps and measured quarter by quarter [PX-0125].
- MRO slots: shops wait on parts, not capacity [PX-0124]. Partner shops carry the capital.
- The fall from 990 to 863 (brief §1): P&W NB engines go from 990 (2039) to 927 (2044) and 863 (2049-60).
  - OE draw on pacing parts falls by 127 engines a year from the peak (12.8%), and by 64 (6.9%) from 2044.
  - The installed base still grows every year and ages into heavier shop visits. The board shows 7,695 P&W NB deliveries in 2037-44; that is not a fleet count, since it has no GTF/Joint Venture split and no retirements.
  - Net: the fall eases OE draw at the margin. Whether it frees capacity for the fleet is not in the brief, and I give no count.
  - Do not cut powder-metal or castings capacity on the OE count.

(5) ENGINEERING LOAD
- No programme is in development. The last GTF2 spend went out in 2035.
- Hot Section kit: kept on offer at shop visits on the company's plan from 2026 [PX-0088][PX-0106]. It is mature, and it is fleet work, not new development.
- Joint Venture derivative work: none is ordered and none is on the board. Any that starts is study and test only, unpriced, and does not draw fleet engineers.
- Fleet support for the Joint Venture engine on NGSA in its first decade is first call on engineers. Early service is where the GTF found its issues.
- Nothing shown is pulling engineers off the fleet. The board charges P&W no strain, so this is advice only.

(6) VETO CHECKS ON hold/hold AND THE OTHER MOVES
- Ground 1, durability before EIS: PASS.
  - No order puts an engine on an airframe or compresses a programme.
  - The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 for NGSA's 2037 EIS.
  - The kit is a certified package offered at shop visits.
  - The derivative rule requires the derivative's own test programme before its own EIS.
  - The statement claims no durability.
- Ground 2, parts and capacity: PASS. The brief shows no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, and there is no launch.
- No binding veto.

(7) STATEMENT CHECK: passes all four of my rules, with one accuracy fix.
- No durability claim beyond the fleet record. It says 'we will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows', and it names standards without claiming them. Pass.
- No dated AOG recovery: 'we give no dated recovery'. Pass.
- No airframer dates, rates or shares. It gives no Boeing or Airbus share and does not attribute our drift to either. 'In service on NGSA since 2037' is a past public fact about our engine, not a forecast. Pass.
- No programme cost figures. Pass.
- FIX (advice, not binding): change 'the engine we developed with Rolls-Royce in our Joint Venture' to 'our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design'.
  - The engine is GTF2's certified design. 'Developed with Rolls-Royce' implies Rolls-Royce content in it, which cuts against point (c), and Rolls-Royce has said publicly 'we are actually bringing a technology'.
  - With the derivative suits open [PG-0039], keep the wording exact.
- Advice: 'If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan' is a promise I have to keep. I once said 'not a surprise coming' [PX-0112].

(8) 2050, STANDING
If the 2050 brief offers any engine order, my test is readiness by the EIS of a live airframe, not yet in service, that could select P&W. None exists today. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2056, the last NB year the board counts. My default proposal is hold.

tests.name: Architecture and the Joint Venture close-out (the Board's round-2 four points)

Ground 1: durability not proven before entry into service. If triggered, the team rule makes it binding.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Toward a ground-1 veto, or a statement that leads with a finding:
- Measured fleet data showing the Joint Venture engine or the GTF fleet short on time on wing or LLP life, especially in hot-and-harsh operation [PX-0122].
- Any safety-critical-part finding, for example in powder metal or castings.
Either goes to Governance and Public Policy and the full Board before the 2050 orders, leads the public statement with the plan, and blocks any durability wording the record does not support.

Toward opposing a derivative (red line, not a veto):
- A Joint Venture or UltraFan derivative that needs our gear or core, merges the gear systems, or comes by licence.
- A derivative entering service before its own test programme is complete.

Toward a ground-2 veto:
- A brief showing a live fleet, quality or supply problem: rising AOG, a quality escape, or a powder-metal or castings shortfall. The fleet then comes first, and any order that adds load fails.

Toward an engine order in 2050:
- Only a live airframe, not yet in service, that could select P&W, with the engine ready by its EIS. None exists today.

Hold/hold itself cannot change: the brief offers nothing else.
ops.memo:
The bad number first: I can't give you a fleet record. The brief has no time on wing, no life-limited-part life, no shop-visit or AOG count for the Joint Venture engine or the GTF fleet, and I won't fill one in. Nothing here proves full life at entry into service either.

What the record does show: the Joint Venture engine, the folded GTF2, was ready in 2036, a year ahead of NGSA's 2037 entry into service. The schedule held. Nothing was compressed or reset.

My proposal is gtf2_solo hold and jv_with_rr hold. The brief offers nothing else, and no live airframe is left to serve.

Joint Venture close-out: the gear and core stay one P&W module with design authority, there's no licence, and under the 2035 freeze the fold left GTF2's certification baseline alone. Rolls-Royce's technology comes in only as a derivative, tested on its own clock, and it never touches our gear and core.

Order of call: safety-critical parts first, then lift for both fleets, then A320neo deliveries, then NGSA new builds. We weigh it daily, with Airbus on the weekly drumbeat. Our deliveries fall from 990 to 863, but the installed base keeps growing, so we don't cut powder-metal or castings capacity.

One fix to the statement: say the engine carries GTF2's design, not that we developed it with Rolls-Royce.

No veto. My record is one day in June 2023, before the recall; the rest is the seat's doctrine. We earn the dependable engine reputation every day.

other_moves.move: GTF durability kit (Hot Section) for the installed fleet
other_moves.detail: We keep offering the Hot Section durability kit at shop visits. It is sold on standard terms, not given away [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. There are no launch-style discounts and no free upgrades [PX-0055]. We give no dated recovery of the AOG count: the brief has no count, and both Eddy's dated recoveries and mine have slipped before [PX-0098][PX-0104]. Mitchill passes it on ground 3 and Eddy passes it on ground 1, as a certified, mature package and fleet work rather than new development. It has no effect on the game board.

other_moves.move: Fleet report to the Board each round (replaces the GTF2 readiness report)
other_moves.detail:
Eddy reports each round on measured data for two fleets, the Joint Venture engine fleet on NGSA and the GTF fleet: time on wing and shop-visit intervals split by environment (hot-and-harsh against cooler) [PX-0122], LLP life against the full-life standard [PX-0128], the AOG count, and the share of the fleet on the latest configuration including the Hot Section kit [PX-0116].

THIS ROUND: the brief and bulletin hold none of these measures, so the report gives no figure. Full LLP life at NGSA's 2037 entry into service is NOT confirmed, because the brief holds no LLP data. The delivery shares are set by the airframe split and the equal-shares rule, so they say nothing about durability either way. We do not use the airframe-split reading to imply that the fleet is fine.

ESCALATION: any durability or safety-critical-part finding goes, with the plan, to Governance and Public Policy and the full Board before the 2050 orders, and is disclosed early [P-1360][P-1214][PG-0050]. No dated recovery is given.

other_moves.move: Order of call on pacing parts, shops and engineers
other_moves.detail:
Eddy's order, adopted:
1. Safety-critical parts and any airworthiness action, on any fleet [PX-0035].
2. Lift for the in-service fleets: GTF fleet MRO and support for the Joint Venture engine fleet on NGSA.
3. A320neo engine deliveries.
4. Joint Venture new-engine production for NGSA.
5. Derivative or development hardware. None is live.

Steps 2 to 4 are weighed daily and reviewed jointly with Airbus on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0099][PX-0123][PX-0131]. The order is a tie-break ('the fleet beats a new engine' [PX-0080]), not a starvation rule.
- Powder-metal capacity is added only with records discipline [P-1040].
- Castings are built up in steps and measured quarter by quarter [PX-0125].
- MRO slots are carried by the partner shops.
- P&W NB deliveries fall from 990 (2039) to 863 (2049 on), but the installed base keeps growing and ageing. So we do not cut powder-metal or castings capacity on the OE count, and we give no count of freed capacity.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture close-out note to the Board, and the derivative rule
other_moves.detail:
Eddy's four-point report, sent privately to the Board:
(a) The gear and core remain one P&W module with P&W design authority. CONFIRMED on the 2035 published terms [P-1233][P-1240], mirrored by Rolls-Royce's 'each side's technology protected'. No hand-over is on the record.
(b) No technology licence. CONFIRMED.
(c) GTF2's certification baseline was left untouched by the fold. CONFIRMED as an inference from the 2035 configuration freeze and from the ready year, 2036 = GTF2 launch + 6, neither reset to 2041 nor compressed. The brief holds no certification file.
(d) Ready in 2036. CONFIRMED by the bulletin. The bulletin's 'in service since 2036' is the ready year; the engine has flown since NGSA's 2037 entry into service.

DERIVATIVE RULE. Rolls-Royce's technology, or any merged Joint Venture or UltraFan content, reaches the engine only as a derivative of the certified engine:
- with its own full test programme, severe-environment testing included, and all LLPs at full life at its own entry into service;
- as a new build standard or a certified kit at shop visits;
- never through a licence, and never into the gear and core.
The integrated-team rule [P-1240] holds only while team boundaries follow module boundaries: the gear and core stay one P&W team with design authority, Rolls-Royce's content sits in modules it owns behind controlled interfaces, and one engine-level authority runs certification. A derivative that crosses the gear-and-core boundary is opposed under red line P-1233 and flagged to the Board.

Risk, investment and revenue stay shared on the 49% partner model [P-1563]. Rolls-Royce's technology is protected on the same terms as ours, and we keep the partner whole [PX-0038]. No derivative spend goes out without a live airframer need.

other_moves.move: Annual programme NPV review of GTF2 and the Joint Venture (Mitchill)
other_moves.detail:
ΔPV -2.93 = engine value -0.93 + R&D -2.00. The R&D is one undiscounted line, booked once in 2035 as the folded GTF2 share. Nothing has been charged since: no fresh $2B and no write-off.

Cash went out at about $0.33B a year in 2030-35. Discounted, that phasing would be about -1.09, and we book none of the difference.

Engine value against the status quo, nominal $B:
- level 2026-37;
- +0.1 in 2038, +0.3 in 2039, +0.1 in 2040;
- level 2041-42;
- then losses from 2043: -0.2, -0.3, -0.4, -0.6, -0.7, -0.8, then -1.0 a year in 2049-53 and -1.1 a year in 2054-56.
In PV terms the gains are +0.15 and the losses -1.12, a net -0.97 against the brief's -0.93 (rounding). That fits the board's 2056 NB cut.

Why the share drifts: P&W's NB share tracks Airbus's NB share at 0.317 pp per point (Mitchill's fit, exact to 0.1 pp for 2037-44). No P&W order reaches that.

LOOK-BACKS (inference, private):
- About +24.8 against being left off NGSA (-2.93 against -27.76). This is the top of the range, not a point estimate: round 2 showed that a Joint Venture without GTF2 could reach the same engine value, but only on events that were not on the record in 2030.
- +5.51 for the 2035 commit, read off the round-2 grid, for $0 of new R&D.

other_moves.detail:
New R&D in 2045 is $0, which is 0% of the ~$6B self-funded envelope [PX-0268]. The last GTF2 tranche, about $0.33B in 2035, was 5.5% of it. The dividend is covered and comes first [PX-0081]. Debt goes back to pre-ASR levels next [P-0686], then buybacks as the fill-in [P-0669].

The board carries no debt path, so Mitchill gives no date rather than invent one; he will report it at 2050 if that brief carries it. The Board's once-in-the-game envelope stretch was never used and has nothing to fund. At the 10% grid rate a buyback scores ΔPV 0, and it is the benchmark any future spend must beat.

other_moves.move: Standing 2050 rule
other_moves.detail:
No engine order unless a live airframe not yet in service selects P&W, on the public record, and the engine can be ready by its entry into service [P-0746][PX-0109].

A 2050 unconditional launch would be ready in 2056, the last NB year the board counts. At best it is worth about +$0.26B PV against $2.00B, an edge of at most -1.74 in every column, with no cancel round. Mitchill's ground 2 and the Board's Committed-airframe and Return-hurdle tests would both veto it.

launch_if_selected only where it is legal and a live airframe outside service could select us. Eddy's default 2050 proposal is hold.

decision.public_statement:
Let me start with what is not where we want it. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries was 23.2% in 2044, down from 24.8% in 2039. That is not where we want to be, and we will not buy it back with price. We earn it with time on wing, and with engines delivered when we promised them.

What is done: our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design, has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. The Joint Venture formed in 2035 on the terms we published. It shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney's gear and core remain our own module, with no technology licence, and each partner's technology is protected.

Control what you can control. The fleet is where this engine earns its place, and the fleet record is how we will be judged: time on wing, life-limited-part life and shop visits. We will report what that record shows, not what we hope it shows, and we give no dated recovery. If we find a durability or safety issue, we will say so early, with the plan. The GTF fleet, the new engine fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The GTF Hot Section durability kit stays on offer at shop visits, on standard terms. There are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

We are not starting a new engine programme today. Any new engine we commit will follow an airframer's selection. It will be ready six years from launch, with durability proven before entry into service. Our capital priorities have not changed: the dividend first, then debt, then share repurchase.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices.
decision.rationale:
THE DECISION: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr hold. premium_b 0. predictions S1 1.00. expected_pv_b -2.93. overrides empty. No Board item.

1. START FROM EDDY'S PROPOSAL. Eddy proposed hold/hold. It is the only row in brief §3.
- A cancel is gone: GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 and has been ready since 2036, and the rules allow a cancel only until an engine is ready.
- A withdraw is gone: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and the rules allow a withdraw only before formation.
- launch and launch_if_selected are not offered, and no live airframe is outside service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040).
I adopt the proposal unchanged.

2. STRIKE WHAT FAILS A BINDING VETO.
- Mitchill invoked one binding veto, on ground 3 (aggressive terms): any share-recovery or pricing campaign to close the Capitalise gap. I had already struck it in my frame, and it stays struck. It also fails my own rule, value not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The board does not price it, and it cannot reach the gap, which comes from the airframe split.
- Mitchill's ground 2 (on a 2050 launch) and ground 4 (on the final text) are standing conditions, not invoked. I checked the final statement against ground 4. It carries no share forecast, no dated recovery, no durability claim, no partner money, no look-back figure and no programme cost figure.
- Eddy invoked neither ground. Ground 1 passes: no order puts an engine on an airframe or compresses a programme, and the engine was ready in 2036 for NGSA's 2037 entry into service. Ground 2 passes: the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem.
- No colleague flagged a company red-line breach.

3. CONSTRAINT FIRST, THEN OPTIMISE [PX-0035].
- The safety and durability constraint now applies to the fleet, not to a launch. We claim no durability that the fleet record does not show, and the brief holds no record. Any finding goes to Governance and Public Policy and the full Board before the 2050 orders.
- Inside the constraint there is one row, so the optimum is hold/hold: -2.93 in S1, worst column -2.93, nothing against hold.

4. TIE-BREAKS.
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080], so I adopt Eddy's order of call. Steps 2 to 4 are weighed jointly with Airbus [PX-0099].
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] asks for nothing. The cycle was answered in 2030 and 2035, and no live airframe can still select us.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer.

5. PREMIUM AND OBJECTIVE.
- premium_b 0. No row differs from hold, so no doctrine or objective premium can arise, and the $1B cap is unused.
- Restore credibility: MET. The Joint Venture engine has been in service on NGSA, a new airframe, since 2037.
- Capitalise: NOT MET at -2.93. No order on the grid reaches it, and I will not chase it with price or terms.
- PV given up for either: $0.

6. ANNUAL PROGRAMME NPV REVIEW (Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own operating dates).
- ΔPV -2.93 = engine value -0.93 + R&D -2.00. The R&D is undiscounted, booked once in 2035, with no fresh share and no write-off since.
- Engine value against the status quo: small gains in 2038-40 (7.6 against 7.5, 7.9 against 7.6, 7.9 against 7.8), worth +0.15 PV. Losses from 2043 (8.1 against 8.3), reaching -1.0 a year by 2049-53, worth -1.12 PV. Net -0.97 on rounded figures against -0.93.
- The drift tracks Airbus's NB share at 0.317 pp per point. That attribution stays private; in public we speak for no airframer [PX-0062].
- Look-backs, inference and private. About +24.8 against being left off NGSA, which is the top of the range, not a point estimate. +5.51 for the 2035 commit, for $0 of new R&D.
- Answer to the shareowner: the $2B defended the franchise, and the residual gap is the airframe split.

7. WHAT CHANGED FROM MY FRAME. Two wording fixes to the statement, both advice and both taken:
- Eddy's and Mitchill's: 'our Joint Venture engine with Rolls-Royce, which carries GTF2's design', in place of 'the engine we developed with Rolls-Royce'. It keeps point (c) exact while the derivative suits are open [PG-0039].
- Mitchill's: 'formed on the terms we published' is printed only now that Eddy has confirmed points (a) to (c).
I also added the conditional, dated offer for any future engine: after an airframer's selection, ready six years from launch, durability proven before entry into service.

8. BIASES NAMED.
- Optimism on operating dates: the statement and the fleet report carry no dated recovery.
- Architecture loyalty: the airframe-split reading is supported by the bulletin, but we hold no fleet data, so I do not use it to say the fleet is fine.
- Partner discipline: Rolls-Royce is now a partner under strain, and its technology is protected on the same terms as ours [PX-0038].

9. RECORD VERSUS DOCTRINE.
- My own record grounds fleet first, value not share, the capital order and fast disclosure.
- The Joint Venture close-out and the derivative rule rest on company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1563] and on Eddy's engineering, not on my record (Low).

10. 2050. The standing rule is in other_moves. A 2050 unconditional launch would be ready in 2056 and fails Mitchill's ground 2 and the Board's tests. My 2050 default is hold unless a live airframe not yet in service selects P&W.

memo_weighing.cfo:

- He confirmed hold/hold at -2.93 in S1, the one column, with weight 1.00.
- He reconciled the NPV review: -0.97 on rounded figures against -0.93, the 2056 cut and the single 2035 R&D line.
- He confirmed no fresh $2B and no write-off.
- He tightened my share-drift arithmetic to an exact fit of 0.317 pp per point of Airbus share.
- He qualified the +24.8 look-back as the top of the range, not a point estimate, and I record it that way.
- His binding ground-3 veto on any pricing or share-recovery campaign is respected; the option was already struck.
- His ground 2 and ground 4 conditions are standing. I checked the final text against ground 4 and it passes.
- I took his two accuracy notes: 'carries GTF2's design', and printing 'formed on the terms we published' only after Eddy's confirmation.
- He gives no debt date because the board carries no debt path. I accept that rather than invent one.

memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed as binding on the technical grounds and as the best engineering read available. His seat's record is one event, June 2023, Low; the rest is seat doctrine, and I say so.
- I adopted his proposal (hold/hold), his four-point Joint Venture close-out and his derivative rule.
- I adopted his order of call. His bias is fleet lift first [PX-0123]; mine is to balance Airbus and the fleet jointly [PX-0099]. So steps 2 to 4 are weighed daily with Airbus as a tie-break, not a starvation rule.
- His plain fleet report, 'none in the brief, no figure', is preferred to an invented one.
- He was candid that full LLP life at NGSA's 2037 entry into service is not confirmed.
- His point (c), the certification baseline, rests on the 2035 freeze and the ready date, not on a file. I label it inference.
- Neither of his grounds is engaged. His standing conditions on durability claims, derivatives and capacity carry into 2050.
- I took his wording fix to the statement. I keep the promise to disclose early that he flagged, because fast disclosure is my record [PX-0030][PX-0034].

No date for any next build standard and no Joint Venture date. Nothing on any airframer's or Pratt & Whitney's plans, dates, rates or engine choices [RX-0053, RX-0296, R-1476, R-0970].

other_moves.detail: UltraFan technology keeps feeding the Trent fleet for time on wing, using public R&D money where available. No product launch, no ready date and no entry date. Qualitative only [RX-0094, RG-0065].

other_moves.detail: This carries over the 2035 support build: partner-shop agreements on our Singapore model, castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts, and the spares pool and field service stood up before NGSA's entry. Now scaled to the fleet: 914 RR-share narrowbody engines in 2045, 863 a year from 2049, about 8,600 delivered by end-2045 and about 13,000 by 2050. Field service sits near NGSA operators. The gap is the gear and core. To close it, we seek P&W's repair data, or a gear-and-core module-exchange pool, under the shared-risk terms, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops (the GTF fleet keeps first call on them). Capacity is advice, not a ground [RX-0283, RX-0286, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: Technical review rights and in-service reporting to the Board
other_moves.detail: We carry shared risk on a gear and core that P&W designs and certifies, with no technology licence. So we ask, under the shared-risk terms, for RR access to P&W's test, certification and fleet data. RR tracks time on wing and life-limited parts itself. Our engineers give their own view of maturity, from test and fleet evidence, not slides. Watson's in-service report goes to the Board before the 2050 orders, and any safety or durability flag goes to the Board at once [RG-0027, RX-0296, RX-0284].

other_moves.move: Off-grid shared-risk sizing on the Joint Venture engine (McCabe)
other_moves.detail: The reasonable worst case, on our own Trent 1000 precedent (£2.4bn of cash over seven years) at RR's 49% on P&W's published partner model, scaled to our fleet: about £1.2-2.9bn in total, with a peak year of about £0.3-0.7bn (7-19% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance). At twice that, about £5.7bn, peaking near £1.4bn, it still fits: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched, with extra distributions flexing first. It books nothing and is not a veto ground. It is rebased on any durability flag, or on time-on-wing or shop-visit data worse than plan [RG-0033, RX-0242, RX-0260].

other_moves.move: Capital frame held: no new programme spend
other_moves.detail: Nothing new is funded on the board this round. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the 30-40% dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. No equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0042, RX-0214, RX-0242, RG-0059].

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline
other_moves.detail: No price concessions on the Joint Venture engine or the Trent fleet. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee. Joint Venture terms stay shared risk and investment, with no RR funding of P&W's costs [RX-0097, RX-0081, R-1582].

UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061. We plan on the strain staying, and confirm it from the 2050 grid [R-1574, R-0361, RG-0068].

rolls_royce.public_statement: So, our narrowbody engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service, and our job now is the fleet. Safety is at the top. Then time on wing, full-life parts and support through our partner shops. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Widebody is our franchise. Durability work on the Trent fleet goes on, and there is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. UltraFan technology continues as technology. We are not starting a new programme this year. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
rolls_royce.rationale:
So, frankly, nothing on this grid adds cash, and we buy nothing. All four fields stay at hold. No Board item. Premium $0B.

1. Proposal. My framing lean was all four at hold. Both memos recommend the same orders.

2. Grid, each item against 'UltraFan NB: hold' (S1 / S2):
- Hold row (the submitted orders): +20.55 / +20.80. Best in both columns. Worst column +20.55.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade': +14.07 / +14.34. Item -6.48 / -6.46, which is $2B of bill + $5B of strain against +0.52 / +0.54 of engine value. Without strain it would still be about -1.48.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB': +11.55 / +12.78. Item -9.00 / -8.02, which is $4B + $5B against 0 / +0.98 of engine value. Ready in 2051 (2045 + 6), a year after S2's 2050 Re-engines enter service.
- The upgrade and UltraFan WB are exclusive, so no combined row.

3. Weights and expected scenario. S1 0.90 / S2 0.10, confirmed by McCabe. S2 needs both Re-engines and can be no likelier than its weaker leg. Boeing's '787 next step once this airplane is in service' is a signal (0.2). Airbus's 'the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus' is nothing (0.1).
- Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold.
- Hold EV: +20.58 (+20.59 on the Board's 0.85 / 0.15; +20.56 on 0.95 / 0.05).
- Upgrade item EV: -6.48 under any weights; row EV +14.10.
- UltraFan WB item EV: -8.90 (-8.85 on the Board's case); row EV +11.67.
- No sign changes under any weights: both widebody items are negative in both columns.

4. Binding vetoes.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature on `t1000_upgrade: launch` and `ultrafan_wb: launch`, on hurdle and unselected downside. Both are binding. Both are respected: neither is ordered.
- She invokes no balance-sheet veto. All-hold needs no funding. No narrowbody R&D remains: our $4.00B Joint Venture share and the $1.71B write-off were booked in 2035. We hold net cash, and leverage stays at or below about 1.5x.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto. His two conditions are met in this package. (a) The statement and the public other moves carry no new-engine date, no Joint Venture date and no date for any next build standard. (b) The in-service support plan and his report to the Board are carried as private other moves.
- `overrides` is empty.

5. Doctrine-favoured orders and premium.
- My record favours the Trent 1000 upgrade: 'do we believe we can regain market share? Absolutely' and 787 share 'Why not?' [RX-0101, RX-0117]. My rule keeps it only as a declared premium within $3B. Its shortfall is $6.48B, beyond the cap and over three times its own bill. Struck. Not at any price: we are not after market share [RX-0054, R-1582].
- UltraFan WB fails airframers first [RX-0058]. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing has named no UltraFan on a 787 Re-engine. Its $8.90B shortfall is far above both the $1B sub-cap and the $3B cap. Struck.
- Premium: $0B. The chosen row is the best row in both columns.

6. Red lines.
- No colleague flags a breach on the final orders.
- Watson notes that the red lines as written (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development; no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo) are not engaged by either widebody option, because no UltraFan is in development and no Solo is live. I accept that. On this board the strain is the economic form of 'one big programme at a time' [R-0929, R-1127]. It is priced in the grid, not deducted again.
- No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column. Both widebody items fail that test in both columns, so both stay at hold. That test is Board doctrine [RG-0033], not my record.
- Nothing is cancelled: no programme is in development and no cancel is offered.

7. Housekeeping, plainly.
- The 2045 withdrawal review is moot and closed: the Joint Venture formed in 2035.
- The 2035 widebody plan assumed the strain would lift once UltraFan NB left development. It did not: on this board the formed Joint Venture is a running narrowbody project. That assumption was wrong, and I say so.
- What the miss costs: without strain the upgrade would read about -1.48, a premium we could have chosen to declare inside $3B. With strain it is off the table.
- What the Joint Venture brought: 24.1% of NGSA engines from entry, both legs of the objective met, and the $2.29B of Solo spend not needed in 2036-37.

8. Off-grid, as the Board asked.
- Watson: the gearbox that flies is P&W's, under P&W's design authority, on GTF2's clock. It was ready in 2036 with no slip, RR was fitted at NGSA's entry (965 engines, 24.1%), and there is no durability or safety flag on the record. The board does not model time on wing or full-life parts, so he gives no number, and neither do I.
- His oversight note becomes a private move: RR technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data, and gear-and-core repair data or a module pool, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops.
- McCabe sizes our share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge at about £1.2-2.9bn, with a peak year of £0.3-0.7bn. Twice that still fits without equity, without leverage above about 1.5x and with the dividend untouched; extra distributions flex first. It books nothing.

9. Where my record is thin. Joint Venture terms and P&W are Low confidence for me (erginbilgic.md §6). On the gear and core, support and shop capacity I defer to Watson. On the shared-risk sizing I take McCabe's test as the evidence. The in-service oversight and the worst-case sizing are company doctrine and Board asks (profile.md §4; RG-0027, RG-0033), not my own words.

'Actually, I've seen this movie before': two programmes in parallel, and the strain eats the return. We control what we control: the fleet, durability and cash.

- CFM/GE holds. The ducted engine and Embraer stay in service, RISE stays as technology, and the GEnx upgrade keeps its 2.8 pp of widebody.
- P&W stays in the Joint Venture on its published terms. The GTF fleet keeps first call on its shops.
- The Joint Venture engine stays in service with no durability or safety flag on the record. Watson's in-service report reaches the Board before the 2050 orders.
- RR on hold: narrowbody share 21.6% from 2049; widebody 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. Both legs of the objective are met.
- The $5B strain stays on any widebody item in 2050, to be confirmed from that grid.
Expected ΔPV of the chosen orders: +20.58 $B on my weights (+20.59 on the Board's case). S1 outcome +20.55; S2 outcome +20.80.

board_response.recommendation: R3-1: Hold all four fields and say why in rationale: protect what is working.
board_response.response: Taken up in full. All four fields are at hold. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns: +20.55 / +20.80, +20.58 on our weights and +20.59 on yours. Both legs of the objective are met. Premium $0B. No Board item. The why is in rationale items 2-5.

board_response.recommendation: R3-2: Close the 2035 widebody plan; for 2050 bring a widebody item only with a Re-engine on the record and within its own bill and the caps.
board_response.response: Taken up. The plan is closed formally in a private move, and I admit plainly that it rested on the strain lifting, which it does not. The cost: without strain the upgrade would read about -1.48, inside the $3B cap; with strain it is -6.48. For 2050 the rule is a Re-engine on the record and a grid row within the item's own bill and the caps ($3B; $1B for UltraFan WB), with the upgrade first per Watson. Noted: UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061. McCabe makes an upgrade launched in 2050 about +0.28 of engine value against $7B of bill and strain.

board_response.recommendation: R3-3: Product safety in service: Watson to report the 2036 review on gearbox durability, time on wing and full-life parts, partner-shop support, and any flag.
board_response.response: Taken up. Watson reports that the gearbox in service is P&W's, under P&W's design authority, on GTF2's clock. It was ready in 2036 with no slip or reset, and RR was fitted at NGSA's entry at 24.1% (965 engines), holding equal shares with P&W through 2044. There is no safety or durability flag on the record. The board does not model time on wing or full-life parts, so he gives no figure. Two private moves answer the maturity point: RR technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data under the shared-risk terms, and gear-and-core repair data or a module-exchange pool, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops. RR tracks time on wing and life-limited parts itself. His in-service report, and any flag, reach you before the 2050 orders.

board_response.recommendation: R3-4: Precaution on shared risk: McCabe to size, off the grid, RR's share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge on the Joint Venture engine.
board_response.response: Taken up. McCabe bases it on our own Trent 1000 precedent (£2.4bn over seven years), taken at RR's 49% on P&W's published partner model and scaled to our fleet: about £1.2-2.9bn in total, with a peak year of about £0.3-0.7bn (7-19% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance). At twice that it still fits: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched, with extra distributions flexing first. It books nothing and is not a veto ground. She rebases it on any durability flag or on fleet data worse than plan.

board_response.recommendation: R3-5: Capital: no new programme spend; distributions from sustainable free cash flow in the capital-frame order; R&D broadly flat; Trent durability and UltraFan technology continue.
board_response.response: Taken up. No new programme spend on the board. The capital frame is held as a private move: balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. McCabe confirms it fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the post-2028 distribution plan. Trent durability (about £1bn over four years) and UltraFan as technology (public R&D money where available) continue as public, qualitative moves.

board_response.recommendation: R3-6: Widebody watch: the franchise test does not trigger; watch for a 787 next step and any A350 Re-engine in 2050; time on wing is the lever today.
board_response.response: Taken up. 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, with S2 at or above S1 (Watson). The test does not trigger. The 2050 watch is a private move: a Boeing 787 next step, any A350 Re-engine, and any further CFM widebody gain on our 5.2 pp of headroom. Watson puts the GEnx upgrade's 2.8 pp at about $0.53B of PV, already in the hold row. Time on wing on the Trent fleet is the lever we fund today; it is worth $0 on this grid but keeps the fleet earning.

board_response.recommendation: R3-7: Public statement, pricing and housekeeping: Joint Venture engine in service with durability and support first; no new-engine date, no Joint Venture date, nothing on airframers' or P&W's plans; 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine'; no price concessions; close the 2045 withdrawal review.
board_response.response: Taken up. The statement leads with safety, time on wing, full-life parts and partner-shop support. It carries no date of any kind and nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, and it keeps 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine' and 'We do not want to underestimate the risks'. Watson checked it for early dates. Pricing discipline is a private move: no concessions, and every contract through the Investment Committee. The 2045 Joint Venture withdrawal review is closed formally as moot: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdraw does not exist after formation.

board_response.recommendation: R2-1 (closing): zero margin at NGSA; the 2036 review to clear gearbox durability on test evidence; in 2045 report what it found and whether RR was fitted at entry.
board_response.response: Closed. After the fold the engine flew on GTF2's clock, ready in 2036 with one year of margin to NGSA's 2037 entry, better than the zero margin UltraFan alone carried. The review's subject became that engine, whose gear P&W designs. The record shows entry on schedule, RR fitted at entry (24.1%) and no flag. No 2036 date was ever put on an RR engine in public. The 2035 line 'ready in 2037' is superseded by the fold and is not repeated.

board_response.recommendation: R2-2 (closing): the 2045 withdrawal review: a sealed withdrawal unless the grid supports the commitment, in the same round as any widebody item; settle the fold question.
board_response.response: Closed as moot. P&W committed in 2035, so the Joint Venture formed that round and withdraw is not on the 2045 menu. The fold question is moot too. The strain concern did materialise, through the formed Joint Venture as a running project rather than through a later formation. That is why both widebody items stay at hold.

board_response.recommendation: R2-3 (closing): keep the private Joint Venture conditions: RR funds only its $4B share, a folded programme keeps its own test clock, no P&W gear or core change, support not counting on P&W's shops.
board_response.response: Kept. RR's R&D on the board is its $4.00B share. The $1.71B write-off is our own UltraFan spend before formation, not a P&W cost. No combined design was offered: the engine took GTF2's own clock with P&W's gear and core. Our support does not count on P&W's shops. The one gap, the gear-and-core module, is now addressed through repair data or a module pool under the shared-risk terms.

board_response.recommendation: R2-4 (closing): support and capacity: confirm the 2035 contracts placed, and the spares pool and field service standing in 2036; capacity is advice.
board_response.response: Confirmed by Watson. Partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model and the castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts were placed in 2035, and the spares pool and field service stood up in 2036, before NGSA's entry. They are now scaled to 914 narrowbody engines in 2045 and 863 a year from 2049, against 188 widebody. Capacity is recorded as advice.

board_response.recommendation: R2-5 (closing): cash: report the remaining Solo spend; if not spent, that saving is no reason to bring widebody spend beside the commitment.
board_response.response: Confirmed. The Joint Venture took GTF2's schedule, so the remaining $2.29B (about £1.68bn) of Solo spend was never needed. It is not redeployed into widebody: both widebody items stay at hold, and gross R&D stays broadly flat.

board_response.recommendation: R2-6 (closing): widebody franchise for 2045: bring the Trent 1000 upgrade first, against a Re-engine on the record or as a declared premium inside $3B; UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap.
board_response.response: Brought and priced, then held. The upgrade is -6.48 / -6.46 against hold because the $5B strain stays beside the formed Joint Venture. That is beyond its own $2B bill and the $3B cap, so it cannot be a declared premium, and McCabe withholds her signature. UltraFan WB has no Re-engine on the record and runs -9.00 / -8.02, far beyond the $1B sub-cap. Both are at hold. The watch carries to 2050.

board_response.recommendation: R2-7 (closing): pricing discipline; in later statements give no Joint Venture ready date and nothing beside any airframer's dates.
board_response.response: Kept. No concessions. This statement carries no Joint Venture date, no new-engine date and nothing on any airframer's dates.

priorities: Product safety comes first, and the engine is now in service. The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine has flown on NGSA since 2036, on the schedule it inherited from GTF2 (bulletin). What matters most to us now is the fleet: time on wing, full-life parts, and support through partner shops. Any safety or durability flag must reach us before the next round's orders. No date for a new engine goes public this round [RG-0027, RG-0025, RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0287].

Protect what is working. Both parts of the objective are met on hold. RR's narrowbody share is 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050. Its widebody share is 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns (+20.55 in S1, +20.80 in S2). Keeping either part needs no premium and no new programme. 'We won't do anything not profitable' [R-1561, R-1582, R-1005, R-1574].

One big programme at a time, and the strain is still in the grid. In 2035 we expected the Trent 1000 upgrade to come back in 2045 without strain, once UltraFan NB was out of development. The grid says otherwise. The Joint Venture counts as a running narrowbody project, so the $5B strain stacks on any widebody item (dashboard_game.md section 2). Against hold, the upgrade is -6.48 / -6.46 and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.02 (S1 / S2). Each loses more than its own bill and breaks the premium caps. Both stay at hold [RG-0019, RG-0033, R-0929, R-1127, RX-0214].

The balance sheet and returns. Narrowbody R&D is behind us: our $4B Joint Venture share and the $1.71B write-off are already booked. Cash follows the capital frame: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D stays broadly flat and Trent durability stays funded. No equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. This test does not apply unless McCabe invokes a balance-sheet veto [RX-0242, R-0900, R-0909, RG-0059, RG-0041, RX-0214].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: Risk aversion is 4 of 5 and time horizon 2.5 of 5. This round is about harvesting and protecting. The Joint Venture engine is in service and both parts of the objective are met on hold. We accept no new programme that can lose more than its own bill, and none on this grid passes. The balance-sheet test does not apply unless McCabe invokes a veto.
board_guidance.expect_to_see:
The package should contain the following.
(1) Grid rows. The row of the submitted orders and the row with each Board item at hold, column by column (S1 / S2). On all-hold that is 'UltraFan NB: hold' at +20.55 / +20.80. For a widebody item, its row against that row: 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' (+14.07 / +14.34) or 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' (+11.55 / +12.78).
(2) The CEO's expected scenario and `predictions`, with weights on S1 and S2 under the ExCo rule. Our illustrative case is S1 0.85, S2 0.15. Boeing said in 2035 it would look at the 787's next step once fps is in service, which is a signal for one Re-engine. Airbus's statement that the A350 family remains its focus is nothing on the other, and S2 needs both. All-hold is then +20.59 expected.
(3) McCabe. Her co-signature on any launch, her weights, the worst column for each item and capex a year. On all-hold, we want her to confirm three things: no narrowbody R&D remains; the plan fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the distribution plan after 2028; and leverage stays at or below about 1.5x. We also ask for an off-grid figure: our exposure under the Joint Venture's shared-risk terms to an in-service charge on the Joint Venture engine. It books nothing.
(4) Watson. His report should cover what the 2036 EIS-readiness review found on gearbox durability, and RR fitted at NGSA's entry (24.1% of narrowbody engines in 2037). It should also cover the Joint Venture engine's in-service time on wing and full-life parts, and support through our partner shops without relying on P&W's shops. For any widebody item, he should give the ready year (UltraFan WB 2051; the upgrade counts from 2048), the years of strain and the support plan.
(5) Both veto checks, with every red-line flag struck or rebutted in `rationale` and `overrides` empty.
(6) `premium_b` item by item. We expect $0 on all-hold.
(7) A public statement with no date for any new engine, no Joint Venture date and nothing on any airframer's dates.
(8) `board_response` to each round-2 recommendation. The 2045 withdrawal review should be closed formally: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, so it is moot.
If a figure is missing, we will compute it from the brief and say so.
would_approve: All four fields at hold. For `ultrafan_nb_solo` and `jv_with_pw`, hold is the only legal value, and the Joint Venture stands as formed. `ultrafan_wb` and `t1000_upgrade` also stay at hold. None of these is a Board item, and we never veto a hold. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns: +20.55 (S1) and +20.80 (S2), or +20.59 on our illustrative case (S1 0.85, S2 0.15). Both parts of the objective are met (narrowbody 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050; widebody at least 55.2%). Premium is $0B.

Qualitative other moves raise no Board item and we would support them: Trent fleet durability (time on wing, about £1bn over four years); UltraFan technology funded as technology, using public R&D money where it is available; in-service support for the Joint Venture engine; and pricing discipline. They change no payoff on the grid.
would_veto: `t1000_upgrade: launch`. Its item value ('UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') is -6.48 (S1) and -6.46 (S2), so -6.48 under any weights. It fails the reasonable worst case: both columns are below minus its $2B bill, because the $5B strain stacks on the bill while the Joint Venture runs. It fails declared premium: the $6.48B shortfall is above the $3B cap for the round. Without strain it would still be about -1.48 (inference: +0.52 of engine value against $2B of R&D), so it does not pay even then. The company's one-programme rule is not engaged as written, since no UltraFan is in development, but the strain is the cost of running a second programme beside the Joint Venture. Acceptable alternative: `hold` [RG-0033, RG-0068, R-1574, RX-0214, R-1127].

`ultrafan_wb: launch`. Its item value ('UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold') is -9.00 (S1) and -8.02 (S2), or -8.85 on our case. It fails the airframe test: no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record. S2 is a grid column, not the record, and Boeing's 2035 remark on the 787's next step is a signal, not a launch. It fails declared premium: the shortfall is far above both the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap and the $3B cap. It fails the reasonable worst case: S1 at -9.00 is below minus its $4B bill. Even in S2 it would be ready in 2051 against Re-engines in service in 2050, and would earn about +0.98 against $9B of R&D and strain. Acceptable alternative: `hold` [R-1574, R-1005, RG-0033, RG-0021, R-0929].

Any Board item that lacks McCabe's co-signature (as defined in our profile), or that comes in a package where a binding ExCo veto went unrespected, a red-line flag is left unresolved or `overrides` is not empty. Acceptable alternative: `hold` [RX-0213, R-1579, RG-0044].

recommendations.text: Hold all four fields and say why in `rationale`: this round we protect what is working. The Joint Venture engine is in service, both parts of the objective are met on hold, and 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns. The CEO has our total support for this frame.

Close the 2035 widebody plan. We recommended then that the Trent 1000 upgrade come back in 2045, once UltraFan NB was out of development, against a Re-engine or as a declared premium inside $3B. That rested on the strain lifting, and the grid shows it does not: the Joint Venture is a running narrowbody project, so the $5B strain stays on any widebody item for the rest of the game. For 2050, bring a widebody item only if a Re-engine is on the record and the grid puts the item within its own bill and the caps. Note that UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061.

Product safety in service. Watson should report four things. First, what the 2036 EIS-readiness review found on gearbox durability. Second, the Joint Venture engine's time on wing and full-life parts since 2036. Under P&W's published terms, P&W held design authority through certification, so we want our own view of maturity. Third, support through our partner shops on the Singapore model: P&W has said the GTF fleet has first call on its shops. Fourth, any safety or durability flag, which must reach us before the next round's orders. 'We have a moral obligation to do these things properly.'

Precaution on shared risk. McCabe should size, off the grid, RR's share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge on the Joint Venture engine under its shared-risk terms. P&W's published terms cite partners carrying 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge. She should confirm that it fits without equity, without leverage above about 1.5x and without touching the dividend. It books nothing and is not a veto ground.

Capital. No new programme spend this round. Distributions should come from sustainable free cash flow, after the cash needs of the business, in the order of the capital frame: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then extra distributions. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. Trent durability (about £1bn over four years) continues, and UltraFan technology continues as technology, using public R&D money where available.

Widebody watch. The franchise test does not trigger. Our share is 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, and no rival-engined Re-engine is on the record. The GEnx upgrade has taken 2.8 pp since 2042. In 2050, watch for a 787 next step from Boeing and any A350 Re-engine. Time on wing on the Trent fleet is the lever we hold today.

The public statement, pricing and housekeeping. The statement should cover the Joint Venture engine in service, with durability and support first. It should give no date for any new engine and say nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, and it should keep 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine'. 'We do not want to underestimate the risks.' Make no price concessions. Formally close the 2045 Joint Venture withdrawal review: the Joint Venture formed in 2035.

frame.question: So, the 2045 question, in cash and quality of earnings. The Joint Venture engine is in service and is now a business. On hold the board gives us +20.55 (S1) and +20.80 (S2), and both legs of the objective are met. The question is whether anything on this grid adds cash. It does not. The Joint Venture counts as a running narrowbody project, so the $5B strain sits on top of either widebody item. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.48 / -6.46 against hold, and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.02. Each loses more than its own bill in both columns, under any weights. So this round is about harvesting and protecting what we have: the fleet, the Joint Venture engine's durability and support, and the Trent franchise. We fund durability, not new engines. We are not after market share [RX-0054, R-1582]. We won't do anything not profitable [RX-0058].
frame.situation:
Public record, 2045.
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, in service since 2037, code 7 (RR, PW and CFM). Fitted: CFM + PW + RR.
- fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on the 10-year path, in service since 2040, code 3 (CFM).
- Joint Venture with P&W: formed 2035, when both of us committed. Our UltraFan NB Solo and P&W's GTF2 folded in. The engine took GTF2's schedule and has been in service since 2036.
- P&W's published terms: shared risk, investment and revenue on the partner model under which partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge. P&W's gear and core stay its own module, and it keeps design authority through certification. There is no technology licence. The GTF fleet has first call on P&W's shops.
- Rivals: CFM ducted engine in service since 2036, CFM-Embraer since 2037, RISE kept as technology. The GEnx upgrade has been in service since 2033 and has counted since 2042, taking 2.8 pp of widebody from us (58.0% to 55.2%).
- Widebody: no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record. Boeing says it will look at the 787's next step once fps is in service. That is a signal for a 787 Re-engine, not a launch, and Boeing has named no engine. Airbus says the A350 family, including the A350F, remains its focus: nothing toward a Re-engine.
- Observed 2044: narrowbody engines CFM 53.7 / P&W 23.2 / RR 23.2; widebody engines CFM/GE 44.8 / RR 55.2.

Our position on hold: ΔPV +20.55 $B, yield 118.68%.
- Components: engine value +26.26; R&D -4.00 (our Joint Venture share); write-offs -1.71 (UltraFan NB spend beyond our share). All of it was booked in 2035. No narrowbody R&D remains on the board (Helen to confirm).
- RR narrowbody engines: 965 in 2037, a peak of 990 in 2039, 914 in 2045, 863 a year from 2049. Our share drifts down from 24.8% to 21.6% as fps gains on CFM only. That is airframe mix, not a lever we hold.
- Widebody engines: 188 a year from 2042.
- The board counts narrowbody to 2056 and widebody to 2061.

Objective: both legs met on hold.
- Narrowbody entry: 22.9% in 2045, 21.6% in 2050.
- Widebody dominance: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. The worst year is 55.2%, 5.2 pp of headroom.
- The S2 hold row is +0.25 above S1, which I read as no loss of widebody share in S2 (inference; Rob to confirm against the 50% line).

Grid, each item against 'UltraFan NB: hold' (S1 / S2):
- T1000 upgrade: -6.48 / -6.46. That is the $2B bill plus the $5B strain against about +0.52 / +0.54 of engine value.
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.02. That is the $4B bill plus the $5B strain against 0 / +0.98 of engine value. It would be ready in 2051, after S2's Re-engines enter service in 2050.

Housekeeping: the 2045 withdrawal review set in 2035 is moot, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035; I close it formally. The 2035 widebody plan (bring the upgrade back once UltraFan NB was out of development) assumed the strain would lift. The grid shows it does not, so I close that plan too.

Board guidance (risk aversion 4 of 5, horizon 2.5): it would approve all four fields at hold, with premium $0B. It would veto `t1000_upgrade: launch`, `ultrafan_wb: launch`, and any item lacking McCabe's co-signature or sitting in a package with an unrespected veto, an unresolved red-line flag or non-empty overrides.

cfo.memo:
We've always said safety, then we said the balance sheet. This round we harvest and protect.

Weights: I confirm S1 0.90 / S2 0.10. S2 needs both Re-engines, so it can be no likelier than its weaker leg. The Board's 0.85 / 0.15 changes no sign.

All-hold: +20.55 / +20.80, +20.58 expected (+20.59 on the Board's case). Best row in both columns, worst column +20.55, premium $0B. No narrowbody R&D remains: our $4.00B share and the $1.71B write-off were booked in 2035.

I withhold my signature on the Trent 1000 upgrade: -6.48 / -6.46 against hold, over three times its $2B bill. That is $2B of bill and $5B of strain against +0.52 of engine value. I withhold it on UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.02, -8.90 expected, against a $4B bill. The grid confirms the strain, and the rules give the Joint Venture no end date as a running project. Plan on it for 2050.

Off the grid, our own Trent 1000 experience is the reasonable worst case: £2.4bn over seven years. At 49%, scaled to our fleet, our share is about £1.2-2.9bn, peak year £0.3-0.7bn, 7-19% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance. Twice that still fits: no equity, net cash kept, the dividend untouched; extra distributions flex first. It books nothing.

My record is thin on engine-launch economics and the Joint Venture: these are the board's numbers. So hold it this way: nothing new out, durability funded, cash in the frame. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture engine (in service; reported for the Board)
tests.threshold: Formation + 6, or earlier at a folded programme's bulletin date. It must be ready by the EIS of the airframe it serves. Zero margin is a pass with a note.
tests.numbers: Formed 2035. Formation + 6 on its own would be 2041. The bulletin shows it ready in 2036, inheriting GTF2's schedule (GTF2 launched 2030, + 6 = 2036). UltraFan NB (2030 + 7 = 2037) folded in. NGSA: launched 2030, EIS 2037, so 1 year of margin, better than the zero margin UltraFan NB carried alone. Fitted at NGSA's entry, as the CEO asked me to confirm: RR at 24.1% of narrowbody engines in 2037 (965 engines), P&W equal at 24.1%, CFM at 51.7%. Then 978 in 2038, the 990 peak in 2039, 914 in 2045 and 863 a year from 2049 (brief's year table). fps: launched 2030 on the 10-year path, EIS 2040, code 3 (CFM), so RR is not selected. No live narrowbody airframe is left (both are in service), so no further narrowbody readiness test applies. My 2035 condition held: the engine flew on GTF2's own clock with no new combined design and nothing compressed.

tests.name: In-service report: Joint Venture engine gearbox, time on wing, full-life parts and flags (the Board's ask; reported, not scored)
tests.threshold: Report test and fleet evidence, not slides. Any safety or durability flag reaches the Board before the 2050 orders.
tests.numbers:
Which gearbox flies: Pratt & Whitney's. The engine took GTF2's schedule. P&W's published terms keep the gear and core as P&W's own module, under P&W design authority through certification, with no technology licence. So the gearbox in service is neither an UltraFan gearbox nor UltraFan fitted with P&W's gear.

The 2036 EIS-readiness review: our plan built it to clear UltraFan's gearbox durability for 2037. After the fold, its subject became the GTF2-clock engine, whose gear we do not design. What the record shows: ready in 2036 on its own clock, with no slip and no reset; RR fitted at NGSA's 2037 entry; equal shares with P&W from 24.1% down to 23.2% through 2044, so no loss of fitment; and no durability or safety event on the public record. Inference: the review cleared entry.

Time on wing and full-life parts: the board does not model them and the brief gives no figure, so I give none. P&W set both as GTF2's standards, to be proven on test before entry (2035 bulletin).

Fleet exposure (brief's year table): about 7,700 RR-share engines delivered 2037-2044, about 8,600 by the end of 2045 and about 13,000 by 2050.

Safety or durability flag: none on the record.

Oversight note (not a flag, not a veto): RR carries shared risk on P&W's partner model, under which partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge, on a gear and core it does not design. Our own engineers' view of maturity is only as good as our access to P&W's test, certification and fleet data. Recommendation: RR technical review rights on that data under the shared-risk terms, with findings to the Board before the 2050 orders.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan WB (option C, if launched)
tests.threshold: Ready at launch + 6. It counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service, so it must be ready by a Re-engine's EIS. A fail is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers: Launched 2045, ready 2051. S1: no Re-engine is on the record, so it never counts: 0 of engine value against the $4B bill + $5B strain = -9.00. S2: both Re-engines launched 2045 enter service in 2050, so UltraFan WB is a year late. It counts from 2051 to the board's 2061 end for +0.98, giving -8.02. Launched in 2050 instead, it is ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061. This is advice: the engine is simply not counted, and McCabe prices the downside. Recommended order: hold.

tests.name: Readiness: Trent 1000 upgrade (option B, if launched)
tests.threshold: Counts at launch + 3, and not before the first Re-engine's EIS (2042 if neither re-engines). No maturity ground on a durability standard for a fleet in service.
tests.numbers: Launched 2045, it counts from 2048; the 2042 floor has passed. The grid's +0.52 (S1) / +0.54 (S2) of engine value matches about 17 widebody engines a year from 2048 on the dashboard economics (my arithmetic, inference), so it counts from 2048 in both columns. It would be retrofitted at shop visits on the model of the June 2025 Trent 1000 package (fleet retrofit within two years). Readiness passes. Its value of -6.48 / -6.46 against hold is McCabe's test; my engineering-load test flags the strain. Recommended order: hold.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 6 (UltraFan WB), launch + 3 (the upgrade's benefit) or the Joint Venture's bulletin date. Nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans (company red line).
tests.numbers: The draft statement gives no date for any engine. 'In service' is the public record, not a date. It gives no Joint Venture date and says nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. 'No new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine' is our own spending condition, not an airframer's plan. If an option were ordered: nothing for UltraFan WB before 2051 (2045 + 6), and nothing for the upgrade's benefit before 2048. The 2035 line 'ready in 2037, seven years from launch' is superseded by the fold, so don't repeat it. Put no date on any next build standard of the Joint Venture engine or on any UltraFan product.

tests.threshold: A support plan through partner shops before any narrowbody EIS (inference). For an engine in service, support scales with the fleet (advice).
