tests.threshold: A narrowbody project beside a widebody project costs $5B of strain; flag the years of overlap. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (seat and company rule, inference).
tests.numbers:
All four at hold: no widebody project, strain $0, 0 years of overlap.

Confirmed: the board treats the Joint Venture as a running narrowbody project even with its engine in service. The grid splits exactly:
- upgrade: -2 bill - 5 strain + 0.52 = -6.48 (S1); + 0.54 = -6.46 (S2);
- UltraFan WB: -4 - 5 + 0 = -9.00 (S1); + 0.98 = -8.02 (S2).

Overlap if ordered: the upgrade 2045-48 (3 years) and UltraFan WB 2045-51 (6 years), each beside the Joint Venture. The $5B is charged once either way. The Joint Venture runs to the board's end (narrowbody is counted to 2056), so I expect the strain on any widebody item in 2050 too (inference; the 2050 grid will confirm).

Red lines as written are not engaged: no UltraFan is in development and no NB Solo is live, so neither option would be a red-line breach. The strain is the cost.

My 2035 plan (bring the upgrade back in 2045, without strain) assumed the strain would lift. It does not, so I withdraw it. The 2035 fold question is moot: the Joint Venture formed in 2035.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable unless the brief reports a constraint. Partner MRO and supplier needs are advice.
tests.numbers:
Brief, on hold: 914 narrowbody + 188 widebody = 1,102 engines in 2045; 863 + 188 = 1,051 a year from 2049; 990 + 197 = 1,187 at the 2039 peak. Narrowbody is 4.9 times widebody in 2045 and 4.6 times from 2049. RR-share narrowbody engines delivered: about 8,600 by the end of 2045 and about 13,000 by 2050. No constraint is reported.

Advice: partner shops on the Singapore model for the narrowbody shop-visit load; high-performing suppliers for castings, forgings and life-limited parts; a gear and core module pool.

Shop visits: I use my CMD figure of 1,100-1,200 a year (widebody era), not Helen's 1,400-1,500; the two were never reconciled. The narrowbody fleet adds a load that neither figure covers and the board does not model.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
S1 on hold: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050. The worst year is 55.2%, 5.2 pp of headroom.

S2: the brief gives no shares by year. S2 moves only the widebody airframes, the widebody engine market is fixed at 340 a year, and the hold row is +0.25 above S1. So RR's widebody value is at least as high, and its share at or above S1's 55.2%, above the 50% line (inference). I confirm the CEO's reading.

The GEnx upgrade's 2.8 pp is 197 to 188 engines, 9 a year, worth about $0.53B of PV at 2026 by my arithmetic on the dashboard economics (inference). It is already in the hold row. The upgrade would win back about 17 engines a year from 2048 for +0.52, at $7B of bill and strain.

Time on wing is worth $0 on this grid, because it moves no share on the board. Off the grid it keeps the Trent fleet flying and earning, and it is what wins the next campaign (inference).

A further CFM widebody move the size of the GEnx upgrade would leave about 52.4%, still above 50% (inference).

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: An idle or folded UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively only; no grid value is adjusted.
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB folded into the Joint Venture in 2035. Its technology is protected under our terms and keeps feeding the Trent fleet for time on wing, with public R&D money where available. It is no argument for any widebody launch. No grid value is changed.

vetoes.plan: A: all four at hold (`ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`)
vetoes.ground:
None invoked. No engine is launched, triggered or committed, so no maturity can be compressed. My concurrence at the veto check rests on two things.
(a) The final statement and the public other moves carry no new-engine date and no Joint Venture date.
(b) The Joint Venture engine's in-service support is carried as a private other move: partner shops on the Singapore model, the spares pool, field service, gear and core repair data or a module-exchange pool under the shared-risk terms, without relying on P&W's shops; and the in-service report goes to the Board before the 2050 orders.
If (a) failed, ground (a) would apply and the team rule would make the veto binding. Dropping (b) is not a veto ground this round, because no narrowbody EIS lies ahead. I would flag it to the Board as a support concern. These grounds rest on attributed transcript turns.

vetoes.plan: Draft public statement ('our narrowbody engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service ... no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine ... not starting a new programme this year')
vetoes.ground: It passes the early-date test, so the veto is not invoked. It gives no engine date, no Joint Venture date, and nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans. Adding any new-engine date, or a date for a next build standard of the Joint Venture engine, would be ground (a), and the team rule would make it binding. Rests on attributed turns.

vetoes.plan: B: `t1000_upgrade: launch`
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. It passes readiness: it counts from 2048. The company red line (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development) is not engaged as written, because no UltraFan is in development. Engineering-load flag: 3 years beside the Joint Venture (2045-48) and $5B of strain, for -6.48 / -6.46 against hold, below minus its own $2B bill in both columns. That is McCabe's ground and the Board's, not mine. Nobody wants those HP turbine blades more than I do, but not at this price. Advice only.

vetoes.plan: C: `ultrafan_wb: launch`
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground on its own. It fails 'Ready by EIS' as advice: ready 2051, with no Re-engine on the record, and a year after S2's 2050 Re-engines. Engineering-load flag: 6 years beside the Joint Venture (2045-51) and $5B of strain, for -9.00 / -8.02 against hold. The overlap red line (UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo) is not engaged, because no Solo is live. It would become a binding Civil ground only if the statement or the rationale gave or counted a ready date before 2051. Advice only.

vetoes.plan: Joint Venture engine in service (Board note on shared risk and the gear and core)
vetoes.ground: Not a veto, and not a durability flag: there is no defect evidence on the record. Oversight note for the Board. RR carries shared risk on P&W's partner model, under which partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge, on a gear and core under P&W design authority with no technology licence. Our own view of maturity, and our partner shops' ability to support that module without P&W's shops, depend on access to P&W's test, fleet and repair data. Ask for it under the shared-risk terms, and report the findings to the Board before the 2050 orders.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Civil veto, binding under the team rule, in either of two cases:
- the final statement or a public other move gives any new-engine date (UltraFan WB before 2051 if launched; the upgrade's benefit before 2048) or a date for a next build standard of the Joint Venture engine;
- the rationale counts any engine before its ready year.

Board flag, not a veto: the orders drop the Joint Venture engine's in-service support (partner shops, spares pool, field service, gear and core repair data or a module pool), or the in-service report to the Board.

A durability or safety finding on the Joint Venture engine, from P&W's test or fleet data, on the gear, the core or life-limited parts. That changes the support plan, the statement and the Board report before the 2050 orders, not these orders.

I would back the Trent 1000 upgrade in 2050, first among the widebody items, in any of three cases:
- the grid puts it within its own $2B bill;
- a rival-engined Re-engine on the record threatens the 50% line;
- the projection falls toward 52%.

UltraFan WB only against an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with Boeing naming UltraFan, with a row within its bill and the $1B sub-cap. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count.

A named airline win on the Joint Venture engine would firm up the support build.
ops.memo:
The Joint Venture engine is flying and earning. It was ready in 2036 on GTF2's own clock, launch plus six, with nothing compressed. We were fitted on NGSA from 2037: 24.1%, 965 engines, and 990 at the 2039 peak. The gearbox that flies is Pratt's, under Pratt's design authority. Our 2036 review was built for UltraFan's gearbox. The record shows entry on schedule and no durability or safety flag through 2044. This board doesn't measure time on wing or full-life parts, and I won't give the Board a number that test and fleet data don't hold.

One note for the Board. We carry shared risk on a gear and core we don't design. We need our own access to Pratt's test and fleet data, plus repair data or module exchange, so our partner shops can support that module without Pratt's shops.

Support: partner shops on our Singapore model, a spares pool and field service. That's 914 narrowbody engines this year and 863 a year from 2049, against 188 widebody. Capacity is advice.

Widebody: 58.0% in 2040, then 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. The 50% line holds in both columns.

Strain: the Joint Venture is a running narrowbody project on this board. I said the upgrade comes back in 2045. At -6.48 it can't. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2051, with no Re-engine to fly it: -9.00.

All four at hold. No Civil veto. We're keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture engine in service: safety, durability and support first
other_moves.detail: The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA. Our priorities for it, in order: safety, then time on wing and full-life parts, then support through our partner shops. No date for any next build standard and no Joint Venture date. Nothing on any airframer's or Pratt & Whitney's plans, dates, rates or engine choices [RX-0053, RX-0296, R-1476, R-0970].

other_moves.move: Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded
other_moves.detail: About £1bn over four years, kept apart from UltraFan money and inside a broadly flat R&D envelope. This is not the t1000_upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0123, RX-0246, RX-0214].

other_moves.move: UltraFan technology continues as technology
other_moves.detail: UltraFan technology keeps feeding the Trent fleet for time on wing, using public R&D money where available. No product launch, no ready date and no entry date. Qualitative only [RX-0094, RG-0065].

other_moves.move: Joint Venture in-service support plan (Watson)
other_moves.detail: This carries over the 2035 support build: partner-shop agreements on our Singapore model, castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts, and the spares pool and field service stood up before NGSA's entry. Now scaled to the fleet: 914 RR-share narrowbody engines in 2045, 863 a year from 2049, about 8,600 delivered by end-2045 and about 13,000 by 2050. Field service sits near NGSA operators. The gap is the gear and core. To close it, we seek P&W's repair data, or a gear-and-core module-exchange pool, under the shared-risk terms, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops (the GTF fleet keeps first call on them). Capacity is advice, not a ground [RX-0283, RX-0286, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: Technical review rights and in-service reporting to the Board
other_moves.detail: We carry shared risk on a gear and core that P&W designs and certifies, with no technology licence. So we ask, under the shared-risk terms, for RR access to P&W's test, certification and fleet data. RR tracks time on wing and life-limited parts itself. Our engineers give their own view of maturity, from test and fleet evidence, not slides. Watson's in-service report goes to the Board before the 2050 orders, and any safety or durability flag goes to the Board at once [RG-0027, RX-0296, RX-0284].

other_moves.move: Off-grid shared-risk sizing on the Joint Venture engine (McCabe)
other_moves.detail: The reasonable worst case, on our own Trent 1000 precedent (£2.4bn of cash over seven years) at RR's 49% on P&W's published partner model, scaled to our fleet: about £1.2-2.9bn in total, with a peak year of about £0.3-0.7bn (7-19% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance). At twice that, about £5.7bn, peaking near £1.4bn, it still fits: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched, with extra distributions flexing first. It books nothing and is not a veto ground. It is rebased on any durability flag, or on time-on-wing or shop-visit data worse than plan [RG-0033, RX-0242, RX-0260].

other_moves.move: Capital frame held: no new programme spend
other_moves.detail: Nothing new is funded on the board this round. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the 30-40% dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. No equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0042, RX-0214, RX-0242, RG-0059].

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline
other_moves.detail: No price concessions on the Joint Venture engine or the Trent fleet. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee. Joint Venture terms stay shared risk and investment, with no RR funding of P&W's costs [RX-0097, RX-0081, R-1582].

other_moves.move: Housekeeping: two 2035 plans formally closed
other_moves.detail: (1) The 2045 Joint Venture withdrawal review is closed as moot. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdraw does not exist after formation. Watson's question on folding an already-ready UltraFan is moot for the same reason. (2) The 2035 widebody plan is closed: it would have brought back the Trent 1000 upgrade in 2045 without strain. The Joint Venture counts as a running narrowbody project on this board, so the $5B strain stays on any widebody item. That plan rested on an assumption that proved wrong, and we say so plainly [RX-0077, R-1573].

other_moves.move: 2050 widebody watch
other_moves.detail: In 2050 we watch for a Boeing 787 next step and any A350 Re-engine on the record, and any further CFM widebody gain on our 5.2 pp of headroom above 50%. A widebody item comes to the ExCo only with a Re-engine on the record and a grid row within its own bill and the caps ($3B; $1B for UltraFan WB). The Trent 1000 upgrade comes first, per Watson. UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061. We plan on the strain staying, and confirm it from the 2050 grid [R-1574, R-0361, RG-0068].

decision.public_statement: So, our narrowbody engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service, and our job now is the fleet. Safety is at the top. Then time on wing, full-life parts and support through our partner shops. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Widebody is our franchise. Durability work on the Trent fleet goes on, and there is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. UltraFan technology continues as technology. We are not starting a new programme this year. Cash goes first to the balance sheet, then to the dividend, then to distributions from sustainable free cash flow. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, frankly, nothing on this grid adds cash, and we buy nothing. All four fields stay at hold. No Board item. Premium $0B.

1. Proposal. My framing lean was all four at hold. Both memos recommend the same orders.

2. Grid, each item against 'UltraFan NB: hold' (S1 / S2):
- Hold row (the submitted orders): +20.55 / +20.80. Best in both columns. Worst column +20.55.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade': +14.07 / +14.34. Item -6.48 / -6.46, which is $2B of bill + $5B of strain against +0.52 / +0.54 of engine value. Without strain it would still be about -1.48.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB': +11.55 / +12.78. Item -9.00 / -8.02, which is $4B + $5B against 0 / +0.98 of engine value. Ready in 2051 (2045 + 6), a year after S2's 2050 Re-engines enter service.
- The upgrade and UltraFan WB are exclusive, so no combined row.

3. Weights and expected scenario. S1 0.90 / S2 0.10, confirmed by McCabe. S2 needs both Re-engines and can be no likelier than its weaker leg. Boeing's '787 next step once this airplane is in service' is a signal (0.2). Airbus's 'the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus' is nothing (0.1).
- Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold.
- Hold EV: +20.58 (+20.59 on the Board's 0.85 / 0.15; +20.56 on 0.95 / 0.05).
- Upgrade item EV: -6.48 under any weights; row EV +14.10.
- UltraFan WB item EV: -8.90 (-8.85 on the Board's case); row EV +11.67.
- No sign changes under any weights: both widebody items are negative in both columns.

4. Binding vetoes.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature on `t1000_upgrade: launch` and `ultrafan_wb: launch`, on hurdle and unselected downside. Both are binding. Both are respected: neither is ordered.
- She invokes no balance-sheet veto. All-hold needs no funding. No narrowbody R&D remains: our $4.00B Joint Venture share and the $1.71B write-off were booked in 2035. We hold net cash, and leverage stays at or below about 1.5x.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto. His two conditions are met in this package. (a) The statement and the public other moves carry no new-engine date, no Joint Venture date and no date for any next build standard. (b) The in-service support plan and his report to the Board are carried as private other moves.
- `overrides` is empty.

5. Doctrine-favoured orders and premium.
- My record favours the Trent 1000 upgrade: 'do we believe we can regain market share? Absolutely' and 787 share 'Why not?' [RX-0101, RX-0117]. My rule keeps it only as a declared premium within $3B. Its shortfall is $6.48B, beyond the cap and over three times its own bill. Struck. Not at any price: we are not after market share [RX-0054, R-1582].
- UltraFan WB fails airframers first [RX-0058]. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing has named no UltraFan on a 787 Re-engine. Its $8.90B shortfall is far above both the $1B sub-cap and the $3B cap. Struck.
- Premium: $0B. The chosen row is the best row in both columns.

6. Red lines.
- No colleague flags a breach on the final orders.
- Watson notes that the red lines as written (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development; no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo) are not engaged by either widebody option, because no UltraFan is in development and no Solo is live. I accept that. On this board the strain is the economic form of 'one big programme at a time' [R-0929, R-1127]. It is priced in the grid, not deducted again.
- No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column. Both widebody items fail that test in both columns, so both stay at hold. That test is Board doctrine [RG-0033], not my record.
- Nothing is cancelled: no programme is in development and no cancel is offered.

7. Housekeeping, plainly.
- The 2045 withdrawal review is moot and closed: the Joint Venture formed in 2035.
- The 2035 widebody plan assumed the strain would lift once UltraFan NB left development. It did not: on this board the formed Joint Venture is a running narrowbody project. That assumption was wrong, and I say so.
- What the miss costs: without strain the upgrade would read about -1.48, a premium we could have chosen to declare inside $3B. With strain it is off the table.
- What the Joint Venture brought: 24.1% of NGSA engines from entry, both legs of the objective met, and the $2.29B of Solo spend not needed in 2036-37.

8. Off-grid, as the Board asked.
- Watson: the gearbox that flies is P&W's, under P&W's design authority, on GTF2's clock. It was ready in 2036 with no slip, RR was fitted at NGSA's entry (965 engines, 24.1%), and there is no durability or safety flag on the record. The board does not model time on wing or full-life parts, so he gives no number, and neither do I.
- His oversight note becomes a private move: RR technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data, and gear-and-core repair data or a module pool, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops.
- McCabe sizes our share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge at about £1.2-2.9bn, with a peak year of £0.3-0.7bn. Twice that still fits without equity, without leverage above about 1.5x and with the dividend untouched; extra distributions flex first. It books nothing.

9. Where my record is thin. Joint Venture terms and P&W are Low confidence for me (erginbilgic.md §6). On the gear and core, support and shop capacity I defer to Watson. On the shared-risk sizing I take McCabe's test as the evidence. The in-service oversight and the worst-case sizing are company doctrine and Board asks (profile.md §4; RG-0027, RG-0033), not my own words.

'Actually, I've seen this movie before': two programmes in parallel, and the strain eats the return. We control what we control: the fleet, durability and cash.

memo_weighing.cfo: Taken in full; she decided the numbers. I adopt her weights (S1 0.90 / S2 0.10, the generous case for the widebody items) and her item values: upgrade -6.48 / -6.46, UltraFan WB -9.00 / -8.02, -8.90 expected. I adopt her worst columns and her premium of $0B. Her withheld co-signatures on the upgrade and UltraFan WB are binding and respected. She invokes no balance-sheet veto: no funding, net cash, leverage at or below about 1.5x. She confirms no narrowbody R&D remains and the fit with a flat R&D envelope and the post-2028 distribution plan. Her capex figures go on the record: about £0.49bn a year for either item, £1.47bn or £2.94bn in total, with £3.68bn of strain on top. Her off-grid shared-risk sizing (£1.2-2.9bn, peak £0.3-0.7bn, twice that still funded from free cash flow) becomes a private cash-plan move that books nothing. Her 2050 view goes to the 2050 watch: strain planned as permanent, and an upgrade launched in 2050 worth only about +0.28 of engine value against $7B. No disagreement with my proposal.
memo_weighing.ops: Taken in full on readiness, support and the franchise. He confirms: the Joint Venture engine ready in 2036 on GTF2's clock with nothing compressed; RR fitted at NGSA's entry (24.1%, 965 engines); no safety or durability flag on the record; widebody at 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, with S2 at or above S1 and so above the 50% line. He confirms the board carries the Joint Venture as a running narrowbody project, so $5B of strain falls on either widebody item; he withdraws his own 2035 upgrade plan. His oversight note on the P&W gear and core becomes two private moves: technical review rights, and repair data or a module-exchange pool. His support plan is carried privately without reliance on P&W's shops, and his in-service report goes to the Board before the 2050 orders. He checked the public statement for early dates; it carries none, and I added only 'UltraFan technology continues as technology', with no date. He invokes no Civil veto. His capacity view and the unreconciled shop-visit figures (1,100-1,200 against 1,400-1,500) are advice, recorded. His ranking for 2050, the upgrade first among widebody items and only within its bill or against a threatening Re-engine, goes into the 2050 watch.

decision.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold (weight 0.90). No 787 or A350 Re-engine this round. Boeing has only signalled a look at the 787's next step once fps is in service, and Airbus keeps the A350 family as its focus. S2 (both Re-engines) is weighted 0.10, capped by its weaker leg.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: 'UltraFan NB: hold' (all four fields at hold): +20.55 in S1, and also the best row in S2 at +20.80. EV +20.58 on 0.90 / 0.10 (+20.59 on the Board's 0.85 / 0.15). It beats 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' (+14.07 / +14.34) by 6.48 / 6.46, and 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' (+11.55 / +12.78) by 9.00 / 8.02.
decision.premium_reason: None. The submitted orders are the best grid row in both columns, so no doctrine-favoured order is kept against PV. Item by item: `ultrafan_nb_solo` hold, $0; `jv_with_pw` hold, $0; `ultrafan_wb` hold, $0; `t1000_upgrade` hold, $0. For the record, choosing the upgrade would have cost $6.48B under any weights, and UltraFan WB $8.90B ($8.85B on the Board's case). Both are above the $3B cap, and UltraFan WB is also above its $1B sub-cap, so neither could be carried as a declared premium.
decision.objective_note: Both legs are met on hold, with no premium and no new programme. Narrowbody entry: RR narrowbody share 22.9% in 2045 and 21.6% in 2050, through the Joint Venture engine on NGSA. Widebody dominance: 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in S1, with 5.2 pp of headroom. S2 is at or above S1 on Watson's reading, since the hold row is +0.25 higher. Neither widebody item is needed to hold 50%. A further CFM widebody gain the size of the GEnx upgrade would leave about 52.4%, still above the line (Watson, inference). The narrowbody drift from 24.8% to 21.6% is airframe mix (fps gains on CFM), not a lever we hold.

board_response.recommendation: R3-1: Hold all four fields and say why in rationale: protect what is working.
board_response.response: Taken up in full. All four fields are at hold. 'UltraFan NB: hold' is the best row in both columns: +20.55 / +20.80, +20.58 on our weights and +20.59 on yours. Both legs of the objective are met. Premium $0B. No Board item. The why is in rationale items 2-5.

board_response.recommendation: R3-2: Close the 2035 widebody plan; for 2050 bring a widebody item only with a Re-engine on the record and within its own bill and the caps.
board_response.response: Taken up. The plan is closed formally in a private move, and I admit plainly that it rested on the strain lifting, which it does not. The cost: without strain the upgrade would read about -1.48, inside the $3B cap; with strain it is -6.48. For 2050 the rule is a Re-engine on the record and a grid row within the item's own bill and the caps ($3B; $1B for UltraFan WB), with the upgrade first per Watson. Noted: UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, with at most five years to count before 2061. McCabe makes an upgrade launched in 2050 about +0.28 of engine value against $7B of bill and strain.

board_response.recommendation: R3-3: Product safety in service: Watson to report the 2036 review on gearbox durability, time on wing and full-life parts, partner-shop support, and any flag.
board_response.response: Taken up. Watson reports that the gearbox in service is P&W's, under P&W's design authority, on GTF2's clock. It was ready in 2036 with no slip or reset, and RR was fitted at NGSA's entry at 24.1% (965 engines), holding equal shares with P&W through 2044. There is no safety or durability flag on the record. The board does not model time on wing or full-life parts, so he gives no figure. Two private moves answer the maturity point: RR technical review rights on P&W's test, certification and fleet data under the shared-risk terms, and gear-and-core repair data or a module-exchange pool, so that our partner shops can support that module without P&W's shops. RR tracks time on wing and life-limited parts itself. His in-service report, and any flag, reach you before the 2050 orders.

board_response.recommendation: R3-4: Precaution on shared risk: McCabe to size, off the grid, RR's share of a reasonable-worst-case in-service charge on the Joint Venture engine.
board_response.response: Taken up. McCabe bases it on our own Trent 1000 precedent (£2.4bn over seven years), taken at RR's 49% on P&W's published partner model and scaled to our fleet: about £1.2-2.9bn in total, with a peak year of about £0.3-0.7bn (7-19% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance). At twice that it still fits: no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x, and the dividend untouched, with extra distributions flexing first. It books nothing and is not a veto ground. She rebases it on any durability flag or on fleet data worse than plan.

board_response.recommendation: R3-5: Capital: no new programme spend; distributions from sustainable free cash flow in the capital-frame order; R&D broadly flat; Trent durability and UltraFan technology continue.
board_response.response: Taken up. No new programme spend on the board. The capital frame is held as a private move: balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then distributions from sustainable free cash flow. McCabe confirms it fits a broadly flat R&D envelope and the post-2028 distribution plan. Trent durability (about £1bn over four years) and UltraFan as technology (public R&D money where available) continue as public, qualitative moves.

board_response.recommendation: R3-6: Widebody watch: the franchise test does not trigger; watch for a 787 next step and any A350 Re-engine in 2050; time on wing is the lever today.
board_response.response: Taken up. 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, with S2 at or above S1 (Watson). The test does not trigger. The 2050 watch is a private move: a Boeing 787 next step, any A350 Re-engine, and any further CFM widebody gain on our 5.2 pp of headroom. Watson puts the GEnx upgrade's 2.8 pp at about $0.53B of PV, already in the hold row. Time on wing on the Trent fleet is the lever we fund today; it is worth $0 on this grid but keeps the fleet earning.

board_response.recommendation: R3-7: Public statement, pricing and housekeeping: Joint Venture engine in service with durability and support first; no new-engine date, no Joint Venture date, nothing on airframers' or P&W's plans; 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine'; no price concessions; close the 2045 withdrawal review.
board_response.response: Taken up. The statement leads with safety, time on wing, full-life parts and partner-shop support. It carries no date of any kind and nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans, and it keeps 'no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine' and 'We do not want to underestimate the risks'. Watson checked it for early dates. Pricing discipline is a private move: no concessions, and every contract through the Investment Committee. The 2045 Joint Venture withdrawal review is closed formally as moot: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdraw does not exist after formation.

board_response.recommendation: R2-1 (closing): zero margin at NGSA; the 2036 review to clear gearbox durability on test evidence; in 2045 report what it found and whether RR was fitted at entry.
board_response.response: Closed. After the fold the engine flew on GTF2's clock, ready in 2036 with one year of margin to NGSA's 2037 entry, better than the zero margin UltraFan alone carried. The review's subject became that engine, whose gear P&W designs. The record shows entry on schedule, RR fitted at entry (24.1%) and no flag. No 2036 date was ever put on an RR engine in public. The 2035 line 'ready in 2037' is superseded by the fold and is not repeated.

board_response.recommendation: R2-2 (closing): the 2045 withdrawal review: a sealed withdrawal unless the grid supports the commitment, in the same round as any widebody item; settle the fold question.
board_response.response: Closed as moot. P&W committed in 2035, so the Joint Venture formed that round and withdraw is not on the 2045 menu. The fold question is moot too. The strain concern did materialise, through the formed Joint Venture as a running project rather than through a later formation. That is why both widebody items stay at hold.

board_response.recommendation: R2-3 (closing): keep the private Joint Venture conditions: RR funds only its $4B share, a folded programme keeps its own test clock, no P&W gear or core change, support not counting on P&W's shops.
board_response.response: Kept. RR's R&D on the board is its $4.00B share. The $1.71B write-off is our own UltraFan spend before formation, not a P&W cost. No combined design was offered: the engine took GTF2's own clock with P&W's gear and core. Our support does not count on P&W's shops. The one gap, the gear-and-core module, is now addressed through repair data or a module pool under the shared-risk terms.

board_response.recommendation: R2-4 (closing): support and capacity: confirm the 2035 contracts placed, and the spares pool and field service standing in 2036; capacity is advice.
board_response.response: Confirmed by Watson. Partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model and the castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts were placed in 2035, and the spares pool and field service stood up in 2036, before NGSA's entry. They are now scaled to 914 narrowbody engines in 2045 and 863 a year from 2049, against 188 widebody. Capacity is recorded as advice.

board_response.recommendation: R2-5 (closing): cash: report the remaining Solo spend; if not spent, that saving is no reason to bring widebody spend beside the commitment.
board_response.response: Confirmed. The Joint Venture took GTF2's schedule, so the remaining $2.29B (about £1.68bn) of Solo spend was never needed. It is not redeployed into widebody: both widebody items stay at hold, and gross R&D stays broadly flat.

board_response.recommendation: R2-6 (closing): widebody franchise for 2045: bring the Trent 1000 upgrade first, against a Re-engine on the record or as a declared premium inside $3B; UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap.
board_response.response: Brought and priced, then held. The upgrade is -6.48 / -6.46 against hold because the $5B strain stays beside the formed Joint Venture. That is beyond its own $2B bill and the $3B cap, so it cannot be a declared premium, and McCabe withholds her signature. UltraFan WB has no Re-engine on the record and runs -9.00 / -8.02, far beyond the $1B sub-cap. Both are at hold. The watch carries to 2050.

board_response.recommendation: R2-7 (closing): pricing discipline; in later statements give no Joint Venture ready date and nothing beside any airframer's dates.
board_response.response: Kept. No concessions. This statement carries no Joint Venture date, no new-engine date and nothing on any airframer's dates.

ops.note:
I concur, with no Civil veto and no red-line breach. Both conditions in my test memo are met in the final package.

**Dates, for the Board**
- **Joint Venture engine:** formed 2035, ready 2036 on GTF2's clock (the bulletin date, from the folded programme). NGSA has been in service since its 2037 EIS, so the engine had a year of margin. RR was fitted at entry with 24.1% (965 engines). It is in service now.

**Items not ordered** (recorded so a later statement does not breach them)
- **UltraFan WB:** if launched in 2045 it would be ready in 2051. That is a "Ready by EIS" fail against S2's 2050 Re-engines. It is advice only and moot at hold.
- **Trent 1000 upgrade:** if launched in 2045 it would count from 2048. It passes readiness and is held on value (-6.48 / -6.46).

**Statement and public moves**
- No engine date, no Joint Venture date, no next-build-standard date.
- Nothing on any airframer's or P&W's plans.
- "UltraFan technology continues as technology" carries no launch, ready or entry date.

**Engineering load:** $0 of strain and no overlap years, because nothing widebody is ordered. On this board the Joint Venture runs as a narrowbody project, so I expect any widebody item in 2050 to carry the $5B strain (inference; the 2050 grid will confirm).

**How the Board should read my concerns**
- **Binding veto:** none.
- **Test fail:** UltraFan WB "Ready by EIS", advice only and moot at hold.
- **Notes, not flags:**

We're keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible. This is hard work for the team, but the fleet is in service and the plan is granular.
